Frey's syndrome is gustatory sweating (sweating of the preauricular skin during eating) that occurs as a postoperative complication of parotid surgery. It is caused by damaged parasympathetic nerve fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve regenerating into the sweat glands of the skin.

Normally, the auriculotemporal nerve (branch of CN V3) carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland. After parotidectomy, these regenerating fibres aberrantly innervate the overlying skin's eccrine sweat glands, causing sweating in response to salivary stimuli (eating/smelling food).

cards.front: What is the approach to evaluating a neck mass by age?
cards.back:
In patients <40 years: most likely inflammatory > congenital/developmental > neoplastic. In patients >40 years: most likely neoplastic > inflammatory > congenital. Any neck mass persisting >2 weeks should be investigated for neoplastic causes.

This age-based prioritization is a key MCCQE1 clinical framework. In young patients, reactive lymphadenopathy from infection dominates. In older patients, malignancy (lymphoma, metastatic squamous cell carcinoma, salivary gland tumours, thyroid cancer) must be the leading concern until proven otherwise.

cards.front: What distinguishes an inflammatory from a neoplastic neck mass on history and physical?
cards.back:
Inflammatory: painful, rapid onset, tender on exam, rubbery. Neoplastic: painless, longer duration (weeks–months), non-tender, rock-hard, immobile/fixed.

These features guide the initial differential. However, lymphoma can present with a rubbery, painless mass, blurring this distinction. Tender nodes can occasionally be malignant (if rapidly growing with central necrosis). Clinical suspicion combined with appropriate investigations (FNA, CT, CBC) is essential.

cards.front: What is the most common congenital neck mass in children?
cards.back:
Thyroglossal duct cyst — the most common congenital cervical anomaly.

Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline remnants of the tract made by the thyroid as it descends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to its final position in the neck. They classically elevate with swallowing and tongue protrusion. Treatment is the Sistrunk procedure.

cards.front: Describe the classic features of a thyroglossal duct cyst.
cards.back:
Midline neck cyst (suprahyoid or infrahyoid) that enlarges with URTIs, elevates with swallowing AND tongue protrusion, may cause dysphagia or globus sensation. Usually presents in childhood or ages 20–40.

The pathognomonic feature is elevation with tongue protrusion (due to the fibrous cord connecting the cyst to the foramen cecum at the tongue base). This distinguishes it from other midline neck masses. The cyst often becomes inflamed during URTIs due to its connection with the pharynx.

cards.front: What surgical procedure is used to treat thyroglossal duct cysts, and what does it involve?
cards.back:
The Sistrunk procedure: complete excision of the cyst, the fibrous cord/tract up to the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue, AND removal of the central portion of the hyoid bone.

Simple cyst excision has a high recurrence rate (~50%). The Sistrunk procedure reduces recurrence to <3% by ensuring complete tract excision including the hyoid bone segment (which the tract passes through). Preoperative antibiotics should be given to reduce inflammation and minimize recurrence risk.

cards.front: What is the most common branchial cleft anomaly, and how does it present?
cards.back:
2nd branchial cleft malformation is most common. Sinuses/fistulae present in infancy as a small opening anterior to the SCM. Cysts present as a smooth, painless, slowly enlarging lateral neck mass, often following a URTI.

Branchial cleft anomalies result from failure of obliteration of embryonic branchial clefts/pouches. They fall into three types: fistula (opens to skin and GI tract), sinus (blind-ended), and cyst (closed). 2nd branchial cleft anomalies are by far most common. Treatment is surgical excision after infection resolves.

cards.front: What is the pathognomonic finding for a 3rd branchial cleft anomaly on CT?
cards.back:
Air on CT scan in or near the thyroid gland, associated with recurrent thyroiditis or thyroid abscess. The tract typically leads to the left pyriform sinus.

3rd branchial cleft anomalies are rare and present as recurrent left-sided thyroiditis or thyroid abscess. The connection to the pyriform sinus allows communication between the pharynx and thyroid, explaining recurrent infections. Air in the thyroid on CT is pathognomonic.

cards.front: What are the premalignant lesions of the oral cavity and their risk of malignant transformation?
cards.back:
Lichen planus: 5–10% risk (follow-up every 6–12 months). Leukoplakia: 5–20% risk (follow-up every 3–12 months). Erythroplakia: associated with carcinoma in situ or invasive tumour in 40% of cases (highest risk).

Erythroplakia carries the highest malignant potential of the three. Leukoplakia is a white keratotic plaque that cannot be rubbed off (distinguishing it from candidiasis). Dysplasia involving the entire mucosal thickness = carcinoma in situ, which has 15–30% progression to invasive cancer.

cards.front: What is the treatment of choice for lichen planus of the oral mucosa?
cards.back:
Topical corticosteroids (first-line); topical calcineurin inhibitors (second-line). Follow-up every 6–12 months due to 5–10% malignant transformation risk.

Oral lichen planus presents as lacy white lines (Wickham's striae) with surrounding erythema. The exact cause is unknown but is thought to be immune-mediated (T-cell lymphocyte attack on basal keratinocytes). Symptomatic lesions require treatment; asymptomatic cases need surveillance.

cards.front: What is the general treatment principle for head and neck malignancies by anatomic site?
cards.back:
Oral cavity: primary surgery with radiotherapy reserved for salvage/poor prognostic indicators. Nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx: primary radiotherapy with surgery reserved for salvage. Advanced (T4) pharyngeal/laryngeal cancer: surgery is standard of care. Metastatic: palliative chemotherapy.

The anatomic site dictates primary treatment modality. Oral cavity tumours are generally resected because they are accessible and well-defined. Laryngeal and pharyngeal tumours are often treated with radiotherapy to preserve function. Laser endoscopic surgery (transoral) is an option for early-stage laryngeal cancer.

cards.front: What is the epidemiology and key risk factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
cards.back:
90% SCC. Mean age: 50–59 yr; M:F = 2.4:1. 100-fold increased incidence in Southern Chinese. Key risk factors: EBV infection, salted fish consumption, nickel exposure. Poor oral hygiene also contributes.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has a striking geographic and ethnic distribution, highly prevalent in Southern China and Southeast Asia. EBV is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis, particularly for the undifferentiated (non-keratinizing) subtype. EBV serology is used in screening in endemic regions.

cards.front: What proportion of oropharyngeal cancers (OPC) are attributable to HPV, and how does HPV status affect prognosis?
cards.back:
Up to 70% of OPC are attributable to HPV (primarily HPV-16). HPV+ OPC patients have significantly better prognosis: 82.4% vs. 51.1% 3-year overall survival and a 58% reduction in risk of death compared to HPV-negative tumours.

The rising incidence of HPV-associated OPC (225% increase from 1988–2004) has shifted the epidemiology of head and neck cancer. HPV+ OPC patients tend to be younger (~10 years), non-smokers, with better treatment response. HPV vaccination (quadrivalent) is a key prevention strategy, independent of smoking and alcohol exposure.

cards.front: What is the most common site of laryngeal carcinoma, and what is the gender predominance?
cards.back:
Glottic larynx (60–65% of laryngeal cancers). Laryngeal cancer has a strong male predominance (M:F = 10:1). Primary risk factors: smoking and alcohol.

Laryngeal cancers arise in three sites: supraglottic (30–35%), glottic (60–65%), and subglottic (1%). Glottic tumours present early (hoarseness) because the vocal cords are directly involved. Supraglottic tumours have poorer prognosis due to late presentation and rich lymphatic drainage. Laryngeal cancer accounts for 45% of all H&N cancers.

cards.front: What is the rule regarding the likelihood of malignancy and salivary gland size?
cards.back:
The smaller the salivary gland, the greater the likelihood that a mass in that gland is malignant. Parotid: 15–25% malignant; submandibular: 37–43% malignant; minor salivary glands: >80% malignant.

This inverse relationship between gland size and malignancy risk is a key MCCQE1 high-yield fact. While the parotid contains most salivary gland tumours, the vast majority are benign. A sublingual or minor salivary gland mass carries very high malignancy risk and demands urgent investigation.

cards.front: What is the most common malignant salivary gland tumour overall?
cards.back:
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (40% of malignant salivary gland tumours), followed by adenoid cystic carcinoma (30%), acinic cell carcinoma (5%), and malignant mixed tumour (5%).

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is also the most common malignant tumour of the parotid. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural invasion and late distant metastases (even decades later). Salivary gland malignancies are associated with radiation exposure as a key risk factor.

cards.front: What is the role of panendoscopy in head and neck oncology?
cards.back:
Panendoscopy (nasopharyngoscopy, laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy with washings and biopsy) is used to identify the primary tumour when cervical lymph node metastasis is identified (unknown primary). The primary is found ~95% of the time.

When a patient presents with a cervical lymph node containing SCC with no obvious primary, panendoscopy is performed to identify the occult primary tumour in the upper aerodigestive tract. If the primary remains occult (~5%), excisional biopsy of the node for histologic diagnosis guides management (radiotherapy ± neck dissection).

cards.front: What targeted therapy is used for advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck?
cards.back:
Anti-EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) treatment — cetuximab or panitumumab — as concurrent therapy with radiation for advanced local and regional SCC of the head and neck.

EGFR is overexpressed in most H&N SCC. Cetuximab (a monoclonal antibody against EGFR) improves survival when added to radiation in advanced disease. It is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate cisplatin-based chemoradiation. Concomitant chemotherapy also increases survival in advanced disease.

cards.front: What is the most common risk factor for hypopharyngeal carcinoma, and what is the most common subsitite?
cards.back:
Smoking and alcohol (synergistic) are the primary risk factors. The most common subsite is the pyriform sinus (60%), followed by the postcricoid region (30%) and posterior pharyngeal wall (10%).

Hypopharyngeal cancers have poor prognosis due to late presentation. They account for 8–10% of all H&N cancers, predominantly affecting males aged 50–70 years. Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron-deficiency dysphagia with esophageal webbing) is associated with postcricoid carcinoma in women.

cards.front: What imaging modality is superior for detecting pathologic cervical lymph nodes and bone cortex invasion in head and neck cancer?
cards.back:
CT scan is superior to MRI for detecting pathologic nodal disease and bone cortex invasion.

While CT excels at detecting cortical bone invasion and lymph node size/morphology, MRI is superior for discriminating tumour from mucus, detecting bone marrow invasion (medullary spread), and soft tissue characterization. PET scans have an emerging role in H&N neoplasm staging and surveillance.

cards.front: What size criteria define pathologically enlarged cervical lymph nodes?
cards.back:
Jugulodigastric node >1.5 cm in diameter; retropharyngeal node >0.8 cm in diameter; any node of any size with central necrosis.

Lymph node size alone is imperfect for detecting metastasis. Central necrosis on imaging (seen as a low-density center on CT) is highly specific for metastatic SCC. Retropharyngeal nodes have smaller threshold criteria because they are not normally visible on imaging.

cards.front: What is lymphatic (cystic hygroma) / venolymphatic malformation, and how does its size affect treatment?
cards.back:
Lymphatic malformations arise from vestigial lymph channels. Macrocystic lesions: soft, painless, compressible, treated by surgical excision or sclerotherapy (doxycycline). Microcystic lesions: noncompressible with mucosal/skin vesicles, difficult to treat — debulking or bleomycin sclerotherapy.

Lymphatic malformations (cystic hygroma) usually present by age 2. They can regress spontaneously after bacterial infection, so surgical intervention should be delayed several months after infection. Sudden enlargement after infection or trauma is a characteristic feature that may cause airway compromise requiring urgent intervention.

cards.front: What is the most common site of oral cavity cancer, and what are its key risk factors?
cards.back:
Most common site: anterior 2/3 of the tongue (50% of oral cavity cancers). Risk factors: smoking, alcohol, poor oral hygiene, leukoplakia, erythroplakia, lichen planus, chronic inflammation, HPV, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, sun exposure (lip), genetic factors.

Oral cavity SCC (95% of oral cavity cancers) is treated primarily with surgery. The tongue is the most common site, and early lesions of the oral tongue have a good prognosis with surgery. Risk factors are additive; smoking and alcohol have a synergistic relationship in causing oral cavity cancers.

cards.front: What are the 5-year survival rates for oral cavity cancer by T-stage?
cards.back:
T1/T2: 75%; T3/T4: 30-35%

Oral cavity cancer prognosis is stage-dependent. Poor prognostic indicators include depth of invasion, close surgical margins, and location (tongue has worse prognosis than floor of mouth). Primary treatment is surgery with local resection ± neck dissection ± reconstruction, with secondary radiation.

cards.front: What is the primary treatment for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC)?
cards.back:
Primary radiation + chemoradiation; surgery reserved for limited or recurrent disease

NPC commonly presents with cervical nodes (60-90%), nasal obstruction, unilateral otitis media with hearing loss, and cranial nerve involvement (III-VI, IX-XII). 5-year survival: T1=79%, T2=77%, T3=50-60%, T4=36-42%.

cards.front: How does HPV status affect oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) prognosis?
cards.back:
HPV-positive OPC has significantly better outcomes: Stage I 92%, II 87%, III 74%, IV 40% vs. HPV-negative: Stage I 70%, II 58%, III 50%, IV 30%

HPV+ OPC predominantly arises at the base of tongue or tonsillar region. HPV status is determined via RT-PCR (presence of HPV DNA) and p16 overexpression. HPV+ patients are candidates for therapy de-intensification. Transoral robotic surgery has an emerging role.

cards.front: What are the Bethesda categories for thyroid FNA cytology and their associated malignancy risk?
cards.back:
I Non-diagnostic: 1-4%; II Benign: 0-3%; III Follicular lesion of undetermined significance/AUS: 5-15%; IV Follicular neoplasm: 15-30%; V Suspicious for malignancy: 60-75%; VI Malignant: 97-99%

The Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (TBSRTC) guides management decisions. Categories III-IV often require molecular testing (BRAF, microRNA classifiers) to distinguish high-risk from low-risk nodules and decide whether surgery is needed.

cards.front: Compare the key features of the 5 types of thyroid carcinoma (papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic, lymphoma).
cards.back:
Papillary (90-92%): lymphatic spread, orphan Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies, positive I-131 uptake, 98% 10-yr survival. Follicular (4-6%): hematogenous spread, capsular/vascular invasion, NOT diagnosable by FNA, 92% 10-yr survival. Medullary (1-2%): associated MEN IIa/IIb, secretes calcitonin, amyloid stroma, 55-80% 5-yr survival Stage I. Anaplastic (<1%): elderly, giant cells/spindle cells, rapid enlarging mass, rapidly fatal. Lymphoma (<1%): associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis (60x risk), diffuse large B-cell most common, non-surgical treatment (CHOP).

Papillary is the most common and has the best prognosis. Follicular cancer is notable for hematogenous spread to lung/bone and cannot be diagnosed by FNA alone (requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion). Medullary cancer can be hereditary (MEN IIa: RET mutation) and requires median/lateral neck dissection based on calcitonin levels. Anaplastic carries the worst prognosis.

cards.front: What is the TI-RADS classification and when is FNA indicated?
cards.back:
TR1 (0 pts): benign, no FNA. TR2 (2 pts): not suspicious, no FNA. TR3 (3 pts): mildly suspicious, FNA if ≥2.5 cm, follow-up if ≥1.5 cm. TR4 (4-6 pts): moderately suspicious, FNA if ≥1.5 cm, follow-up if ≥1 cm. TR5 (≥7 pts): highly suspicious, FNA if ≥1 cm, follow-up if >0.5 cm.

The ACR Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) uses features including composition, echogenicity, shape, margin, and echogenic foci to score thyroid nodules. Higher scores indicate greater suspicion for malignancy and lower size thresholds for FNA.

cards.front: What are the indications for radioiodine (I-131) therapy in thyroid disease?
cards.back:
Treatment of hyperthyroidism; adjuvant treatment after surgery for intermediate-to-high-risk papillary or follicular carcinoma

Radioiodine therapy targets thyroid tissue that takes up iodine. For well-differentiated thyroid cancers, postoperative I-131 scanning guides further treatment. Medullary and anaplastic carcinomas do not take up iodine and are not treated with I-131.

cards.front: What is the definition of acute otitis media (AOM) and what is the primary etiology?
cards.back:
AOM = infection of middle ear space with both presence of middle ear effusion/inflammation (MEE/MEI) AND acute onset of symptoms. Primary defect: Eustachian tube dysfunction/obstruction leading to stasis and pathogen colonization. Most common bacteria: S. pneumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.

AOM is the most frequent diagnosis in sick children and the most common reason for antibiotic prescription. Peak incidence is 6-15 months. Bacterial and viral co-infections are common. Viral pathogens include RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, and rhinovirus.

cards.front: What are the criteria for watchful waiting vs. immediate antibiotics in pediatric AOM?
cards.back:
Watchful waiting (24-48h): healthy child >6 months with unilateral, non-severe AOM (mild illness, otalgia mild, fever <39°C, <48h symptoms). Immediate antibiotics: infant <6 months; moderately/severely ill; fever ≥39°C; symptoms >48h; immunocompromised; craniofacial abnormalities; perforated TM with purulent drainage.

This reflects Canadian evidence-based guidelines. If not improved or worsening at 24-48h follow-up, treat with antimicrobials. For severe or bilateral AOM with MEE and bulging TM, antimicrobials should be started immediately regardless of age.

cards.front: What is the first-line antibiotic treatment for AOM, and what are alternatives for penicillin allergy?
cards.back:
First-line (no penicillin allergy): high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/d divided BID. Penicillin allergy (first-line alternatives): azithromycin 10 mg/kg or clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/d divided BID. If initial therapy fails (no improvement after 2-3 days): high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate 45-60 mg/kg/d.

Duration: 5-day course for most children >2 years with uncomplicated AOM; 10-day course for children 6-24 months, perforated TM, or recurrent AOM. Failure of first-line therapy suggests beta-lactamase-producing organisms (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) requiring amoxicillin-clavulanate.

cards.front: What is the most common complication of AOM, and what are the major intracranial complications?
cards.back:
Most common complication: mastoiditis. Intracranial complications: meningitis, epidural/brain abscess, subdural empyema, lateral and cavernous sinus thrombosis, sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis, carotid artery thrombosis, facial nerve paralysis.

Extracranial complications include hearing loss, TM perforation, cholesteatoma, facial nerve palsy, middle ear atelectasis, ossicular necrosis, and vestibular dysfunction. Other complications include postauricular abscess and Bezold's abscess (extension to neck).

cards.front: What are the criteria for tympanostomy tube insertion in children?
cards.back:
Recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months OR ≥4 episodes in 12 months with ≥1 in recent 6 months) with unilateral or bilateral MEE at time of reassessment; Chronic bilateral OME and documented hearing loss ≥25 dB after ≥3 months with symptoms attributable to OME; At-risk children (permanent HL, speech/language delay, ASD, craniofacial disorders) with unilateral or bilateral OME with type B tympanogram or persistent effusion >3 months.

Per Canadian/AAO clinical practice guidelines on tympanostomy tubes. Evidence shows tubes improve hearing threshold by ~9 dB at 1-3 months vs. watchful waiting, and reduce recurrent AOM episodes, but benefit diminishes by 12-24 months.

cards.front: What is otitis media with effusion (OME) and how does it differ from AOM?
cards.back:
OME = presence of fluid in the middle ear WITHOUT signs or symptoms of acute infection. AOM requires both MEE/MEI AND acute onset symptoms (otalgia, fever). OME presents with conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, amber/dull grey TM with immobility on pneumatic otoscopy, and meniscus fluid level.

OME is the most common cause of pediatric hearing loss. 90% of children clear fluid within 3 months following AOM. Watchful waiting for 3 months is recommended before considering surgery. Intranasal steroids, systemic antibiotics, antihistamines, and decongestants are NOT recommended.

cards.front: What is adenoid facies and what causes it?
cards.back:
Adenoid facies = characteristic facial appearance from chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy: open-mouthed appearance, high arched palate, dental crowding, hypoplastic maxilla, pinched nostrils, short upper lip, and elongated face.

Adenoid hypertrophy peaks around age 5-7 and typically resolves by age 12 (self-resolving due to age-related atrophy). Graded 0 (absent) to 4+ (>75% obstruction). Complications include Eustachian tube obstruction causing serous otitis media, sleep apnea, and orofacial developmental abnormalities.

cards.front: What are the PSG (polysomnography) criteria for OSA severity in children vs. adults?
cards.back:
Children: AHI >1/h abnormal; mild 2-4/h, moderate 6-10/h, severe >10/h. Adults: mild 5.1-15/h, moderate 15.1-30/h, severe >30.1/h.

Children have a lower threshold for abnormality (AHI >1/h vs. >5/h in adults) because children normally have near-absent apneas during sleep. Pediatric OSA peaks at age 2-8 years when tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the pharyngeal airway.

cards.front: What is the surgical treatment of choice for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)?
cards.back:
Bilateral tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy

If OSA persists after tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy, consider adenoid regrowth. For refractory cases not tolerant of CPAP/BiPAP, options include lingual tonsillectomy, midline posterior glossectomy, tongue suspension, or other surgeries targeting resistance sites, guided by drug-induced sleep endoscopy or cine-MRI.

cards.front: What is the classic triad (Quinsy triad) of peritonsillar abscess and what is the most reliable diagnostic sign?
cards.back:
Quinsy triad: trismus, uvular deviation, dysphonia ('hot potato voice'). Most reliable indicator: trismus (due to irritation and reflex spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle).

Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is most common in 15-30 year olds. Most common causative organism is Group A Streptococcus (50%). Complications include aspiration pneumonia (spontaneous rupture), airway obstruction, lateral dissection into parapharyngeal/carotid space, bacteremia, and retropharyngeal abscess.

cards.front: How is peritonsillar abscess treated?
cards.back:
Secure airway; surgical drainage (incision or needle aspiration with C&S); empiric PO antibiotics for 14-day course; IV penicillin G x10d if GAS on cultures; add PO/IV metronidazole or clindamycin x10d if Bacteroides positive; warm saline irrigation; consider elective tonsillectomy after resolution.

Tonsillectomy may be deferred until after a second episode. The recurrence rate of peritonsillar abscess after needle aspiration alone is higher than after tonsillectomy, but tonsillectomy carries surgical risks.

cards.front: What are the absolute indications for tonsillectomy?
cards.back:
Sleep-disordered breathing (most common); recurrent tonsillitis (second most common); tonsillar hypertrophy causing upper airway obstruction, OSA, severe dysphagia, or cardiopulmonary complications (cor pulmonale); suspicion of malignancy (lymphoma, SCC); orofacial/dental deformity; hemorrhagic tonsillitis.

The Paradise Criteria define relative indications: ≥7 tonsillitis episodes in past year, or ≥5 per year for 2 years, or ≥3 per year for 3 years, each with documented sore throat plus one of: fever >38.3°C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive GAS test.

cards.front: What are the Paradise Criteria for tonsillectomy?
cards.back:
Recurrent tonsillitis with: ≥7 episodes in the past year, OR ≥5 episodes per year for 2 years, OR ≥3 episodes per year for 3 years. Each episode must have documented sore throat with ≥1 of: temperature >38.3°C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive test for Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus.

These are relative (not absolute) indications for tonsillectomy to reduce disease burden. The absolute most common indication is sleep-disordered breathing. Hemorrhage (primary within 24h, secondary within 7-10 days) is the major complication of tonsillectomy.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of stridor in neonates/infants?
cards.back:
Laryngomalacia — the most common cause of stridor in children

Laryngomalacia results from supraglottic collapse during inspiration due to immature or floppy laryngeal cartilage. It typically worsens in the supine position and with feeding. Most cases resolve spontaneously by 12-18 months. Vocal cord palsy (birth trauma or Arnold-Chiari malformation) is the second most common cause.

cards.front: How does the quality and timing of stridor indicate the level of airway obstruction?
cards.back:
Inspiratory stridor: vocal cords (glottis) or above (supraglottis). Biphasic stridor: glottis, subglottis, or extrathoracic trachea. Expiratory stridor: distal tracheobronchial tree.

Body position is also informative: stridor worse prone suggests double aortic arch; worse supine suggests laryngomalacia or glossoptosis. Biphasic stridor indicates a fixed obstruction at or below the glottis and is more ominous than purely inspiratory stridor.

cards.front: What is acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)? What is the most common cause?
cards.back:
Croup = inflammation of subglottic space and tracheobronchial tree with mucosal swelling and thick mucopurulent exudate compromising upper airway. Most common cause: parainfluenza type I virus. Croup is the most common infectious cause of stridor in children.

Croup affects children 6 months to 5 years, peaking in fall/winter. Classic presentation: preceded by URTI, worse at night, 'seal-bark' croupy cough, inspiratory or biphasic stridor, sternal/intercostal indrawing. 'Steeple sign' (narrow subglottis) on AP neck X-ray.

cards.front: What is the treatment of croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis)?
cards.back:
Nebulized epinephrine q1-2h PRN (if severe, Westley Croup Score >2); systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg or prednisone); humidified oxygen and hydration; close observation 3-4h; hospitalize if poor response after 4h with persistent stridor at rest; intubation if severe (use smaller ETT than expected for age).

Corticosteroids reduce mucosal edema and are the mainstay of treatment for moderate-to-severe croup. Nebulized epinephrine provides rapid but transient relief (rebound effect possible). Recurrent croup should prompt evaluation for subglottic stenosis with bronchoscopy.

cards.front: How does acute epiglottitis differ from croup in clinical presentation?
cards.back:
Epiglottitis: rapid onset, toxic-appearing, high fever, tripod posture, drooling, muffled voice, inspiratory stridor, slow breathing, dysphagia. No cough. 'Thumb sign' on lateral neck X-ray. Croup: gradual onset, less toxic, barking 'seal' cough, worse at night, 'steeple sign' on AP neck X-ray, supraglottis normal.

This is a classic MCCQE1 distinction. Epiglottitis is a medical emergency — do NOT examine the throat as it may precipitate complete obstruction. Ensure anesthesia/ENT present before any airway manipulation. Post-H. influenzae type B vaccine, causes now include S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, and S. aureus.

cards.front: What is the treatment of acute epiglottitis?
cards.back:
Secure airway (most critical — do NOT examine throat before preparation); IV access with hydration; IV antibiotics: cefuroxime, cefotaxime, or ceftriaxone for 10-14 days; moist air; extubate when epiglottic edema decreases (air leak around ETT) and patient is afebrile; watch for meningitis/sepsis.

The 'thumb sign' on lateral neck radiograph shows swollen epiglottis. Blood and pharyngeal cultures should be taken AFTER intubation. WBC is elevated. The condition was previously most common in children 1-4 years due to H. influenzae type B, but HiB vaccination has made this much less common.

cards.front: What are the contraindications to tonsillectomy?
cards.back:
Relative contraindications: velopharyngeal insufficiency (overt or submucous cleft palate, impaired palatal function); hematologic (coagulopathy, anemia, hemophilia, leukemia, agranulocytosis); active local infection without urgent obstructive symptoms.

Tonsillectomy in patients with submucous cleft palate can unmask velopharyngeal insufficiency, leading to hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation. In patients with coagulopathy, the risk of hemorrhage (primary within 24h or secondary within 7-10 days) is significantly increased.

cards.front: What syndromes are associated with Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent AOM?
cards.back:
Down syndrome (horizontal Eustachian tube position), Crouzon syndrome, cleft palate (even after repair), Apert syndrome, Kartagener syndrome (abnormal cilia). Also: CHARGE syndrome (associated with choanal atresia), Pierre-Robin sequence.

Eustachian tube dysfunction is the primary defect in AOM. At-risk populations include those with craniofacial abnormalities, immunodeficiencies, and ciliary dyskinesia syndromes. These children should be monitored closely for OME and may benefit from earlier consideration of tympanostomy tubes.

cards.front: What are the otoscopic findings that most reliably diagnose AOM?
cards.back:
Bulging tympanic membrane (LR 51, 95% CI 36-73) is most reliable; cloudy TM (LR 34, 95% CI 28-42); immobile TM on pneumatic otoscopy (LR 31, 95% CI 26-37); erythematous TM (LR 8.4, 95% CI 7-11). Ear pain is the most reliable symptom.

The diagnosis of AOM in pediatrics requires both MEE/MEI AND acute onset symptoms. Ear tugging alone is not a reliable indicator of pathology. MEI on otoscopy includes a bulging TM with marked discolouration (hemorrhagic, red, grey, or yellow) with loss of bony landmarks.

cards.front: What is Grisel's syndrome and in what surgical context does it occur?
cards.back:
Grisel's syndrome = atlantoaxial subluxation following head and neck surgery, particularly tonsillectomy. It is a rare complication.

Grisel's syndrome occurs due to inflammatory ligamentous laxity from local infection or surgical trauma near the atlantoaxial joint. It presents with painful torticollis and limited neck motion post-operatively and requires prompt recognition and treatment.

cards.front: What are the indications for adenoidectomy?
cards.back:
Chronic upper airway obstruction with sleep-disordered breathing/OSA + cor pulmonale; chronic nasopharyngitis resistant to medical treatment; chronic serous OM and chronic suppurative OM (with second set of tubes); recurrent AOM resistant to antibiotics; suspicion of nasopharyngeal malignancy; persistent rhinorrhea from nasal obstruction; persistent adenoiditis after two courses of antibiotics; hyponasal speech; dental malocclusion or orofacial growth disturbance.

Adenoidectomy combined with tympanostomy tubes is recommended for recurrent AOM in children ≥4 years. Adenoidectomy alone is not recommended in children <4 years unless there is nasal obstruction or chronic adenoiditis. Contraindications include conditions increasing risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency.

cards.front: What is the role of molecular testing in thyroid nodule evaluation?
cards.back:
Molecular testing (mutational analysis including BRAF, RAS, microRNA classifiers) is used to distinguish 'high-risk' from 'low-risk' thyroid nodules in Bethesda category III (follicular lesion of undetermined significance) and category IV (follicular neoplasm) to determine whether surgical excision is needed.

Nuclear scanning has minimal value in thyroid nodule investigation. All patients with thyroid nodules require serum TSH and thyroid/neck ultrasound. TI-RADS guides FNA vs. ultrasound follow-up decisions. U/S-guided FNA should be used for repeat biopsy of initially non-diagnostic nodules.

cards.front: What are the protective factors and modifiable risk factors for AOM in children?
cards.back:
Protective factors: breastfeeding, xylitol. Modifiable risk factors: lack of breastfeeding, daycare attendance, household crowding, exposure to cigarette smoke/air pollution, pacifier use, vitamin A deficiency, cochlear implants.

Non-modifiable risk factors include young age, family history of OM, prematurity, orofacial abnormalities, immunodeficiencies, Down syndrome, and lower SES. Breastfeeding provides passive immunity and optimal Eustachian tube positioning during feeding, reducing AOM risk.

cards.front: What are common causes of sudden-onset airway obstruction in infants?
cards.back:
Foreign body aspiration, croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis), bacterial tracheitis, caustic ingestion, epiglottitis.

Foreign body aspiration should always be considered in sudden-onset stridor in infants and toddlers, especially with a choking episode history. Bacterial tracheitis (Staphylococcal) can mimic croup but is more toxic-appearing and refractory to standard croup treatment.

cards.front: What is the treatment for medullary thyroid carcinoma and why is family screening important?
cards.back:
Treatment: total thyroidectomy + median and/or lateral compartment neck dissection based on serum calcitonin levels; postoperative thyroxine; radiotherapy; screen relatives. Family screening important because medullary thyroid cancer is associated with MEN IIa and MEN IIb (RET proto-oncogene mutations) — hereditary in 25% of cases.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma secretes calcitonin (diagnostic marker), prostaglandins, ACTH, serotonin, and kallikrein. MEN IIa includes MTC + pheochromocytoma + primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN IIb includes MTC + pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus. Serum calcitonin is used for monitoring.

cards.front: What lymphoid tissues comprise Waldeyer's ring?
cards.back:
Waldeyer's ring is an interrupted circle of protective lymphoid tissue at the upper ends of the respiratory and alimentary tracts, consisting of: pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), tubal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and lingual tonsil (under mucosa of posterior 1/3 of tongue).

Waldeyer's ring acts as the first line of immune defense at the pharyngeal inlet. Chronic inflammation or hypertrophy of any component can cause airway obstruction. Thyroid lymphoma arising in this ring has a strong association with Hashimoto thyroiditis.

cards.front: What is the Cotton-Myer grading system for subglottic stenosis?
cards.back:
Grade I: ≤50% obstruction; Grade II: 51-70%; Grade III: 71-99%; Grade IV: no detectable lumen.

The Cotton-Myer grading system standardizes the degree of subglottic obstruction and guides management decisions, ranging from endoscopic dilation for mild stenosis to laryngotracheoplasty for severe cases.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of acquired subglottic stenosis?
cards.back:
Prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation causing pressure necrosis and subsequent scar formation.

Endotracheal intubation is the most common cause of acquired subglottic stenosis. Nasal intubation is less traumatic than oral intubation for long-term use because of differing tube orientation and less pressure on the subglottis. Stenosis risk is related to both duration of intubation and endotracheal tube size.

cards.front: Which syndromes are frequently associated with congenital subglottic stenosis?
cards.back:
22q11 deletion (DiGeorge), Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), and CHARGE syndrome.

Congenital subglottic stenosis is defined as a subglottic diameter <4 mm in neonates or smaller than average for age. It is commonly associated with chromosomal or developmental syndromes, highlighting the importance of airway evaluation in these patients.

cards.front: What are the clinical features of subglottic stenosis?
cards.back:
Biphasic stridor, respiratory distress, and recurrent or prolonged croup.

Biphasic stridor (both inspiratory and expiratory) reflects fixed airway obstruction at the subglottis. Recurrent croup should prompt evaluation for underlying subglottic stenosis, especially in young children with multiple croup episodes.

cards.front: How is subglottic stenosis treated based on stenosis characteristics?
cards.back:
Soft stenosis: tissue division with knife or laser, balloon dilation + steroids. Firm stenosis: laryngotracheoplasty.

The consistency of the stenotic tissue determines treatment approach. Soft/mucosal stenosis responds to endoscopic techniques and steroids, while firm/cartilaginous stenosis requires open surgical reconstruction (laryngotracheoplasty) to provide a durable airway.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in neonates?
cards.back:
Laryngomalacia — congenital softening of tissues above the glottis causing collapse into the glottis on inspiration.

Laryngomalacia accounts for approximately 60% of all cases of neonatal stridor. The immature laryngeal cartilage and poor supraglottic tone cause dynamic collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration, producing characteristic high-pitched inspiratory stridor.

cards.front: Describe the pathophysiologic cycle in laryngomalacia that perpetuates airway obstruction.
cards.back:
Airway obstruction → supraglottic indrawing on inspiration → negative intrathoracic pressure → laryngopharyngeal reflux of acid → supraglottic edema → worsened obstruction.

This self-reinforcing cycle explains why PPI therapy is part of conservative management. By reducing acid reflux, PPIs decrease supraglottic edema, breaking the cycle and improving airway patency. This also explains why laryngomalacia often worsens postprandially.

cards.front: What are the classic laryngoscopic findings in laryngomalacia?
cards.back:
Omega-shaped epiglottis, short aryepiglottic folds, and redundant mucosa over the arytenoids.

These anatomical findings on flexible laryngoscopy confirm the diagnosis of laryngomalacia. The omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds are the primary structural abnormalities; supraglottoplasty addresses these by dividing the short aryepiglottic folds and/or removing excess arytenoid mucosa.

cards.front: What is the natural history and initial management of laryngomalacia?
cards.back:
Symptoms typically resolve spontaneously by 12-18 months in >90% of cases. Initial management: observation + PPI therapy.

The vast majority of laryngomalacia is self-limiting. PPIs break the acid-reflux cycle that promotes supraglottic edema. Surgical intervention (supraglottoplasty) is reserved for the ~10% with severe disease causing failure to thrive, significant feeding difficulties, or cyanotic episodes.

cards.front: Where does an ingested foreign body most commonly lodge in a child?
cards.back:
At the cricopharyngeus muscle (upper esophageal sphincter).

The cricopharyngeus is the narrowest point of the esophagus and the most common site of food and foreign body impaction. Common objects include coins, toys, and batteries. Batteries require emergency removal due to their ability to erode through the esophagus via electrical and chemical injury.

cards.front: Why is a button battery ingestion a medical emergency compared to a coin?
cards.back:
Button batteries can erode through the esophagus via electrical current and chemical injury; they appear as a 'halo sign' on X-ray (vs. single disc for coin) and must be urgently removed.

Even a brief contact period allows button batteries to generate hydroxide at the negative pole via electrical current, causing liquefactive necrosis of esophageal tissue. Fatal complications (esophago-aortic fistula, tracheoesophageal fistula) can occur within hours. The double-ring or halo sign on X-ray distinguishes a battery from a coin.

cards.front: Where does an aspirated foreign body most commonly lodge and why?
cards.back:
Right main bronchus — because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

The anatomy of the right main bronchus (more vertical, wider, shorter) makes it the preferential path for aspirated foreign bodies. Right-sided aspiration causes unilateral 'asthma-like' symptoms — wheezing, decreased breath sounds — often leading to misdiagnosis. Complete occlusion can lead to atelectasis, lobar pneumonia, or pneumothorax.

cards.front: What are the radiographic techniques used to evaluate suspected foreign body aspiration in children based on age?
cards.back:
Older child (stable): inspiratory AND expiratory chest X-ray. Younger child: right and left lateral decubitus chest X-rays (lack of lung deflation on dependent side suggests foreign body).

Air trapping distal to an obstructing foreign body causes the affected lung to remain hyperinflated. In older cooperative children, expiratory films reveal unilateral hyperinflation. In young children who cannot cooperate, gravity-dependent decubitus views serve the same purpose — a normal lung should deflate when dependent, whereas an obstructed lung remains inflated.

cards.front: What is the definitive treatment for a suspected airway or esophageal foreign body?
cards.back:
Bronchoscopy (airway) or esophagoscopy (esophageal) with removal. Patient must be kept NPO immediately.

Any patient with suspected foreign body ingestion or aspiration should be made NPO immediately to prepare for potential procedural intervention. Rigid bronchoscopy or esophagoscopy under general anesthesia allows direct visualization and extraction.

cards.front: What is the most common source of deep neck space infection in adults vs. children?
cards.back:
Adults: mandibular dental infection (most common). Children: tonsillar infection (most common).

Deep neck space infections are polymicrobial, involving mixed aerobes and anaerobes from the oral flora. Ludwig's angina is the prototypical deep neck infection involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from dental infections in adults.

cards.front: What is Ludwig's angina and what is its anatomical significance?
cards.back:
Ludwig's angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis/infection of the submandibular and sublingual spaces — the prototypical deep neck space infection, most commonly from dental sources.

Ludwig's angina can rapidly compromise the airway through floor-of-mouth elevation and tongue displacement. Airway management is the first priority. The infection is typically polymicrobial. CT with contrast aids in assessment, but imaging should be accompanied by the surgeon given risk of sudden airway loss.

cards.front: What is the treatment triad for deep neck space infections?
cards.back:
1) Secure the airway; 2) Source control (surgical drainage, tooth extraction, debridement); 3) Maximum-dose IV antimicrobials.

The airway must be secured first in deep neck space infections as progressive swelling can cause sudden airway loss — the worst scenario is losing the airway during imaging. Surgical drainage of fluctuant collections is essential as antibiotics alone are insufficient for established abscesses.

cards.front: What is the clinical warning about imaging in deep neck space infections?
cards.back:
Investigations (CT/MRI) should be obtained carefully with the surgeon accompanying the patient, as the worst place to lose an airway is during imaging.

Deep neck space infections can cause rapid airway deterioration. The surgeon should accompany the patient to radiology to manage potential acute airway compromise. If airway compromise is imminent, securing the airway takes priority over imaging.

cards.front: What is rhinitis medicamentosa and which nasal decongestants cause it?
cards.back:
Rhinitis medicamentosa is rebound nasal congestion/decongestant addiction from prolonged use (>5 days) of topical decongestants such as xylometazoline (Otrivin) and oxymetazoline (Dristan).

Topical alpha-adrenergic decongestants cause vasoconstriction of nasal mucosa. With prolonged use, rebound vasodilation occurs upon drug withdrawal, causing worsening congestion. Treatment is gradual cessation, sometimes with topical nasal steroids. Short-term use (<5 days) is recommended to avoid this complication.

cards.front: What is an important caution for ipratropium bromide (Atrovent) nasal spray?
cards.back:
Avoid spraying into eyes — can cause burning or precipitate narrow-angle glaucoma. Also causes increased epistaxis risk when combined with topical nasal steroids.

Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic used for vasomotor rhinitis. Its systemic anticholinergic effects (mydriasis, cycloplegia) can precipitate acute narrow-angle glaucoma if it contacts the eyes. The combination with nasal steroids increases epistaxis risk, requiring patient education.

cards.front: What is the key finding from the NEJM 2016 trial on AOM treatment duration in children aged 6-23 months?
cards.back:
10 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate had more favourable outcomes (16% vs 34% clinical failure) than 5 days; no increase in adverse events or antimicrobial resistance with 10-day course.

This trial demonstrated that shortened courses of antibiotic therapy for AOM in young children (6-23 months) resulted in significantly higher clinical failure rates. Canadian and international guidelines support 10-day courses in this age group to optimize outcomes while limiting resistance.

cards.front: What did the PET-NECK trial (NEJM 2016) demonstrate about surveillance versus planned neck dissection in N2/N3 head and neck SCC?
cards.back:
PET-CT-guided surveillance is non-inferior to planned neck dissection for overall survival in N2 or N3 SCC (2-year survival 84.9% vs 81.5%), with fewer operations.

The PET-NECK trial changed practice by supporting PET-CT surveillance at 12 weeks post-chemoradiotherapy instead of routine planned neck dissection. This avoids significant surgical morbidity in patients who achieve a complete response on imaging while maintaining equivalent survival outcomes.

cards.front: What did the CheckMate 141 trial demonstrate regarding nivolumab in head and neck SCC?
cards.back:
Nivolumab resulted in longer median overall survival (7.5 mo vs 5.1 mo) than standard therapy in platinum-refractory recurrent SCC of the head and neck (HR 0.70, p=0.01).

CheckMate 141 established nivolumab (anti-PD-1 immunotherapy) as a treatment option for platinum-refractory recurrent head and neck SCC. This was a landmark trial for immunotherapy in this setting and led to regulatory approval in Canada and internationally.

cards.front: What did the elective vs. therapeutic neck dissection trial (NEJM 2015) show for node-negative oral cavity SCC?
cards.back:
Elective (upfront) neck dissection had significantly better 3-year overall survival (80% vs 67.5%) and disease-free survival (69.5% vs 45.9%) compared to therapeutic (delayed) neck dissection.

This RCT demonstrated that elective neck dissection at the time of primary tumour resection leads to superior outcomes over watchful waiting with therapeutic neck dissection only when nodal disease becomes clinically apparent. This supports elective neck dissection as standard of care for T1/T2 node-negative oral SCC.

cards.front: What were the key conclusions of the CHAT trial (NEJM 2013) regarding adenotonsillectomy for childhood OSA?
cards.back:
In children aged 5-9 with OSA, adenotonsillectomy did NOT significantly improve attention or executive function, but DID significantly improve behaviour, quality of life, and polysomnographic findings (normalization: 79% vs 46%).

The CHAT trial is a landmark RCT showing that the primary neurocognitive outcomes (attention, executive function) were not significantly different at 7 months post-surgery versus watchful waiting, but subjective measures and polysomnography improved. This informs shared decision-making about adenotonsillectomy in school-age children.

cards.front: What does the KATE trial conclude about adenotonsillectomy for mild vs. moderate OSA in young children (ages 2-4)?
cards.back:
Children with MILD OSA (ages 2-4): watchful waiting may suffice. Children with MODERATE OSA: adenotonsillectomy should be considered (meaningful OAHI improvement: -3.1 vs -1.0).

The KATE trial provides evidence for stratifying surgical intervention by OSA severity in very young children. While mild OSA may resolve with watchful waiting, moderate OSA shows a clinically meaningful benefit from adenotonsillectomy, guiding Canadian paediatric otolaryngology practice.

cards.front: What is ciprofloxacin's important safety consideration in children regarding musculoskeletal effects?
cards.back:
Animal studies suggest systemic quinolones may cause cartilage necrosis (arthropathy) in children; use with caution.

Fluoroquinolones cause arthropathy in juvenile animal studies, raising concerns about use in pediatric populations. In otolaryngology, ciprofloxacin otic drops (Ciprodex) are used topically for otitis externa and complications of otitis media and are considered safe due to minimal systemic absorption, but systemic quinolones are used cautiously in children.

cards.front: What complication is associated with erythromycin (systemic) use in the ear?
cards.back:
Ototoxicity.

Erythromycin and other macrolides are associated with reversible sensorineural hearing loss, particularly at high systemic doses. This is relevant in ENT practice when erythromycin is used as a penicillin alternative. Erythromycin also commonly causes GI side effects (nausea, cramping) via motilin receptor agonism.

cards.front: What is the risk of neomycin/polymyxin B/hydrocortisone (Cortisporin Otic) otic drops if placed in the inner ear?
cards.back:
Risk of hearing loss (cochlear toxicity) if placed in the inner ear (i.e., if the tympanic membrane is perforated).

Aminoglycoside-containing otic drops (e.g., neomycin in Cortisporin) are contraindicated when the tympanic membrane is perforated due to potential ototoxicity from direct contact with inner ear structures. Ciprofloxacin otic drops (non-ototoxic) are preferred when a perforation is present.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of hydrocortisone and acetic acid (VoSol HC) otic drops?
cards.back:
Bactericidal by lowering pH of the ear canal; used for otitis media.

Acidic ear drops work by creating an environment hostile to bacterial growth. Most ear pathogens (including Pseudomonas) cannot survive in a low-pH environment. This mechanism is particularly useful in otitis media and otitis externa management when antibiotic resistance is a concern.

cards.front: What is the advantage of mometasone furoate (Nasonex) and fluticasone (Flonase) nasal sprays regarding systemic absorption?
cards.back:
Flonase and Nasonex are NOT absorbed systemically, making them safer for long-term use in allergic rhinitis.

Minimal systemic bioavailability (<1%) of these intranasal steroids reduces the risk of HPA axis suppression, growth effects in children, and other systemic corticosteroid side effects with long-term use. This is a key advantage over older intranasal steroids. Nasal steroids typically require up to 4 weeks of consistent use to achieve full therapeutic effect.

cards.front: A 3-week-old infant presents with high-pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens with feeding and crying but improves in the prone position. Flexible laryngoscopy reveals an omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
cards.back:
Laryngomalacia. First-line management: observation and PPI therapy. >90% resolve by 12-18 months. Supraglottoplasty if severe (failure to thrive, cyanosis).

This clinical vignette is classic for laryngomalacia — the most common cause of stridor in neonates. Key features include: onset at 1-2 weeks, worsening with feeding/crying/supine position, characteristic laryngoscopic findings. PPIs address the acid reflux cycle. The prone position relieves obstruction by allowing the tongue and supraglottic structures to fall forward.

cards.front: A 2-year-old presents to the ER with sudden onset coughing, wheeze, and decreased breath sounds on the right side without fever. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step?
cards.back:
Aspirated foreign body in the right main bronchus. Next step: make NPO immediately; right and left decubitus chest X-rays (lack of deflation on dependent side suggests obstruction); urgent rigid bronchoscopy.

The classic triad of sudden onset, unilateral wheeze, and decreased breath sounds without fever in a toddler strongly suggests foreign body aspiration. The right main bronchus is most commonly affected. Absence of fever and elevated WBC differentiates from infectious causes. Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

sections.title: Ear Disorders & Hearing Loss
sections.body:
**Q:** What is the most common causative organism of acute otitis media in children?

**A:** Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), followed by non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis

AOM is most common in children 6–24 months. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13/PCV15) has reduced S. pneumoniae AOM. First-line treatment: amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day divided BID for 10 days (high-dose to overcome resistance).

**Q:** What is the Rinne test and what result indicates conductive hearing loss?

**A:** Rinne test compares air conduction (AC) vs. bone conduction (BC) using a tuning fork; negative Rinne (BC > AC) indicates conductive hearing loss

Normal/sensorineural hearing loss: AC > BC (positive Rinne). Conductive hearing loss: BC > AC (negative Rinne) because air conduction is blocked (effusion, ossicular disease, EAC obstruction). Weber test localizes to affected ear in conductive loss.

**Q:** What is Menière disease and what is its classic tetrad of symptoms?

**A:** Endolymphatic hydrops of the inner ear; tetrad: episodic vertigo (>20 min), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness

Menière disease is diagnosed clinically. Treatment: low-sodium diet, diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide + triamterene), vestibular suppressants (dimenhydrinate) for acute attacks. Intratympanic gentamicin or endolymphatic sac decompression for refractory cases.

**Q:** What is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and what is the first-line treatment?

**A:** Canalith displacement into semicircular canal causing brief positional vertigo; first-line: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning)

BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo. Dix-Hallpike test reproduces posterior canal BPPV. Epley maneuver cures 80–90%. No medication needed. Semont maneuver is an alternative. Recurrence rate is 15–50% within 1 year.

**Q:** A 5-year-old with recurrent AOM (>3 per 6 months) and bilateral effusions for >3 months with 30 dB hearing loss is referred for what procedure?

**A:** Tympanostomy tube insertion (ventilation tubes / grommets)

Indications for tubes: recurrent AOM ≥3 in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months; OME >3 months with hearing loss ≥25 dB; OME with speech delay or learning problems. Tubes equalize middle ear pressure and drain effusions.

**Q:** What is otosclerosis and what are the audiological findings?

**A:** Abnormal remodeling of the otic capsule causing fixation of the stapes footplate; findings: progressive conductive hearing loss with Carhart notch (reduced bone conduction at 2000 Hz) and normal TM on otoscopy

Otosclerosis is autosomal dominant, common in white women, worsened by pregnancy. Audiogram: conductive hearing loss with Carhart notch at 2000 Hz, absent stapedial reflexes, type As (low compliance) tympanogram. Treatment: stapedotomy/stapedectomy.

**Q:** What is the most appropriate management of a single episode of sudden sensorineural hearing loss?

**A:** Urgent ENT referral + oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day × 7–14 days) within 72 hours

Sudden SNHL (≥30 dB loss over ≥3 frequencies within 72 h) may be idiopathic, viral, or vascular. High-dose corticosteroids improve recovery. MRI brain/IAC to exclude acoustic neuroma. Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive in some centers.

**Q:** How do you differentiate acute otitis media from otitis externa?

**A:** AOM: ear pain, fever, bulging/red TM, middle ear effusion, recent URI. OE: ear canal pain with tragal tenderness, edematous canal, discharge, no TM abnormality

AOM treatment: amoxicillin 90mg/kg/day. Watch and wait if mild in >2y. OE: topical ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone drops, keep ear dry. Malignant OE in diabetics/immunocompromised: IV antibiotics.

**Q:** How is acute otitis media diagnosed and managed in children?

**A:** Diagnosis: moderate-severe bulging of TM or new otorrhea or mild bulging+recent ear pain/erythema. First-line: amoxicillin 75-90mg/kg/d divided BID x5-10d. Watch-and-wait option if >2yr, unilateral, non-severe

CPS guidelines. High-dose amox overcomes pneumococcal resistance. Second-line if failure at 48-72h: amox-clav 90mg/kg/d. Tympanostomy tubes for recurrent AOM (>=3 in 6mo or >=4 in 12mo). Complications: mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling/erythema), meningitis.

**Q:** How does otitis externa differ from otitis media and how is it managed?

**A:** OE: ear canal pain worse with tragal pressure/pinna traction, canal edema/debris. TM intact. Treat: topical antibiotic+steroid drops (ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone). Keep ear dry. Wick if canal very swollen

OE risk: swimming, hearing aids, cotton swabs. Malignant OE in diabetics/immunocompromised: Pseudomonas, skull base osteomyelitis - requires IV antipseudomonal + CT scan. Fungal OE (otomycosis): fluffy/spore debris, treat with topical antifungal.

**Q:** What are the causes and management of sudden sensorineural hearing loss?

**A:** SSNHL: >=30dB loss over <=3 days in >=3 consecutive frequencies. Causes: idiopathic (viral), vascular, autoimmune, Meniere, acoustic neuroma. Treatment: oral prednisone 1mg/kg x14d taper. Urgent ENT referral + audiogram

SSNHL is an otologic EMERGENCY. Rule out: acoustic neuroma (MRI with gadolinium). Prognosis: 65% partial recovery. Intratympanic steroids if oral fails. Always differentiate from conductive loss (tuning fork: Weber lateralizes to affected ear in conductive, away in SNHL).

**Q:** How is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) diagnosed and treated?

**A:** Diagnosis: Dix-Hallpike test positive (upbeat-torsional nystagmus with 5-20s latency, fatigable, <60s). Posterior canal most common. Treatment: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning). Avoid meclizine (delays compensation)

BPPV caused by otoconia dislodged into semicircular canal. Dix-Hallpike: head turned 45 degrees, rapidly lie back with head extended. Epley: 93% effective after 1-2 treatments. Horizontal canal BPPV: supine roll test, Lempert maneuver.

**Q:** What is the differential diagnosis of vertigo?

**A:** Peripheral (ENT): BPPV (brief, positional), Meniere (hours, hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness), vestibular neuritis (days, post-viral). Central (neurology): stroke (HINTS exam abnormal), MS, tumor

HINTS exam for acute vestibular syndrome: Head Impulse (normal=central), Nystagmus (direction-changing=central), Test of Skew (present=central). >90% sensitive for stroke. Peripheral: horizontal nystagmus, unidirectional, suppressed by fixation.

**Q:** How is Meniere disease diagnosed and managed?

**A:** Diagnosis: >=2 episodes of vertigo 20min-12h + low-mid frequency SNHL + aural fullness/tinnitus. Management: sodium restriction <2g/d, diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide), betahistine, acute: dimenhydrinate/benzodiazepine

Endolymphatic hydrops is the pathological finding. Hearing loss is fluctuating initially, progressive over years. Intratympanic gentamicin or dexamethasone for refractory cases. Endolymphatic sac surgery. Avoid caffeine and alcohol.

**Q:** What is cholesteatoma and how is it managed?

**A:** Abnormal keratinizing squamous epithelium in middle ear. Presents: chronic otorrhea, conductive hearing loss, TM retraction pocket with debris. Complications: ossicular erosion, facial nerve palsy, intracranial abscess

Acquired >> congenital. CT temporal bone for extent. Treatment: SURGICAL (tympanomastoidectomy). Not curable with antibiotics alone. Complications from erosion: labyrinthine fistula (vertigo), sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess. Lifelong surveillance for recurrence.

**Q:** How is conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss differentiated?

**A:** Weber: lateralizes to affected ear (conductive) or normal ear (SNHL). Rinne: BC>AC = conductive loss (negative Rinne). AC>BC normal (positive Rinne). Audiogram confirms type and severity

Conductive: cerumen, effusion, TM perforation, ossicular chain, otosclerosis. Sensorineural: noise, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs, Meniere, acoustic neuroma, congenital. Mixed: chronic otitis media. Audiogram is essential investigation.

**Q:** What are the indications for tympanostomy tubes?

**A:** Recurrent AOM: >=3 in 6mo or >=4 in 12mo. Chronic OME: >=3 months bilateral with hearing loss. Chronic OME unilateral >=6mo. Complicated AOM. Eustachian tube dysfunction causing recurrent symptoms

Tubes ventilate middle ear and allow topical treatment. Usually extrude spontaneously in 6-18mo. Water precautions controversial (surface swimming generally OK). Otorrhea through tubes: topical ciprofloxacin-dex drops. Risks: persistent perforation 2%, tympanosclerosis.

**Q:** What ototoxic drugs should be monitored?

**A:** Aminoglycosides (vestibulotoxic>cochleotoxic): gentamicin. Cisplatin (cochleotoxic, permanent, high-frequency). Loop diuretics (usually reversible). ASA at high doses (tinnitus, reversible). Vancomycin (especially with aminoglycosides)

Baseline audiogram before ototoxic drugs. Monitor during treatment. Aminoglycoside: once-daily dosing with trough monitoring reduces toxicity. Risk factors: renal impairment, prolonged treatment, concurrent ototoxins. Hearing loss from cisplatin is irreversible.

**Q:** What is the differential diagnosis for conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss, and how do Weber and Rinne tests differentiate them?

**A:** Conductive hearing loss (CHL): external/middle ear pathology — cerumen impaction, otitis media/effusion, tympanic membrane perforation, otosclerosis, cholesteatoma. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL): inner ear/CN VIII — presbycusis (age-related), noise-induced, Meniere disease, acoustic neuroma, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin), sudden SNHL. Weber test (tuning fork on forehead): CHL — lateralizes to AFFECTED ear; SNHL — lateralizes to UNAFFECTED ear. Rinne test (tuning fork on mastoid then beside ear): CHL — bone conduction > air conduction (negative Rinne); SNHL — air conduction > bone conduction (positive Rinne, but reduced).

Mnemonic for Weber: 'CHL loves the bad ear' (sound conducted through bone to the ear with conductive block). Rinne: in CHL, bone > air because the middle ear conduction is impaired. Audiometry is the definitive test. In Canada, audiologists perform pure-tone audiometry and are accessible via referral.

**Q:** A 45-year-old wakes up with sudden unilateral hearing loss. What is the diagnosis and urgency of management?

**A:** Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) — an otologic EMERGENCY. Definition: ≥30 dB loss over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours. Management: urgent audiology (audiogram within 24h), high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 10-14 days with taper) — must start within 2 weeks (ideally within 72h) for best outcomes; intratympanic dexamethasone if systemic steroids fail or are contraindicated; MRI with gadolinium to rule out acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Workup: CBC, ESR/CRP, glucose, TSH, syphilis serology, autoimmune screen if bilateral.

SSNHL is often misdiagnosed as cerumen impaction or otitis — always do a Rinne/Weber to confirm sensorineural pattern. ~1/3 recover spontaneously, ~1/3 improve with treatment, ~1/3 have permanent loss. Early steroid treatment is the only intervention with proven benefit. Canadian Otolaryngology guidelines emphasize urgent ENT referral within 24-48 hours.

**Q:** A 50-year-old woman presents with progressive bilateral hearing loss. Otoscopy is normal. Rinne test shows bone conduction > air conduction bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?

**A:** Otosclerosis: abnormal bone remodeling of the stapes footplate causing fixation at the oval window → progressive conductive hearing loss. Features: bilateral (often worse in one ear), family history (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance), Carhart notch (characteristic dip at 2000 Hz on audiometry), Schwartze sign (pink blush behind TM on otoscopy from increased vascularity — not always present), may worsen during pregnancy. Treatment: hearing aids (conservative) or stapedectomy/stapedotomy (surgical — excellent results, >90% improvement).

Otosclerosis is the most common cause of progressive conductive hearing loss in adults with a normal tympanic membrane. It typically presents in the 20s-40s and is more common in females and Caucasians. The Carhart notch is an audiometric artifact, not true sensorineural loss — it resolves after successful stapedectomy. In Canada, stapedectomy is covered under provincial health insurance.

**Q:** What is the first-line antibiotic for acute otitis media (AOM) in children, and what is used for treatment failure?

**A:** First line: amoxicillin 75–90 mg/kg/day BID. Penicillin allergy: cefprozil or cefuroxime-axetil 30 mg/kg/day BID/TID OR ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/day IM x 3 days (minor allergy) OR clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/day BID (severe allergy, inferior bacterial killing). Treatment failure: amoxicillin-clavulanate (T:1 ratio), <35 kg: 45–60 mg/kg/day TID; >35 kg: 500 mg TID.

High-dose amoxicillin overcomes low-level penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae. Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers beta-lactamase producing H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, common causes of treatment failure. Clarithromycin has suboptimal efficacy for AOM due to inferior bacterial killing but is used for severe penicillin allergy.

**Q:** How does the Dix-Hallpike test work and what does a positive result indicate?

**A:** Patient seated with legs extended, head rotated 45°. Rapidly shift patient to supine with head fully supported in slight extension. Observe for rotatory nystagmus and ask about vertigo. A positive test (rotatory nystagmus + vertigo) indicates BPPV.

The Dix-Hallpike test assesses the posterior semicircular canal. BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo and is caused by displaced otoliths (canalith repositioning maneuver/Epley technique is treatment).

**Q:** Compare the features of BPPV, labyrinthitis, Meniere's disease, and acoustic neuroma.

**A:** BPPV: sudden onset, seconds duration, no hearing loss, no tinnitus. Labyrinthitis: sudden onset, days duration, +/- hearing loss, +/- tinnitus. Meniere's: sudden onset, minutes-hours duration, hearing loss, tinnitus. Acoustic neuroma: insidious onset, chronic duration, hearing loss, tinnitus.

Duration is key in differentiating peripheral causes of vertigo. BPPV lasts seconds and is positional. Labyrinthitis lasts days. Meniere's episodes last minutes to hours. Acoustic neuroma causes chronic progressive symptoms.

**Q:** What are ototoxic drugs that can cause dizziness?

**A:** Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin, tobramycin), erythromycin, ASA, antimalarials (ototoxic agents). Furosemide, caffeine, and alcohol can cause hypotension contributing to dizziness.

Aminoglycosides damage hair cells in the cochlea and vestibule, causing both hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction. This is irreversible with prolonged use or high doses, particularly in patients with renal insufficiency.

**Q:** What features in dizziness history suggest a central versus peripheral vestibular cause?

**A:** Central (neurologic): transient diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, ataxia (TIA/VBI/migraine), persistent headache, altered consciousness, sensory/motor deficits. Peripheral (audiologic): hearing loss, tinnitus, otalgia, aural fullness, nausea/vomiting. Worse with head movement = vestibular. Worse with exercise = cardiac/pulmonary.

Central causes of vertigo are dangerous and require urgent neuroimaging. The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) can differentiate central from peripheral vertigo at the bedside.

**Q:** What types of dizziness should be clarified in the history and how does each differ?

**A:** Vertigo: illusion of movement (spinning). Pre-syncope: feeling of impending faint. Disequilibrium: sense of imbalance (often with walking). Lightheadedness: vague, non-specific. Each points to different etiologies: vertigo (vestibular), pre-syncope (cardiac/autonomic), disequilibrium (cerebellar/proprioceptive), lightheadedness (psychiatric/hyperventilation).

Clarifying the type of dizziness is the most important initial step. 70% of affected patients initially see GPs. Dizziness is the most common complaint in ambulatory patients >75 years.

sections.title: ENT Emergencies
sections.body:
**Q:** A 3-year-old child is brought to the ED with sudden-onset stridor at rest, drooling, and a muffled "hot potato" voice. He appears toxic and is sitting upright. What is the immediate priority?

**A:** Maintain airway; do NOT examine the throat or lay the child down — emergent anesthesia/ENT for intubation in OR

This presentation is epiglottitis until proven otherwise (H. influenzae type b or S. aureus). Manipulating the throat can trigger complete airway obstruction. Call anesthesia and ENT immediately. After airway secured: ceftriaxone IV, dexamethasone.

**Q:** What is the most common complication of untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis?

**A:** Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) — collection of pus between the tonsil and superior constrictor muscle

PTA presents with unilateral bulging of the soft palate, uvular deviation, severe dysphagia, trismus, and "hot potato" voice. Treatment: needle aspiration or I&D + penicillin IV, then PO amoxicillin-clavulanate. Quinsy tonsillectomy for recurrent PTA.

**Q:** An adult presents with 3 days of right-sided facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, fever, and maxillary teeth pain worse on leaning forward. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

**A:** Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS); treat with amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 10 days if moderate-severe or no improvement after 7 days of symptomatic therapy

ABRS requires: symptoms >10 days without improvement, or severe symptoms (fever >39°C, unilateral facial pain) from onset, or double-worsening. Most viral ARS resolves in 7–10 days. Saline irrigation and decongestants provide symptomatic relief.

**Q:** What are the danger signs of orbital cellulitis (vs periorbital/preseptal cellulitis)?

**A:** Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia (restricted/painful eye movements), diplopia, decreased visual acuity, and afferent pupillary defect — all indicate postseptal (orbital) cellulitis

Orbital cellulitis is a surgical emergency requiring CT orbits + sinuses, IV antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftriaxone), and ophthalmology/ENT consultation. Periorbital cellulitis (preseptal) is treated with oral antibiotics.

**Q:** What is the management of a posterior epistaxis that fails conservative measures?

**A:** Posterior nasal packing (or Foley catheter balloon) + anterior packing; consult ENT for arterial ligation or embolization if packing fails

Posterior epistaxis is from the sphenopalatine artery. It is less common but more dangerous than anterior bleeds (Kiesselbach plexus). Posterior packing requires hospital admission for monitoring (risk of hypoxia, pressure necrosis).

**Q:** A 45-year-old presents with sudden onset severe unilateral otalgia, vesicles in the ear canal, facial nerve palsy, and vertigo. What is the diagnosis?

**A:** Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus — reactivation of VZV in geniculate ganglion)

Triad: otic pain, vesicles in the ear/pinna, and ipsilateral facial palsy. Treatment: oral acyclovir/valacyclovir + prednisone within 72 hours. Prognosis for facial nerve recovery is worse than Bell palsy. Audiometry for SNHL.

**Q:** What is the appropriate management of a fish bone foreign body in the pharynx/esophagus?

**A:** Direct or indirect laryngoscopy ± rigid esophagoscopy under GA for retrieval if lodged below cricopharyngeus

Fish bones are radiopaque on lateral neck X-ray but are often missed. Bones above the cricopharyngeus can be removed in the ED with forceps. Bones in the esophagus require rigid endoscopy. Flexible endoscopy is second choice. CT neck/chest if X-ray negative but high suspicion.

**Q:** What is the management of epistaxis?

**A:** Anterior: direct pressure 15min, nasal packing (Merocel/RhinoRocket) if persistent, cauterize with silver nitrate. Posterior: posterior packing (Foley catheter) or balloon, ENT consultation, possible embolization

90% anterior (Kiesselbach plexus). Posterior from sphenopalatine artery — higher risk. Check BP, coagulation studies, medications (anticoagulants). Topical oxymetazoline before packing.

**Q:** How is anterior epistaxis managed?

**A:** 1) Sit forward, pinch soft nose 15min continuous. 2) Topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline). 3) Silver nitrate cautery if bleeding point visible. 4) Anterior nasal packing (Merocel/Rapid Rhino). 5) ENT if refractory

90% epistaxis is anterior (Kiesselbach plexus/Little area). Posterior epistaxis: posterior pack or balloon, admit. Check BP, coagulation, medications (anticoagulants, antiplatelets). Do NOT cauterize both sides of septum (perforation risk).

**Q:** How is peritonsillar abscess (PTA) diagnosed and treated?

**A:** Presentation: severe sore throat, trismus, hot-potato voice, uvular deviation, unilateral tonsillar swelling. Diagnosis: clinical +/- CT or US. Treatment: needle aspiration or I&D + antibiotics (amox-clav or clindamycin). IV fluids

PTA is most common deep neck space infection. Complication: parapharyngeal abscess, airway compromise, Lemierre syndrome (IJV thrombophlebitis from Fusobacterium). Tonsillectomy recommended if recurrent PTA (>2). Always assess airway before instrumentation.

**Q:** What is the approach to a patient with stridor?

**A:** Inspiratory stridor: supraglottic/glottic obstruction (croup, epiglottitis, foreign body, anaphylaxis). Biphasic: glottic/subglottic (croup, subglottic stenosis). Expiratory: lower airway (asthma, bronchiolitis). Assess severity: can they speak, drooling, position?

Croup (6mo-3yr): barky cough, viral, dexamethasone 0.6mg/kg PO single dose + nebulized epinephrine if severe. Epiglottitis: drooling, toxic, do NOT examine throat, urgent anesthesia/ENT for intubation. Adult epiglottitis still occurs.

**Q:** How is acute sinusitis managed?

**A:** Viral (most common, <10d): supportive (saline irrigation, analgesics, intranasal corticosteroids). Bacterial (symptoms >10d, or worsening after 5-7d, or severe onset): amoxicillin 500mg TID x5-7d. Second-line: amox-clav

CTFPHC recommends delayed antibiotics for most sinusitis. Bacterial signs: purulent discharge, unilateral facial pain/pressure, fever, double sickening. Imaging NOT needed for uncomplicated. CT only for complications or chronic. Complications: orbital cellulitis, intracranial abscess.

**Q:** What are the red flags for serious causes of sore throat?

**A:** Drooling/unable to swallow (PTA, epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess). Trismus. Respiratory distress/stridor. Neck swelling/erythema (Ludwig angina). Unilateral swelling. Hot-potato voice. Toxic appearance

Ludwig angina: bilateral submandibular space infection, floor of mouth elevation, potential airway emergency. Lemierre syndrome: sore throat + septic thrombophlebitis of IJV (Fusobacterium). Retropharyngeal abscess: neck stiffness, dysphagia, CT confirms.

**Q:** How is group A strep pharyngitis diagnosed and managed?

**A:** Centor/McIsaac criteria: fever>38, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical LAD, no cough (+1 if age 3-14, -1 if >45). Score 0-1: no test. 2-3: rapid strep then culture. 4+: empiric abx. Treat: penicillin V 600mg BID x10d or amoxicillin

Treatment prevents rheumatic fever (rare in Canada) and reduces symptoms by ~1 day. Alternatives: cephalexin, azithromycin if penicillin allergic. Complications: PTA, rheumatic fever, PSGN (not prevented by antibiotics), scarlet fever.

**Q:** What is the approach to a foreign body in the ear or nose?

**A:** Ear: irrigation if not button battery or live insect (kill insect first with mineral oil). Nose: positive pressure (parent blow or Katz extractor). Button battery: EMERGENCY removal (mucosal necrosis in 2h)

Button battery in nose or esophagus is a TRUE EMERGENCY - causes liquefactive necrosis rapidly. Do not delay for imaging. Nasal FB: occlude unaffected nostril, parent blows into mouth. Ear FB: do not push deeper. ENT referral if failed removal.

**Q:** How is a nasal fracture assessed and managed?

**A:** Assess: deformity, crepitus, epistaxis, septal hematoma (fluctuant swelling - drain immediately to prevent necrosis/saddle nose). XR not needed. Closed reduction if displaced (within 7-10 days for adults)

Septal hematoma is a surgical EMERGENCY - avascular necrosis of cartilage if not drained. Simple nasal fracture: ice, analgesia, reassess in 5-7 days when swelling reduced, reduce if cosmetic deformity. Rule out: CSF rhinorrhea (beta-2 transferrin), orbital blowout fracture.

**Q:** What is the 2-week rule for head and neck cancer referral?

**A:** Urgent ENT referral (2wk) for: hoarseness >3wk, persistent neck lump, unilateral ear pain with normal ear, oral ulcer/lesion >3wk, unexplained dysphagia, unilateral nasal obstruction with bloody discharge

Head and neck SCC risk factors: tobacco, alcohol, HPV (oropharyngeal). HPV+ oropharyngeal cancer increasing in young non-smokers, better prognosis. Pan-endoscopy for staging. Treatment: surgery and/or chemoradiation depending on site and stage.

**Q:** How is obstructive sleep apnea diagnosed and managed?
