Damage occurs with exposure to 85-90 dB over months-years or single impulses >135 dB. Speech reception is not altered until HL exceeds 30 dB at speech frequencies, so considerable damage occurs before symptoms arise.

**Q:** What is the characteristic audiogram finding in otosclerosis?

**A:** Conductive hearing loss with a characteristic dip at 2000 Hz (Carhart's notch) and normal tympanic membrane.

Otosclerosis involves fusion of the stapes footplate to the oval window. It is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, more common in females, and progresses during pregnancy. Schwartz's sign (pink blush on TM) indicates active neovascularization. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy/stapedotomy.

**Q:** How do you differentiate peripheral from central vertigo?

**A:** Peripheral: moderate-severe imbalance, severe N/V, common auditory symptoms, rare neuro symptoms, unidirectional horizontal/rotatory nystagmus, rapid compensation. Central: mild-moderate imbalance, variable N/V, rare auditory symptoms, common neuro symptoms, bidirectional/vertical nystagmus, slow compensation.

The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) helps distinguish central from peripheral causes. A central pattern (no saccades on head impulse, vertical/direction-changing nystagmus, abnormal skew) suggests stroke and requires urgent neuroimaging.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of episodic vertigo, and how is it diagnosed?

**A:** Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Diagnosed by a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver showing geotropic rotatory nystagmus with latency and fatigability.

BPPV is caused by canalithiasis (free-floating otoliths) in the semicircular canals, with the posterior canal affected in >90% of cases. Attacks last seconds, triggered by head position changes. Treatment is the Epley maneuver for particle repositioning. Vestibular suppressants delay recovery and should be avoided.

**Q:** What are the four classic symptoms of Meniere's disease?

**A:** Episodic vertigo (minutes to hours), fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.

Meniere's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops. Peak incidence is 40-60 years, bilateral in 35% of cases. Triggers include high salt, caffeine, stress. Acute management: antiemetics and betahistine. Long-term: low-salt diet, diuretics. Intratympanic gentamicin destroys the vestibular end-organ but causes complete SNHL.

**Q:** What is an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma), and what is the gold standard for diagnosis?

**A:** A schwannoma of the vestibular portion of CN VIII. Gold standard diagnosis: MRI of the internal auditory canal with gadolinium contrast.

Acoustic neuroma is the most common CPA tumor and the most common intracranial tumor causing SNHL. It usually presents with unilateral progressive SNHL or tinnitus. True vertigo is rare because slow tumor growth allows compensation. Bilateral acoustic neuromas suggest NF2. In the elderly, unilateral tinnitus or SNHL is acoustic neuroma until proven otherwise.

**Q:** What is the most common organism causing otitis externa, and what is the cardinal sign?

**A:** Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Cardinal sign: pain aggravated by traction of the pinna or pressure over the tragus.

OE is inflammation of the external auditory canal, most commonly bacterial (90%). Risk factors include water exposure (swimmer's ear), trauma from cotton swabs, and hearing aids. Treatment includes microdebridement, topical antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin), and keeping the ear dry.

**Q:** What is malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa, and in whom does it occur?

**A:** Osteomyelitis of the temporal/mastoid bone, most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, occurring in elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients.

It presents with otalgia and purulent otorrhea refractory to medical therapy, with granulation tissue on the floor of the auditory canal. CN VII palsy is the most common cranial nerve complication. It is a medical emergency requiring IV antibiotics, hospitalization, and possibly surgical debridement.

**Q:** What is a cholesteatoma, and what is the classic otoscopic finding?

**A:** A cyst of keratinized desquamated epithelium in the middle ear/mastoid that causes progressive bony destruction. Classic finding: retraction pocket in the TM containing keratinous debris, often with malodorous unilateral otorrhea.

Cholesteatoma can be congenital (white pearl behind intact TM) or acquired (associated with chronic otitis media). Complications include ossicular erosion (CHL), labyrinthine erosion (SNHL, vertigo), facial nerve paralysis, and intracranial complications (meningitis, abscess). Treatment is surgical: mastoidectomy with tympanoplasty.

**Q:** What is the second most common cause of CHL in patients aged 15-50?

**A:** Otosclerosis.

Otosclerosis is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (~40%). It is more common in females and progresses during pregnancy. It presents with progressive CHL first noticed in teens/twenties, sometimes with Schwartz's sign (pink blush on TM) and Carhart's notch at 2000 Hz on audiogram. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy.

**Q:** What tympanogram pattern indicates middle ear effusion?

**A:** Type B tympanogram — flat curve with no pressure peak, indicating poor TM mobility.

Type A is normal (peak at 0 mmH2O). Type B shows no peak, indicating effusion or TM perforation (differentiated by ear canal volume: >2 cc in children or >2.5 cc in adults suggests perforation). Type C shows a negative pressure peak, indicating Eustachian tube dysfunction or early otitis media without effusion.

**Q:** What differentiates Bell's palsy from Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

**A:** Bell's palsy: idiopathic (likely HSV), 80-90% of peripheral facial palsies, >90% prognosis. Ramsay Hunt syndrome: VZV reactivation in CN VII/VIII, vesicles on pinna/ear canal, associated SNHL, worse prognosis (only 22% full recovery).

Both cause peripheral facial nerve paralysis (all muscle groups on one side including frontalis). Bell's palsy is treated with steroids +/- antivirals. Ramsay Hunt syndrome requires acyclovir and steroids. Both need corneal protection. Spontaneous remission of Bell's palsy should begin within 3 weeks.

**Q:** What are the orbital complications of sinusitis (Chandler's classification)?

**A:** I: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis. II: Orbital cellulitis. III: Subperiosteal abscess. IV: Orbital abscess. V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

These are the most feared complications of sinusitis and require hospitalization. Preseptal cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and does not compromise vision. Postseptal involvement (stages II-V) can cause proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and vision loss. Cavernous sinus thrombosis carries high mortality.

**Q:** What is the most common site of epistaxis, and what is the relevant vascular anatomy?

**A:** Anterior-inferior nasal septum at Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), where the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and greater palatine arteries anastomose.

Most epistaxis is anterior and can be controlled with direct pressure for 15-20 minutes, topical decongestants, and silver nitrate cautery. Do not cauterize both sides of the septum simultaneously (risk of perforation). Posterior epistaxis requires packing, admission, and possibly sphenopalatine artery ligation.

**Q:** What are vocal cord nodules, and how do they differ from vocal cord polyps?

**A:** Nodules: bilateral, symmetric, at the junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of cords, gradual onset, treated primarily with voice therapy. Polyps: unilateral, asymmetric, acute onset from capillary breakage, may require surgical excision.

Nodules are also called 'singer's nodules' and result from chronic voice strain. They occur at the point of maximal cord vibration. Polyps are the most common benign tumor of vocal cords and are more common in males aged 30-50. Both require elimination of irritants and voice therapy as first-line treatment.

**Q:** What is the connexin 26 (GJB2) gene mutation significant for?

**A:** It is the most common cause of non-syndromic congenital sensorineural hearing loss (autosomal recessive).

Non-syndromic causes account for 70% of hereditary SNHL, while syndromic causes account for 30%. Important syndromes include Waardenburg (white forelock, heterochromia), Pendred (euthyroid goiter), Treacher-Collins (branchial cleft anomalies), and Alport (hereditary nephritis).

**Q:** What is the HINTS exam and how does it help differentiate central from peripheral vertigo?

**A:** Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew. Central (stroke): normal head impulse (no saccades), vertical/direction-changing nystagmus, abnormal skew. Peripheral (vestibular neuritis): corrective saccade present, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, normal skew.

The HINTS exam is more sensitive than early MRI for detecting posterior fossa stroke in patients with acute vestibular syndrome. A central pattern on any ONE of the three tests should raise concern for stroke. This is critical in emergency settings to avoid misdiagnosing a cerebellar infarct as vestibular neuritis.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of sudden SNHL?

**A:** Idiopathic (80-90% of cases). Treatment: intratympanic or oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 7-14 days), ideally started within 3 days.

Sudden SNHL is defined as loss of at least 30 dB affecting three consecutive frequencies. It may be confused with ischemic brain events, especially in elderly patients. MRI is needed to rule out tumor; CT if neurological signs suggest stroke. 70% resolve within 10-14 days, but 10% experience permanent hearing loss.

**Q:** What aminoglycosides are vestibulotoxic vs. cochleotoxic?

**A:** Vestibulotoxic: streptomycin and gentamicin. Cochleotoxic: kanamycin and tobramycin.

Aminoglycosides destroy sensory hair cells (outer first, then inner) by any route. Duration of treatment is the most important predictor of ototoxicity. Once-daily dosing presents less risk than divided doses due to saturable kinetics. Otoacoustic emissions are lost first since they originate from outer hair cells.

**Q:** What is the most important predictor of hearing aid response?

**A:** Speech discrimination score. A poor score indicates significant neural degeneration, and hearing aids may not be the best option.

Speech discrimination is tested at 40 dB above the patient's speech reception threshold. Normal hearing or CHL patients score >90%. The rollover effect (decreased discrimination with increased intensity) is typical of retrocochlear lesions like acoustic neuroma. Asymmetry >20% between ears also suggests retrocochlear pathology.

**Q:** What is the recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, and what HPV types cause it?

**A:** Benign wart-like growths in the respiratory tract, most commonly caused by HPV types 6 and 11. It is the most common laryngeal tumor in children.

It has a biphasic distribution: juvenile (birth to puberty) and adult onset. Juvenile forms may resolve at puberty. It is highly resistant to complete removal with high recurrence rates. Treatment is suspension microlaryngoscopy with laser removal. The quadrivalent HPV vaccine can prevent and treat as systemic adjuvant.

**Q:** What is sialolithiasis, and which gland is most commonly affected?

**A:** Ductal stones (mainly hydroxyapatite) causing chronic sialadenitis. 80% occur in the submandibular gland.

The submandibular gland is most susceptible because its duct (Wharton's duct) is longer, curves upward, and produces more mucous secretions. Symptoms include intermittent swelling related to meals. Diagnosis is by ultrasound first, then CT for localization. Treatment includes sialogogues, massage, and if refractory, surgical excision.

**Q:** What are the three ossicular bones of the middle ear, and what is their function?

**A:** Malleus, incus, stapes; they transmit and amplify sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window (inner ear).

The ossicular chain converts acoustic (air) energy into mechanical energy and amplifies it approximately 20-fold through lever action and the area ratio between the tympanic membrane and oval window. Disruption causes conductive hearing loss.

**Q:** What are the three divisions of the ear?

**A:** External ear (pinna, external auditory canal, tympanic membrane), middle ear (ossicles, Eustachian tube), inner ear (cochlea, semicircular canals, vestibule).

The external ear collects and funnels sound. The middle ear transmits and amplifies sound via the ossicular chain. The inner ear contains the cochlea (hearing) and vestibular apparatus (balance). Understanding this division is essential for localizing hearing loss as conductive (external/middle) or sensorineural (inner).

**Q:** What are the two parts of the tympanic membrane visible on otoscopy?

**A:** Pars flaccida (superior, loose) and pars tensa (inferior, larger, taut portion).

The pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) lacks the fibrous middle layer and is the most common site of cholesteatoma formation. The pars tensa is the main vibrating portion and contains the cone of light (anteroinferior light reflex) and attachment of the malleus handle. The umbo is the deepest point at the tip of the malleus.

**Q:** What are the four paranasal sinuses?

**A:** Maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses.

The maxillary sinuses are largest and most commonly affected by rhinosinusitis. The ethmoid sinuses (multiple small air cells) drain via the ostiomeatal complex. The sphenoid sinuses are posterior and close to the optic nerve and cavernous sinus — a dangerous site for spread of infection. The frontal sinuses are superior.

**Q:** What is the arterial supply of the nasal septum and what is Kiesselbach's plexus?

**A:** Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anterior nasal septum receives contributions from: anterior ethmoid a., sphenopalatine a. (branch of external carotid), superior labial a., and greater palatine a.

Kiesselbach's plexus is the most common site of anterior epistaxis (~90% of epistaxis). It receives supply from both internal carotid (anterior ethmoid via ophthalmic artery) and external carotid (sphenopalatine, superior labial, greater palatine) systems. This dual supply makes it highly vascular.

**Q:** What are the true vocal cords vs. false vocal cords (vestibular folds)?

**A:** True vocal cords (vocal folds) vibrate to produce voice; false vocal cords (vestibular folds/vestibular ligaments) are superior folds that do not vibrate and function in airway protection.

The true vocal cords contain the vocalis muscle and are lined by stratified squamous epithelium — important for squamous cell carcinoma development. The false cords are superior folds that assist in Valsalva maneuvers and airway protection. On indirect laryngoscopy, they appear as the upper pair of folds.

**Q:** What are the branches of the facial nerve (CN VII) from superior to inferior?

**A:** Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular (marginal mandibular), cervical. Mnemonic: 'To Zanzibar By Motor Car'.

The facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen and immediately enters the parotid gland where it divides into these five branches. Parotid surgery risks injury to these branches. The marginal mandibular branch is most commonly injured in parotid surgery, causing lower lip/chin asymmetry.

**Q:** What are the four functions of the facial nerve summarized in the mnemonic 'Ears, Tears, Face, Taste'?

**A:** Ears: motor to stapedius (hyperacusis if damaged); Tears: lacrimal gland and salivation (submandibular, sublingual glands via chorda tympani); Face: muscles of facial expression; Taste: anterior 2/3 of tongue via chorda tympani.

The parasympathetic ganglia supplied by CN VII include: pterygopalatine (lacrimal gland, nasal mucosa) and submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands). Loss of stapedius function causes hyperacusis. The chorda tympani carries taste from anterior 2/3 tongue and preganglionic parasympathetics to submandibular ganglion.

**Q:** What are the boundaries and contents of the anterior triangle of the neck?

**A:** Bounded by: anterior border of SCM, midline of neck (jugular notch to mentum), inferior border of mandible. Contains: carotid triangle (tail of parotid, submandibular gland, hypoglossal nerve, carotid bifurcation) and muscular triangle (internal jugular vein, vagus nerve).

The anterior triangle is subdivided into submental (unpaired, midline), digastric/submandibular, carotid, and muscular triangles. Knowledge of these borders and contents is essential for understanding neck dissections, lymph node levels, and the approach to neck masses.

**Q:** What are the boundaries and contents of the posterior triangle of the neck?

**A:** Bounded by: posterior border of SCM, anterior border of trapezius, middle third of clavicle. Contains: accessory nerve (CN XI), brachial plexus roots/trunks, phrenic nerve, occipital and supraclavicular lymph nodes.

The posterior triangle is subdivided by the inferior belly of the omohyoid into the occipital (superior) and subclavian (inferior) triangles. The accessory nerve (CN XI) traverses the posterior triangle superficially and is vulnerable to surgical injury during lymph node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness.

**Q:** What does enlargement of the left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node) suggest clinically?

**A:** Abdominal malignancy or malignancy below the clavicle (e.g., gastric, pancreatic cancer).

Virchow's node is the left lower jugular (Level IV) supraclavicular lymph node. It receives lymph drainage from the thoracic duct, which drains the abdominal and pelvic viscera. Left-sided Virchow's node enlargement (Troisier's sign) classically suggests an abdominal malignancy such as gastric cancer.

**Q:** What does right-sided supraclavicular lymphadenopathy suggest?

**A:** Malignancy of the mediastinum, lungs, or esophagus.

Right-sided supraclavicular lymphadenopathy receives drainage from the right thoracic duct, which drains the right chest, lung, and mediastinum. Therefore, right supraclavicular adenopathy suggests thoracic malignancies such as lung cancer or esophageal cancer, in contrast to left-sided Virchow's node which suggests abdominal primaries.

**Q:** What does occipital and/or posterior auricular lymphadenopathy suggest?

**A:** Rubella.

Posterior auricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy is a classic finding of rubella (German measles) in addition to a maculopapular rash and low-grade fever. This pattern of lymphadenopathy should prompt consideration of rubella, especially in unvaccinated individuals or those in early pregnancy where rubella can cause congenital rubella syndrome.

**Q:** What lymph node level drains the thyroid gland and is called the anterior compartment?

**A:** Level VI (anterior compartment); located between the hyoid bone and suprasternal notch between the common carotid arteries.

Level VI nodes include pretracheal, precricoid, paratracheal, and perithyroidal nodes. They drain the thyroid gland, glottic and subglottic larynx, apex of piriform sinus, and cervical esophagus. This level is dissected in total thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

**Q:** What are the findings suggestive of central vs. peripheral vertigo?

**A:** Central: acute onset and continuous, normal head impulse test, multidirectional nystagmus, skew deviation present. Peripheral: nystagmus/vertigo compensates within weeks (unless cerebellar ischemia history), abnormal head impulse test, unidirectional nystagmus.

Central vertigo (e.g., stroke, MS, tumour) is more dangerous and requires urgent neuroimaging. The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus direction, Test of Skew) distinguishes central from peripheral causes. A normal head impulse test with multidirectional nystagmus and skew deviation strongly suggests central pathology.

**Q:** What are the 5 Ds of vertebrobasilar insufficiency causing central vertigo?

**A:** Drop attacks, Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dizziness, Dysphagia.

Vertebrobasilar insufficiency results from posterior circulation ischemia affecting the brainstem and cerebellum. These five features (5 Ds) indicate involvement of multiple posterior circulation structures and should prompt urgent investigation for stroke or TIA. Treatment is antiplatelet therapy and risk factor modification.

**Q:** What is referred otalgia and which cranial nerves mediate it?

**A:** Pain perceived in the ear arising from a distant source. Mediated by CN V (trigeminal), CN VII (facial), CN IX (glossopharyngeal), and CN X (vagus).

The ear receives sensory innervation from multiple cranial nerves, making it a common site for referred pain. The '10 Ts of referred otalgia' include: Teeth, TMD, Tubal area, Tonsils, Throat, Tongue, Trachea/larynx, Thyroid, Temporal arteritis, and Trauma. A normal ear exam with otalgia must prompt evaluation for oropharyngeal/laryngeal malignancy.

**Q:** A 60-year-old smoker presents with right ear pain but a normal ear exam. What must be ruled out?

**A:** Oropharyngeal/laryngeal malignancy causing referred otalgia via CN IX or CN X.

Otalgia with a normal ear examination should always raise suspicion for referred pain. In a middle-aged or elderly smoker/drinker, oropharyngeal cancer (tonsillar, base of tongue) or laryngeal cancer are high on the differential. Thorough inspection of the oral cavity, oropharynx, and larynx is mandatory, followed by flexible laryngoscopy.

**Q:** What are the parasympathetic ganglia of the head supplied by CN VII, and what structures do they innervate?

**A:** Pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal gland, nasal mucosa) and submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands) via chorda tympani.

CN VII carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to two ganglia. The greater petrosal nerve reaches the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimal and nasal secretion. The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve to reach the submandibular ganglion for salivation. Loss of these functions occurs with Bell's palsy proximal to the geniculate ganglion.

**Q:** What is the otic ganglion supplied by, and what does it innervate?

**A:** Supplied by CN IX (glossopharyngeal); innervates the parotid gland.

The preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from CN IX travel via the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion, which then provides secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland. This pathway is relevant in Frey's syndrome (auriculotemporal syndrome) where aberrant regeneration after parotidectomy causes gustatory sweating.

**Q:** What is the ciliary ganglion supplied by, and what does it control?

**A:** Supplied by CN III (oculomotor); controls pupillary constriction (miosis) and accommodation.

Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in CN III synapse in the ciliary ganglion, which sends postganglionic fibers to the sphincter pupillae (constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation). Third nerve palsy causes mydriasis (dilated pupil) and loss of accommodation, along with ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia.

**Q:** What is the strap muscle anatomy of the neck relevant to thyroid surgery?

**A:** Sternohyoid and sternothyroid (infrahyoid strap muscles) overlie the thyroid gland; must be divided or retracted for thyroid access.

The strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid) are thin infrahyoid muscles innervated by the ansa cervicalis. They overlie the thyroid and must be managed during thyroid surgery. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) and superior/inferior parathyroid glands are key structures at risk.

**Q:** What is the Thyroidea ima artery, and why is it clinically relevant?

**A:** An anomalous artery present in ~3% of the population arising from the aortic arch or innominate artery, supplying the thyroid gland inferiorly; relevant to emergency cricothyrotomy and thyroid surgery.

The Thyroidea ima artery is an anatomical variant that travels in the midline and can be encountered during emergency airway access (cricothyrotomy, tracheotomy) or thyroid surgery. Injury can cause significant bleeding. Its presence should be anticipated and managed during inferior thyroid dissection.

**Q:** What lymph node level drains the nasopharynx and oropharynx and is located in the posterior triangle?

**A:** Level V (posterior triangle nodes, VA and VB); located between the posterior border of SCM, anterior border of trapezius, from skull base to clavicle.

Level V nodes drain the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and cutaneous structures of the posterior scalp and neck. They are important in the staging and surgical management of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and oropharyngeal cancers. A neck dissection for these primaries often includes Level V.

**Q:** What does the submental triangle contain and what are its boundaries?

**A:** Bounded by both anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and the hyoid bone; drains the floor of mouth, anterior tongue, anterior mandibular alveolar ridge, and lower lip. It is the only unpaired triangle.

The submental triangle (Level IA) is unpaired and midline. It contains submental lymph nodes that drain anterior oral cavity structures. These nodes are relevant in surgical management of squamous cell carcinoma of the anterior oral cavity and lower lip.

**Q:** What imaging modality is used to evaluate a patient with suspected nerve involvement in Eustachian tube dysfunction?

**A:** MRI with gadolinium is the imaging of choice for Eustachian tube, nasopharyngeal, and middle ear pathology with suspected neural involvement.

The Eustachian tube and nasopharynx are closely related anatomically and functionally. MRI provides superior soft-tissue resolution for evaluating these structures. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma classically presents with Eustachian tube dysfunction causing unilateral otitis media with effusion in adults, necessitating nasopharyngeal evaluation.

**Q:** What are the contents of the eustachian tube region in the neck lymph node drainage?

**A:** The tubal area (nasopharynx including Eustachian tube opening) drains to upper jugular nodes (Level IIA/IIB) and posterior triangle nodes (Level V).

The Eustachian tube opens into the nasopharynx at the fossa of Rosenmüller. Nasopharyngeal malignancy commonly presents with cervical lymphadenopathy at Levels II and V, as well as Eustachian tube obstruction causing unilateral serous otitis media. This is a 'red flag' presentation requiring urgent nasopharyngoscopy.

**Q:** What are the structures of the larynx visible on indirect laryngoscopy from superior view?

**A:** Epiglottis, vallecula, arytenoid cartilages, vestibular folds (false cords), vocal folds (true cords), pyriform fossae, posterior commissure.

Indirect laryngoscopy (mirror or flexible scope) provides a superior view. The vallecula is between the base of tongue and epiglottis — a site where foreign bodies lodge and where epiglottitis causes the 'thumb sign' on lateral X-ray. The pyriform fossae are lateral to the aryepiglottic folds and are sites of hypopharyngeal carcinoma.

**Q:** What is the trigeminal nerve (CN V) contribution to ear sensory innervation and its clinical relevance?

**A:** CN V (auriculotemporal branch of V3) supplies the anterior external auditory canal and anterior pinna; relevant as a source of referred otalgia from dental/TMJ pathology.

The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of the mandibular division V3) supplies the anterior EAC and anterior pinna. Dental disease, TMJ dysfunction, and masseter muscle disorders commonly cause referred otalgia via CN V. This is one of the most common causes of referred ear pain in clinical practice.

**Q:** What is the Eustachian tube and why is its dysfunction important in otolaryngology?

**A:** The Eustachian tube connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear, equalizing pressure and draining middle ear secretions. Dysfunction leads to otitis media with effusion (OME), acute otitis media (AOM), and hearing loss.

Normal Eustachian tube function maintains negative pressure equalization and mucociliary drainage of the middle ear. Dysfunction (e.g., due to adenoid hypertrophy, nasopharyngeal mass, rhinitis) impairs drainage, causing middle ear effusion (glue ear) — the most common cause of conductive hearing loss in children. Persistent unilateral OME in adults must prompt nasopharyngeal evaluation to exclude malignancy.

**Q:** What are the signs and symptoms of a Glomus Tympanicum/Jugulare tumour?

**A:** Pulsatile tinnitus, hearing loss (HL), blue mass behind the tympanic membrane (TM), and Brown's sign (blanching of the TM with pneumatic otoscopy).

Glomus tumours are paragangliomas arising in the middle ear or jugular foramen. The blue-red mass visible through the TM and pulsatile tinnitus are classic. Brown's sign (blanching of the vascular mass with pneumatic pressure) is pathognomonic.

**Q:** What is the most common differential for a neck mass in a patient under age 20?

**A:** Congenital causes (e.g., thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial cleft cyst, cystic hygroma).

The rule of thumb for neck masses: under 20 = congenital, ages 20–40 = inflammatory/infectious, over 40 = neoplastic (malignant until proven otherwise). This guides the initial diagnostic workup.

**Q:** What is the most common differential for a neck mass in a patient over age 40?

**A:** Malignancy (neoplastic) — a neck mass in a patient over 40 is considered malignant until proven otherwise.

Squamous cell carcinoma metastatic from a head and neck primary is the most common cause of a neck mass in those over 40. Lymphoma, thyroid malignancy, and other primaries must also be considered. Early biopsy and workup are essential.

**Q:** Describe the conductive auditory pathway from the external ear to the cochlea.

**A:** Sound travels down the EAC → vibrates the tympanic membrane → sequential vibration of ossicles (malleus → incus → stapes) → stapes footplate transmits amplified vibrations to the oval window → vibrations through cochlear fluid create movement along the basilar membrane.

Understanding the conductive pathway is essential for localizing conductive hearing loss (CHL). Pathology at any of these structures (EAC, TM, ossicles, oval window) can cause CHL without affecting sensorineural structures.

**Q:** Describe the neural auditory pathway from the cochlea to the cortex.

**A:** Basilar membrane vibration → hair cells in organ of Corti → bipolar neurons in spiral ganglion → cochlear division of CN VIII → cochlear nucleus → superior olivary nucleus → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate → Sylvian fissure of temporal lobe.

The neural pathway has multiple relay stations. Lesions at the level of CN VIII (e.g., acoustic neuroma), brainstem, or cortex produce sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Identifying the level of the lesion is critical for management.

**Q:** What are the three types of hearing loss?

**A:** 1. Conductive hearing loss (CHL): impaired conduction to the cochlea (external/middle ear disease). 2. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL): defect in conversion or transmission of neural signals (inner ear, CN VIII, brainstem, cortex). 3. Mixed hearing loss: combination of CHL and SNHL.

Distinguishing CHL from SNHL guides investigation and treatment. CHL is often surgically correctable; SNHL may require hearing aids or cochlear implants. Mixed loss requires addressing both components.

**Q:** Interpret the Rinne and Weber tests: a patient has right-sided CHL and a normal left ear.

**A:** Weber lateralizes to the RIGHT (ipsilateral to CHL). Rinne is NEGATIVE on the right (BC > AC, abnormal).

Weber lateralizes toward the side of CHL because the affected side is relatively quieter externally, making bone-conducted sound seem louder. A negative Rinne (BC > AC) indicates CHL on that side. This pattern is classic for unilateral conductive pathology.

**Q:** Interpret the Rinne and Weber tests: a patient has right-sided SNHL and a normal left ear.

**A:** Weber lateralizes to the LEFT (contralateral to SNHL). Rinne is POSITIVE on both sides (AC > BC bilaterally).

Weber lateralizes away from SNHL because the affected cochlea cannot process bone-conducted sound as well. Rinne remains positive (AC > BC) in SNHL because while both are reduced, the ratio is preserved. A negative Rinne would indicate CHL.

**Q:** What tuning fork frequency is used for Rinne and Weber tests, and why?

**A:** 512 Hz. It is the most sensitive for detecting clinically significant hearing loss and falls within the speech frequency range (500–2000 Hz).

Lower frequency forks (e.g., 256 Hz) require a larger air-bone gap (15 dB) to reverse the Rinne, making them less sensitive. The 512 Hz fork requires only a ~30 dB gap and is optimal for detecting conductive losses relevant to speech.

**Q:** What is the pure tone average (PTA) and which frequencies does it use?

**A:** The PTA is the average threshold at 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz — the range of human speech frequencies. It determines the degree of hearing loss.

These three frequencies correspond to the range of human speech (500–2000 Hz), making the PTA the most clinically relevant measure of functional hearing. The range of human hearing is 20–20,000 Hz, but the most sensitive is 1000–4000 Hz.

**Q:** What audiogram pattern is seen in noise-induced (occupational) hearing loss, and at what frequency?

**A:** A notch at 4000 Hz (the 'Boilermaker's notch'), with better hearing at adjacent frequencies.

Noise-induced hearing loss characteristically affects the 4000 Hz frequency first due to its sensitivity to mechanical trauma. This 4000 Hz notch is a hallmark finding on audiogram and is important for occupational health assessments and medicolegal evaluation.

**Q:** What audiogram pattern is associated with otosclerosis, and what is it called?

**A:** Carhart's notch — a notch at 2000 Hz on the bone conduction audiogram, seen in otosclerosis.

Carhart's notch is a mechanical artefact of otosclerosis, not true cochlear involvement. It reflects reduced mechanical resonance at 2000 Hz due to stapes fixation. It improves after successful stapedectomy, distinguishing it from true SNHL.

**Q:** How do you distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss on audiogram?

**A:** CHL: BC in normal range, AC outside normal range, air-bone gap >10 dB. SNHL: both AC and BC below normal, air-bone gap <10 dB. Mixed: both below normal with air-bone gap >10 dB.

The air-bone gap is the key distinguishing feature. In CHL, the inner ear (bone conduction) is intact but sound cannot reach it (air conduction reduced). In SNHL, the cochlea or nerve is damaged so both AC and BC are reduced proportionally.

**Q:** What is the Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) and when is the result considered suspicious for a retrocochlear lesion?

**A:** SRT is the lowest HL level at which a patient can repeat 50% of spondee words. If SRT and the best pure tone threshold at 500–2000 Hz disagree by >5 dB, suspect a retrocochlear lesion or functional hearing loss.

In normal or cochlear hearing loss, the SRT closely matches the PTA (within 5 dB). A large discrepancy suggests pathology beyond the cochlea, such as an acoustic neuroma (CN VIII schwannoma), which disrupts neural transmission more than expected from the pure tone threshold.

**Q:** What is the rollover effect in speech discrimination testing, and what does it indicate?

**A:** A decrease in speech discrimination score as sound intensity increases. It is typical of a retrocochlear lesion (e.g., acoustic neuroma).

Normally, speech discrimination improves or plateaus with increasing intensity. Rollover — where scores paradoxically worsen at higher intensities — indicates abnormal neural firing patterns, characteristic of acoustic neuroma or CN VIII pathology.

**Q:** Interpret a Type B tympanogram.

**A:** Flat curve with no pressure peak, indicating poor TM mobility. Causes: middle ear effusion (MEE) or perforated TM. Canal volume >2 cc in children or >2.5 cc in adults with Type B suggests TM perforation or patent ventilation tube.

The tympanogram measures middle ear compliance against pressure. A flat Type B indicates no compliance change, suggesting fluid in the middle ear (MEE, otitis media with effusion) or a perforated TM. Distinguishing these requires measuring ear canal volume.

**Q:** Interpret a Type C tympanogram.

**A:** Negative pressure peak (peak shifted to the negative pressure side), indicating Eustachian tube dysfunction or early otitis media without effusion.

A Type C tympanogram shows the compliance peak at negative pressure, reflecting impaired Eustachian tube function that cannot equalize middle ear pressure with ambient. This is an early sign of otitis media and can progress to MEE (Type B) if untreated.

**Q:** What are the conditions required for an acoustic stapedial reflex to be present?

**A:** CN VII must be intact, and there must be no CHL in the monitored ear. The acoustic reflex threshold is normally 70–100 dB above hearing threshold.

The stapedius muscle (innervated by CN VII) contracts bilaterally in response to loud sound. Absent reflex without CHL or severe SNHL suggests CN VII lesion. In CHL, the reflex is absent on the affected side. This test is valuable in distinguishing sites of facial nerve and hearing pathology.

**Q:** What acoustic stapedial reflex findings are seen in acoustic neuroma (retrocochlear HL)?

**A:** Absent acoustic reflexes OR marked reflex decay (>50%) within 5 seconds. The acoustic reflex decay test reveals inability of the stapedius to sustain contraction at 500 and 1000 Hz.

Acoustic neuroma damages CN VIII, impairing the afferent limb of the stapedial reflex arc. Reflex decay — unlike in cochlear lesions — is pathological and suggests retrocochlear pathology. This finding warrants MRI of the internal auditory canal.

**Q:** What is the Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) test and what are its key clinical advantages?

**A:** ABR measures neuroelectric potentials (5 waves) at different anatomic sites along the auditory pathway. Key advantages: (1) does not require patient cooperation (useful in children and malingerers); (2) can localize the site of lesion; (3) delay in brainstem response suggests cochlear or retrocochlear abnormalities.

ABR is an objective test (no voluntary response required), making it invaluable for pediatric hearing assessment, medico-legal evaluations, and surgical monitoring. In acoustic neuroma, the 5th wave latency is characteristically delayed.

**Q:** What are Otoacoustic Emissions (OAEs) and what is their clinical use?

**A:** OAEs are echoes generated by outer hair cells in response to click stimuli. Uses: newborn hearing screening, detecting malingering (absent OAE = true HL vs. normal OAE = functional HL). Absent emissions indicate HL, middle ear fluid, or narrow EAC.

OAEs are an objective test that bypasses voluntary response. Outer hair cell function is a proxy for overall cochlear (inner hair cell) function. They are the standard test for universal newborn hearing screening in Canada and can unmask malingering.

**Q:** What is a cochlear implant and what are the established indications?

**A:** A cochlear implant is an electrode inserted into the cochlea for direct stimulation of the auditory nerve. Established indications: profound bilateral SNHL refractory to conventional hearing aids, including postlingually deafened adults and pre/postlingually deaf children.

Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells by directly stimulating the auditory nerve. Prelingually deaf infants are the best candidates for aural rehabilitation because early intervention maximizes benefit from ongoing brain plasticity during language development.

**Q:** What is a Bone-Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) and who are suitable candidates?

**A:** A BAHA is a hearing aid attached to the skull that transmits sound vibrations through the external abutment to a titanium implant via bone conduction. Candidates: patients with CHL, unilateral HL, and mixed HL who cannot wear conventional hearing aids.

BAHA bypasses the outer and middle ear entirely, making it ideal for congenital aural atresia, chronic otitis media, or single-sided deafness. It is surgically implanted and requires intact cochlear function on the implanted side.

**Q:** Differentiate peripheral from central vertigo across key clinical features.

**A:** Peripheral: moderate-severe imbalance, severe N/V, common auditory symptoms, rare neuro symptoms, rapid compensation, unidirectional horizontal or rotatory nystagmus. Central: mild-moderate imbalance, variable N/V, rare auditory symptoms, common neuro symptoms, slow compensation, bidirectional or vertical nystagmus.

Distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo is critical because central causes (brainstem/cerebellar infarct) are life-threatening. Vertical nystagmus, neurologic deficits, and slow compensation all suggest a central process requiring urgent MRI.

**Q:** What is the HINTS exam and how does it differentiate central from peripheral vertigo?

**A:** HINTS = Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew. Central (stroke): no saccade on head impulse, vertical/torsional/gaze-evoked nystagmus, abnormal skew. Peripheral (vestibular neuritis): saccade present on head impulse, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, normal skew.

The HINTS exam is more sensitive than early MRI for posterior fossa stroke in acute vestibular syndrome. A 'HINTS positive for stroke' (no saccade + vertical/directional nystagmus + abnormal skew) mandates urgent neuroimaging despite possibly normal early DWI MRI.

**Q:** What is Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)? What causes it and what canal is most commonly affected?

**A:** BPPV: acute attacks of transient rotatory vertigo (<1 min) triggered by head position change, with torsional nystagmus. Caused by canalithiasis (free otoliths in endolymph) or cupulolithiasis. Posterior semicircular canal is affected in >90% of cases.

BPPV is the most common cause of episodic vertigo (50% of peripheral vestibular dysfunction). Free-floating otoliths create abnormal signals when the head moves. The posterior canal's anatomical position makes it most susceptible to otolith accumulation.

**Q:** How is BPPV diagnosed and what are the signs seen on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver?

**A:** Positive Dix-Hallpike (sensitivity 82%, specificity 71%): patient rapidly moved from sitting to supine with head turned 45° and neck extended 20°. Positive signs: latency of ~20s, crescendo/decrescendo vertigo lasting ~20s, geotropic rotatory nystagmus (fast phase toward floor), reversal on sitting up, fatigability with repeated stimulation.

The characteristic features (latency, fatigability, geotropic nystagmus) distinguish BPPV from other causes of positional vertigo. No additional diagnostic testing is needed for typical posterior canal BPPV once Dix-Hallpike is positive.

**Q:** What is the treatment for BPPV?

**A:** First-line: particle repositioning maneuvers — Epley maneuver (physician-performed or self-performed with DizzyFIX™) or Brandt-Daroff exercises. Anti-emetics for N/V. Refractory cases: posterior semicircular canal occlusion or singular neurectomy. Note: vestibular suppressants delay recovery and are NOT used.

Canalith repositioning (Epley) moves otoliths out of the semicircular canal back into the utricle using gravity and sequential head positioning. It has >80% success rate. Vestibular suppressants (meclizine, etc.) impair central compensation and are contraindicated as primary therapy in BPPV.

**Q:** Describe the clinical course and features of Ménière's disease.

**A:** Peak incidence 40–60 yr. Bilateral in 35%. Classic tetrad: episodic vertigo (min to h), fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, aural fullness. Drop attacks (Tumarkin's crisis). Triggers: high salt, caffeine, stress, nicotine, alcohol. Early: fluctuating SNHL. Late: persistent tinnitus, progressive SNHL.

Ménière's results from inadequate endolymph absorption causing endolymphatic hydrops. Over time, the SNHL becomes permanent even as vertigo may diminish. Tumarkin's crisis (sudden fall without loss of consciousness) occurs due to sudden otolith organ stimulation.

**Q:** What are the medical and surgical treatment options for Ménière's disease?

**A:** Acute: bed rest, antiemetics, antivertiginous drugs (betahistine/Serc®, meclizine, diphenhydramine), anticholinergics. Long-term medical: low-salt diet, diuretics (HCTZ, triamterene, amiloride), Serc® prophylaxis, intratympanic gentamicin (destroys vestibular end-organ → complete SNHL), intratympanic dexamethasone. Surgical: selective vestibular neurectomy, labyrinthectomy, endolymphatic sac decompression.

Management is stepwise: lifestyle modification and diuretics first, then intratympanic therapy, then surgery. Intratympanic gentamicin ablates vestibular function but causes hearing loss. Since 35% of cases are bilateral, the contralateral ear must be monitored before ablative therapy.

**Q:** Differentiate vestibular neuronitis from labyrinthitis.

**A:** Vestibular neuronitis: inflammation of the vestibular portion of CN VIII → vertigo, N/V, imbalance WITHOUT hearing loss. Labyrinthitis: inflammation of both vestibular and cochlear portions of CN VIII → same symptoms PLUS tinnitus and hearing loss.

The key distinguishing feature is cochlear involvement. Labyrinthitis can complicate AOM, bacterial meningitis, cholesteatoma, and temporal bone fractures. Vestibular neuronitis is thought to be viral in origin.

**Q:** What are the clinical features of acute vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis?

**A:** Acute phase (1–5 days): severe vertigo, N/V, imbalance, irritative nystagmus (fast phase TOWARD affected ear), ataxia (veering toward affected side), + tinnitus/HL in labyrinthitis. Convalescent phase: imbalance and motion sickness, spontaneous nystagmus AWAY from affected side, gradual vestibular adaptation over weeks to months.

The nystagmus direction changes from irritative (toward affected ear) to the convalescent phase (away from affected ear, reflecting the loss of vestibular input). This evolution is diagnostically helpful. Vestibular exercises accelerate central compensation.

**Q:** What is the treatment of vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis?

**A:** Acute phase: bed rest, antivertiginous drugs, corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) + antivirals. Bacterial labyrinthitis: IV antibiotics, drainage of middle ear ± mastoidectomy. Convalescent phase: progressive ambulation, vestibular exercises (eye/head movements, sitting/standing/walking) to promote central compensation.

Corticosteroids help reduce vestibular nerve inflammation. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are key in the convalescent phase to promote central compensation — particularly important in the elderly, who compensate more slowly and are at greater fall risk.

**Q:** What is an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)?

**A:** A schwannoma of the vestibular portion of CN VIII. It starts in the internal auditory canal, expands into the cerebellopontine angle (CPA), and compresses the cerebellum and brainstem. It is the most common intracranial tumour causing SNHL and the most common CPA tumour.

Despite the name, acoustic neuromas arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular (not cochlear) nerve. They grow slowly, allowing compensation and explaining why true vertigo is rare. Bilateral acoustic neuromas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

**Q:** What are the clinical features of acoustic neuroma?

**A:** Usually: unilateral SNHL (chronic, progressive) or tinnitus. Dizziness/unsteadiness may occur but true vertigo is RARE (slow growth allows compensation). Late complications: facial nerve palsy (CN VII) and trigeminal sensory deficit (V1; corneal reflex). In the elderly, unilateral SNHL is acoustic neuroma until proven otherwise.

The slow growth of acoustic neuromas explains the lack of dramatic vestibular symptoms. Any adult with unexplained progressive unilateral SNHL, poor speech discrimination, or absent stapedial reflexes should have gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canal.

**Q:** How is acoustic neuroma diagnosed?

**A:** Gold standard: MRI of the internal auditory canal with gadolinium contrast. Supportive findings: audiogram (SNHL, poor speech discrimination), absent/decayed stapedial reflexes, ABR (increased 5th wave latency), vestibular tests (asymmetric caloric weakness — early sign).

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI can detect tumours as small as 1–2 mm. Asymmetric caloric weakness on electronystagmography is an early sign of unilateral vestibular dysfunction. Poor speech discrimination disproportionate to the degree of pure tone loss is a classic audiometric signature.

**Q:** What are the treatment options for acoustic neuroma?

**A:** Expectant management (watch-and-wait): small tumours or elderly patients. Definitive: surgical excision. Alternatives: gamma knife radiosurgery, radiation therapy.

Management is individualized based on tumour size, growth rate, patient age, and hearing status. Observation with serial MRI is appropriate for small tumours, especially in elderly patients. Gamma knife is increasingly used for small-to-medium tumours as an alternative to open surgery.

**Q:** What is tinnitus and how is it classified?

**A:** Tinnitus is auditory perception in the absence of acoustic stimuli, due to abnormal firing of central auditory neurons from loss of peripheral input. Classified as: subjective vs. objective, pulsatile vs. non-pulsatile, unilateral vs. bilateral.

Most tinnitus is subjective (only heard by patient) and non-pulsatile. Pulsatile tinnitus suggests a vascular cause (e.g., glomus tumour, AV malformation, venous sinus stenosis) and requires CT/MRA/MRV. Non-pulsatile unilateral tinnitus requires MRI to rule out acoustic neuroma.

**Q:** What is the investigation algorithm for tinnitus?

**A:** All: cranial nerve exam, otoscopy, auscultate for bruits, audiology. If pulsatile: CT or MRA/MRV of head and neck (rule out vascular abnormalities). If non-pulsatile and unilateral: non-contrast MRI (rule out acoustic neuroma).

The investigation is guided by tinnitus character. Pulsatile tinnitus may represent a surgically treatable vascular lesion. Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus can be the presenting symptom of acoustic neuroma, mandating imaging even in the absence of hearing loss.

**Q:** What is the natural history of tinnitus when no treatable cause is found?

**A:** 15% resolve, 20% improve, 50% remain unchanged, 15% worsen.

This natural history data is important for counselling patients. Management focuses on reassurance, sound amplification (hearing aids, white noise), tinnitus retraining therapy, and conservative measures (sleep hygiene, caffeine/alcohol reduction). SSRIs/TCAs are considered if anxiety/depression coexist.

**Q:** What is cerumen impaction, and what are its indications and contraindications for removal?

**A:** Cerumen impaction is the most common cause of CHL in those aged 15–50. Indication: totally occlusive cerumen with pain, decreased hearing, or tinnitus. Contraindications: active infection, previous ear surgery.

Cerumen is a mixture of ceruminous gland secretions, epithelial squames, dust, and debris. Risk factors include hairy/narrow canals, hearing aids, and cotton swab use. Treatment options: cerumenolytics (water is effective), irrigation (if TM intact), or manual removal.

**Q:** What are exostoses of the external auditory canal (EAC) and how do they present?

**A:** Exostoses are bony protuberances (lamellar bone) in the EAC, associated with swimming in cold water. Usually an incidental finding; if large, can cause cerumen impaction or otitis externa. Treatment only if symptomatic (frequent OE, CHL).

Cold water exposure causes periosteal irritation leading to bony proliferation in the EAC. Unlike osteomas (solitary, pedunculated), exostoses are typically multiple and broad-based. Surfer's ear (exostoses) is an important occupational/recreational hazard.

**Q:** What organisms cause acute otitis externa (OE), and what is the most common pathogen?

**A:** Bacterial (90% of OE): most common is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Others: Pseudomonas vulgaris, E. coli, Staphylococcus aureus. Fungal: Candida albicans, Aspergillus niger.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa thrives in the warm, moist environment of the ear canal and is the dominant pathogen in swimmer's ear. Treatment is with antipseudomonal topical agents (e.g., ciprofloxacin). Fungal OE often follows prolonged antibiotic use and presents with more pruritus.

**Q:** What are the clinical features that distinguish acute from chronic otitis externa?

**A:** Acute OE: otalgia, itching, fullness ± HL ± ear canal pain on chewing; ear canal edema, erythema ± otorrhea ± lymphadenitis ± cellulitis; SEVERE pinna traction tenderness and tragus pressure pain. Chronic OE: pruritus, excoriation, atrophic scaly lining ± otorrhea ± HL; wide meatus, NO pain with auricle movement; normal TM.

The hallmark of acute OE is exquisite pain on manipulation of the pinna or tragus — this distinguishes it from otitis media (where pinna traction does not worsen pain). Chronic OE results from repeated trauma, moisture, or dermatologic conditions.

**Q:** What topical agents are used to treat acute otitis externa and what is an important contraindication?

**A:** Antipseudomonal agents: ciprofloxacin or combination Ciprodex® (ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone). IMPORTANT contraindication: ototoxic topical agents (gentamicin, neomycin, neomycin/polymyxin B/hydrocortisone) must NOT be used with a perforated TM.

Topical treatment is first-line for uncomplicated OE. Ciprofloxacin-based drops are preferred as they are antipseudomonal and non-ototoxic. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, neomycin) are ototoxic to the cochlea if the TM is perforated and should be avoided when integrity cannot be confirmed.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man presents with progressive unilateral right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Audiogram shows SNHL with poor speech discrimination. Stapedial reflexes are absent on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis and what investigation is gold standard?

**A:** Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Gold standard: gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canal.

The combination of progressive unilateral SNHL, poor speech discrimination (disproportionate to hearing loss), and absent stapedial reflexes is the classic acoustic neuroma triad. In the elderly, unilateral SNHL is acoustic neuroma until proven otherwise. MRI with gadolinium detects even small tumours.

**Q:** A 35-year-old woman presents with episodic vertigo lasting 30 minutes to 2 hours, left-sided low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Audiogram confirms left SNHL. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?

**A:** Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops). First-line management: acute — antiemetics, antivertiginous drugs (betahistine, meclizine), anticholinergics; long-term — low-salt diet, diuretics (HCTZ, triamterene, amiloride), betahistine (Serc®) prophylaxis.

The classic tetrad of Ménière's is vertigo (20 min–12 h), fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Treatment is stepped: diet/lifestyle → diuretics → intratympanic therapy → surgery. Since 35% are bilateral, the contralateral ear must be monitored.

**Q:** A 25-year-old presents with sudden onset severe vertigo, vomiting, and imbalance after a flu-like illness. No hearing loss. Nystagmus is present with fast phase toward the left ear. What is the likely diagnosis and initial treatment?

**A:** Vestibular neuronitis (inflammation of vestibular CN VIII, likely viral). Nystagmus fast phase toward the AFFECTED (irritated) ear in acute phase. Initial treatment: bed rest, antivertiginous drugs, corticosteroids (methylprednisolone), antivirals.

Vestibular neuronitis presents with acute severe vertigo without hearing loss (distinguishing it from labyrinthitis). The irritative nystagmus (fast phase toward the affected ear) in the acute phase later reverses to paretic nystagmus (away from affected ear) in the convalescent phase.

**Q:** What is the Weber test lateralization rule, and what makes it more reliable than the Rinne test for detecting CHL?

**A:** Weber lateralizes IPSILATERAL to CHL (or contralateral to SNHL). Weber is more sensitive than Rinne for CHL because it only requires a >6 dB difference between ears, whereas Rinne requires a larger air-bone gap to reverse (false negative Rinne occurs when the good cochlea picks up BC vibrations in severe SNHL).

A vibrating tuning fork on the mastoid stimulates both cochleae bilaterally. In severe unilateral SNHL, the Rinne on the affected side can falsely appear negative (BC appears better than AC) because the intact opposite cochlea detects the bone-conducted sound — a false negative Rinne. Weber catches this by lateralizing to the normal ear.

**Q:** What is the differential diagnosis of nasal obstruction? List congenital and acquired causes.

**A:** Acquired: rhinitis (acute/chronic/vasomotor/allergic), rhinosinusitis, foreign bodies, enlarged turbinates, nasal polyps/inverting papilloma, malignant tumours (SCC, esthesioneuroblastoma, adenocarcinoma), septal deviation/dislocation/hematoma-abscess, adenoid hypertrophy, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, GPA, JNA. Congenital: pyriform aperture stenosis, choanal atresia, dermoid cyst, encephalocele, glioma, septal deviation/dislocation/hematoma.

Bilateral nasal obstruction in a neonate should raise immediate concern for choanal atresia, as neonates are obligate nasal breathers. Unilateral nasal obstruction with clear discharge in a child suggests a foreign body. Inverting papilloma is a benign lesion with malignant potential requiring complete excision.

**Q:** What are the neurological causes of hoarseness and how do they differ by laterality?

**A:** Central: vocal cord paralysis from CVA, MS, skull base tumours, Arnold-Chiari malformation, head injury. Peripheral unilateral: lung malignancy (most common), iatrogenic (thyroid/parathyroid surgery, carotid endarterectomy, PDA ligation). Peripheral bilateral (iatrogenic): bilateral thyroid surgery, forceps delivery. Neuromuscular: myasthenia gravis.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X) has a long course and is vulnerable to injury at multiple sites. Left-sided paralysis is more common due to the longer intrathoracic course. Bilateral vocal cord paralysis can cause airway compromise requiring urgent intervention.

**Q:** What is the diagnostic significance of a poor speech discrimination score as a predictor of hearing aid outcomes?

**A:** Poor speech discrimination score indicates significant neural degeneration. A poor score means hearing aids may NOT be the best option for the patient, as amplification cannot overcome neural processing deficits.

Hearing aids amplify sound but cannot restore neural coding fidelity. If the cochlear nerve or auditory cortex is significantly damaged, even amplified sound cannot be processed intelligibly. These patients may be better candidates for cochlear implants or other assistive devices.

**Q:** What is Kiesselbach's plexus and where is it located?

**A:** Kiesselbach's plexus is an anastomotic network of vessels on the anterior-inferior portion of the cartilaginous nasal septum (Little's area). It receives contributions from the anterior/posterior ethmoidal arteries (internal carotid), sphenopalatine artery, superior labial artery, and greater palatine artery (all from external carotid).

Kiesselbach's plexus is the most common site of anterior epistaxis. Its rich anastomotic supply from both internal and external carotid systems explains why anterior nosebleeds are so frequent. Little's area is the clinical correlate — the anterior-inferior cartilaginous septum.

**Q:** An adolescent male presents with unilateral, recurrent epistaxis. What diagnosis must be considered?

**A:** Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) — the most common benign tumour of the nasopharynx. It occurs in adolescent males and presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis.

JNA is a highly vascular, locally aggressive benign tumour arising in the nasopharynx. Despite being benign, it causes significant morbidity through recurrent epistaxis and local invasion. Biopsy is risky due to vascularity; imaging (CT/MRI) is preferred for diagnosis before surgical planning.

**Q:** What is the first-line treatment for epistaxis in the emergency setting?

**A:** Apply constant firm pressure for 15–20 minutes on the cartilaginous part of the nose (not the bony pyramid) with the patient leaning forward and the head in a neutral position. First-line topical treatment is a topical decongestant (e.g., Otrivin®).

Leaning forward prevents blood from flowing posteriorly into the airway or being swallowed (which can cause nausea/vomiting and obscure assessment). Pressure on the cartilaginous septum compresses Kiesselbach's plexus. Topical decongestants cause vasoconstriction to help achieve hemostasis.

**Q:** Why should silver nitrate cauterization never be applied to both sides of the nasal septum simultaneously?

**A:** Bilateral simultaneous cauterization risks septal perforation due to loss of septal blood supply from both sides.

The nasal septum is avascular cartilage that relies on the overlying mucoperichondrium for its blood supply. Cauterizing both sides simultaneously destroys this supply bilaterally, causing avascular necrosis and septal perforation — a serious complication.

**Q:** What type of nasal packing is preferred for patients with coagulopathy or on anticoagulation who require nasal packing for epistaxis?

**A:** Lubricated absorbable packing (e.g., Gelfoam wrapped in Surgicel®) is preferred to prevent recurrent epistaxis caused by packing removal, which can disrupt newly formed clot.

Conventional packing (Merocel®, Rapid Rhino®) is non-absorbable and must be removed, risking re-bleeding in coagulopathic patients. Absorbable materials dissolve in situ, eliminating the trauma of removal and the risk of dislodging a fragile clot.

**Q:** What are the complications of posterior nasal packing for epistaxis?

**A:** Hypoxemia (nasopulmonary reflex), toxic shock syndrome, pharyngeal fibrosis/stenosis, alar/septal necrosis, and aspiration.

Posterior packs are associated with more serious complications than anterior packs. The nasopulmonary reflex (posterior pack stimulates a vagal response causing bronchospasm and hypoxemia) mandates hospital admission and monitoring. Packs left >48 hours or any posterior pack require prophylactic antibiotics against toxic shock syndrome.

**Q:** When are antibiotics indicated for nasal packing in epistaxis management?

**A:** Antibiotics are required for any posterior nasal pack OR any anterior pack left in place for >48 hours, due to risk of toxic shock syndrome.

Nasal packs create an anaerobic environment that can promote S. aureus colonization and toxin production, leading to toxic shock syndrome. This is particularly true with prolonged packing. Canadian guidelines recommend antibiotic prophylaxis in these scenarios.

**Q:** What surgical and interventional options are available when anterior/posterior nasal packs fail to control epistaxis?

**A:** Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation + anterior ethmoid artery ligation (by otolaryngology) OR embolization of the culprit arterial supply (by interventional radiology). Septoplasty may also be added.

Sphenopalatine artery ligation addresses the dominant posterior supply. Anterior ethmoid artery ligation addresses the superior anterior supply. Embolization is an alternative that preserves the artery but blocks flow. These are used when packing fails or is not tolerated.

**Q:** Define dysphonia vs. aphonia.

**A:** Dysphonia: a general alteration in voice quality (including hoarseness and voice weakness). Aphonia: no sound emanates from the vocal folds.

Hoarseness is the subjective perception of voice harshness or weakness. Dysphonia is broader and encompasses all voice quality changes. Aphonia represents complete loss of voice. Both reflect abnormalities anywhere along the vocal tract from oral cavity to lungs. Hoarseness persisting >2 weeks requires evaluation to rule out malignancy.

**Q:** Hoarseness present for more than 2 weeks requires what evaluation?

**A:** Laryngoscopy to rule out malignancy (e.g., laryngeal carcinoma).

Persistent hoarseness (>2 weeks) is a red flag symptom in otolaryngology. While most causes are benign (chronic laryngitis, nodules, polyps), laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma must be excluded via direct or flexible laryngoscopy. This is a key Canadian clinical threshold.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of acute laryngitis?

**A:** Infectious causes, most commonly viral (influenza, adenovirus, HSV).

Acute laryngitis is defined as <2 weeks of inflammatory changes in the laryngeal mucosa. Viral infection is the most common trigger. Mechanical causes (voice strain), environmental irritants (toxic fume inhalation), and bacterial infections (Group A Streptococcus) are other etiologies.

**Q:** What are the treatment principles for acute laryngitis?

**A:** Usually self-limited (resolves in 1–2 weeks). Treatment: voice rest, humidification, hydration, avoid irritants (smoking, caffeine). Add antibiotics if concurrent bacterial pharyngitis; add PPI if reflux is contributing.

The mainstay of acute laryngitis management is supportive. Because viral etiology is most common, antibiotics are not routinely indicated. GERD is a recognized precipitant/aggravator and PPIs can help in that context. Steroids are not standard for acute laryngitis unless airway compromise exists.

**Q:** What is the position of a paralyzed vocal cord in unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy, and what are the consequences?

**A:** The affected cord lies in the paramedian position, causing inadequate glottic closure → breathy voice and aspiration risk. Usually medializes with time, improving phonation and aspiration. Treatment options: voice therapy, injection laryngoplasty (e.g., Radiesse), or thyroplasty/nerve reinnervation.

The RLN innervates all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Paralysis causes the cord to assume the paramedian (adducted/abducted intermediate) position. The contralateral cord may compensate by crossing the midline. Injection laryngoplasty medializes the cord to improve voice and swallow.

**Q:** What are the respiratory consequences of bilateral vocal cord paralysis, and how is it managed?

**A:** Both cords rest near the midline → airway obstruction → stridor. If no respiratory compromise, monitor for improvement. If airway is compromised, surgical options include vocal cord lateralization, arytenoidectomy, posterior costal cartilage graft, or tracheotomy.

Bilateral RLN palsy is an airway emergency if the cords are adducted (midline). Paradoxically, phonation may be preserved if the cords are close to the midline. Management prioritizes airway over voice quality. Selective nerve reinnervation (Marie Technique) may restore movement in experienced hands.

**Q:** What are the systemic and local causes of chronic laryngitis?

**A:** Local: repeated acute laryngitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with postnasal drip, chronic voice strain, chronic irritants (dust, smoke, chemicals), alcohol. Systemic: GERD, Zenker's diverticulum, hiatal hernia, allergy, hypothyroidism, Addison's disease.

Chronic laryngitis (>3 weeks) has multiple etiologies. GERD is a particularly important and treatable systemic cause — acid reflux causes posterior laryngeal erythema and granuloma formation. Hypothyroidism causes myxedematous changes to the vocal cord mucosa. All causes should be addressed to prevent malignant transformation.

**Q:** Contrast vocal cord polyps vs. vocal cord nodules in terms of laterality, onset, and characteristics.

**A:** Polyps: unilateral, asymmetric, acute onset, may resolve spontaneously, soft/smooth/pedunculated, subepithelial capillary breakage. Nodules: bilateral, symmetric, gradual onset, chronic course, bilateral at anterior 1/3–posterior 2/3 junction, early = hemorrhagic, chronic = hard, white, fibrosed.

This distinction is clinically and therapeutically important. Polyps result from acute subepithelial vascular injury during extreme vocal exertion. Nodules result from chronic repetitive micro-trauma (vocal abuse) leading to callus formation at the point of maximum cord vibration. Treatment differs: polyps may require surgery; nodules are primarily treated with voice therapy.

**Q:** What is the primary treatment for vocal cord nodules?

**A:** Voice rest and voice therapy (primary treatment). Add hydration and avoidance of irritants. Surgery is rarely indicated and only for refractory nodules.

Vocal cord nodules are a behavioral disorder — they result from chronic vocal misuse/abuse. Voice therapy addresses the underlying vocal behaviors and is curative in most cases. Surgery is generally avoided as a first-line treatment because nodules recur unless the vocal behavior is corrected.

**Q:** Vocal cord nodules are found at what specific location on laryngoscopy?

**A:** Bilateral symmetric nodules at the junction of the anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of the vocal cords — the point of maximal cord vibration.

This is a high-yield anatomical fact. The anterior 1/3–posterior 2/3 junction is where vibratory stress is greatest during phonation, making it the site of nodule formation. Finding bilateral symmetric lesions at this precise location is pathognomonic of vocal cord nodules (vs. polyps, which are typically unilateral).

**Q:** What HPV types cause recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP)?

**A:** Most commonly HPV types 6 and 11. Types 16, 18, 31, and 33 can also be responsible.

HPV 6 and 11 cause the benign condylomatous lesions of RRP. HPV 16 and 18 (high-risk oncogenic types) are associated with malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. RRP is thought to be acquired during vaginal delivery (vertical transmission), with possible hormonal influence.

**Q:** What is the most common laryngeal tumour in children?

**A:** Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) — caused by HPV (types 6, 11).

RRP has a biphasic distribution: juvenile-onset (birth to puberty) and adult-onset (>12 yr). The juvenile form is the most common laryngeal tumour in children. It presents with progressive hoarseness, stridor, and respiratory distress. While benign, it has high recurrence and can seed the tracheobronchial tree.

**Q:** What is the gold standard treatment for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP)?

**A:** Suspension microlaryngoscopy with laser removal (preferably CO2 or KTP laser) with preservation of normal mucosa. This is NOT curative; the goal is improvement in voice and/or breathing.

RRP is highly resistant to complete removal and has a high tendency for recurrence. The goal of surgery is to improve function, not achieve cure. If >4 surgeries/year are required, adjuvant systemic therapy is considered: quadrivalent HPV vaccine, bevacizumab, cidofovir, interferon, or indole-3-carbinol.

**Q:** What is sialadenitis and what are the most common causative organisms?

**A:** Sialadenitis is inflammation of the salivary glands. Most commonly viral (mumps). Bacterial causes include S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae.

Obstructive sialadenitis results from salivary stasis (e.g., sialolithiasis, duct stenosis) with retrograde bacterial flow. Non-obstructive forms include viral (mumps — bilateral parotitis + SNHL + orchitis) and immune-mediated (Sjögren's). Treatment mnemonic: MASH — Massage, Antibiotics, Sialogogues, Heat/Hydration.

**Q:** What is the MASH mnemonic for sialadenitis treatment?

**A:** M – Massage; A – Analgesics/Antibiotics; S – Sialogogues (agents that stimulate saliva, e.g., lemon candies); H – Heat/Hydration.

This mnemonic covers the conservative management of sialadenitis. If bacterial infection is confirmed, cloxacillin is added. Abscess drainage is required if a fluctuant abscess forms. Bilateral parotid enlargement should prompt evaluation for systemic causes (mumps, HIV, Sjögren's, eating disorders).

**Q:** What are the predisposing factors for sialadenitis?

**A:** HIV, anorexia/bulimia, Sjögren's syndrome, Cushing's syndrome, hypothyroidism, DM, hepatic/renal failure, sialolithiasis, and medications that increase stasis (diuretics, TCAs, beta-blockers, anticholinergics, antibiotics).

Any condition reducing salivary flow creates stasis and increases risk of ascending bacterial infection. Medications with anticholinergic effects are a common and often overlooked cause. Anorexia/bulimia causes parotid hypertrophy from repeated purging (Stensen's duct reflux).

**Q:** What percentage of sialolithiasis (salivary duct stones) occurs in the submandibular gland, and why?

**A:** 80% of salivary stones occur in the submandibular gland. This is because submandibular saliva is more alkaline, mucous, and calcium-rich, and Wharton's duct is longer, wider, and drains against gravity.

The submandibular gland's anatomy and secretion properties favor stone formation. The classic presentation is intermittent painful swelling of the submandibular gland related to meals (when salivary flow increases). Parotid gland accounts for <20% of cases; sublingual gland ~1%.

**Q:** What is the investigation of choice for sialolithiasis?

**A:** Ultrasound (U/S) is first-line. If a stone is identified, CT is used for precise localization. Sialogram may also be considered.

U/S is non-invasive and effectively identifies most submandibular stones. CT provides precise 3D localization to guide surgical planning. Sialography (contrast injection into the duct) can outline the ductal system and demonstrate filling defects but is less commonly used.

**Q:** What is the distribution of salivary gland neoplasms, and what is the most common benign and malignant type in the parotid?

**A:** Parotid 70–85%, submandibular 8–15%, sublingual 1%, minor salivary glands 5–8%. Parotid: 80% benign (most common: pleomorphic adenoma), 20% malignant (most common: mucoepidermoid carcinoma). Warthin's tumour is the 2nd most common benign parotid tumour.

The 'rule of 80s' for parotid: 80% of all salivary gland tumours are in the parotid; 80% of parotid tumours are benign; the most common benign tumour is pleomorphic adenoma. Inversely, the smaller the gland, the higher the likelihood of malignancy (minor salivary glands: >80% malignant).

**Q:** What clinical feature of a parotid mass increases suspicion for malignancy?

**A:** Facial nerve involvement (facial paralysis/paresis) is a sign of malignancy in a parotid mass.

The facial nerve (CN VII) traverses the parotid gland and divides within it. Malignant parotid tumours may invade the nerve, causing facial weakness or paralysis. Bilateral parotid masses suggest a benign process (Warthin's tumour, Sjögren's, bulimia, mumps) or lymphoma. A mass above the line from tragus to mandibular angle is a parotid lesion until proven otherwise.

**Q:** Why are pleomorphic adenomas excised rather than observed?

**A:** Pleomorphic adenomas have a 5% risk of malignant transformation over a prolonged period of time.

Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumour) is the most common salivary gland neoplasm. Despite its benign nature, it carries a risk of malignant transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma. Additionally, incomplete excision leads to seeding and recurrence. Incisional biopsy is contraindicated — it risks seeding and should not be performed.

**Q:** What is Frey's syndrome and why does it occur?

**A:** Frey's syndrome is gustatory sweating (sweating of the preauricular skin during eating) that occurs as a postoperative complication of parotid surgery. It is caused by damaged parasympathetic nerve fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve regenerating into the sweat glands of the skin.

Normally, the auriculotemporal nerve (branch of CN V3) carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland. After parotidectomy, these regenerating fibres aberrantly innervate the overlying skin's eccrine sweat glands, causing sweating in response to salivary stimuli (eating/smelling food).

**Q:** What is the approach to evaluating a neck mass by age?

**A:** In patients <40 years: most likely inflammatory > congenital/developmental > neoplastic. In patients >40 years: most likely neoplastic > inflammatory > congenital. Any neck mass persisting >2 weeks should be investigated for neoplastic causes.

This age-based prioritization is a key MCCQE1 clinical framework. In young patients, reactive lymphadenopathy from infection dominates. In older patients, malignancy (lymphoma, metastatic squamous cell carcinoma, salivary gland tumours, thyroid cancer) must be the leading concern until proven otherwise.

**Q:** What distinguishes an inflammatory from a neoplastic neck mass on history and physical?

**A:** Inflammatory: painful, rapid onset, tender on exam, rubbery. Neoplastic: painless, longer duration (weeks–months), non-tender, rock-hard, immobile/fixed.

These features guide the initial differential. However, lymphoma can present with a rubbery, painless mass, blurring this distinction. Tender nodes can occasionally be malignant (if rapidly growing with central necrosis). Clinical suspicion combined with appropriate investigations (FNA, CT, CBC) is essential.

**Q:** What is the most common congenital neck mass in children?

**A:** Thyroglossal duct cyst — the most common congenital cervical anomaly.

Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline remnants of the tract made by the thyroid as it descends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to its final position in the neck. They classically elevate with swallowing and tongue protrusion. Treatment is the Sistrunk procedure.

**Q:** Describe the classic features of a thyroglossal duct cyst.

**A:** Midline neck cyst (suprahyoid or infrahyoid) that enlarges with URTIs, elevates with swallowing AND tongue protrusion, may cause dysphagia or globus sensation. Usually presents in childhood or ages 20–40.

The pathognomonic feature is elevation with tongue protrusion (due to the fibrous cord connecting the cyst to the foramen cecum at the tongue base). This distinguishes it from other midline neck masses. The cyst often becomes inflamed during URTIs due to its connection with the pharynx.

**Q:** What surgical procedure is used to treat thyroglossal duct cysts, and what does it involve?

**A:** The Sistrunk procedure: complete excision of the cyst, the fibrous cord/tract up to the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue, AND removal of the central portion of the hyoid bone.

Simple cyst excision has a high recurrence rate (~50%). The Sistrunk procedure reduces recurrence to <3% by ensuring complete tract excision including the hyoid bone segment (which the tract passes through). Preoperative antibiotics should be given to reduce inflammation and minimize recurrence risk.

**Q:** What is the most common branchial cleft anomaly, and how does it present?

**A:** 2nd branchial cleft malformation is most common. Sinuses/fistulae present in infancy as a small opening anterior to the SCM. Cysts present as a smooth, painless, slowly enlarging lateral neck mass, often following a URTI.

Branchial cleft anomalies result from failure of obliteration of embryonic branchial clefts/pouches. They fall into three types: fistula (opens to skin and GI tract), sinus (blind-ended), and cyst (closed). 2nd branchial cleft anomalies are by far most common. Treatment is surgical excision after infection resolves.
