**Q:** What is the pathognomonic finding for a 3rd branchial cleft anomaly on CT?

**A:** Air on CT scan in or near the thyroid gland, associated with recurrent thyroiditis or thyroid abscess. The tract typically leads to the left pyriform sinus.

3rd branchial cleft anomalies are rare and present as recurrent left-sided thyroiditis or thyroid abscess. The connection to the pyriform sinus allows communication between the pharynx and thyroid, explaining recurrent infections. Air in the thyroid on CT is pathognomonic.

**Q:** What are the premalignant lesions of the oral cavity and their risk of malignant transformation?

**A:** Lichen planus: 5–10% risk (follow-up every 6–12 months). Leukoplakia: 5–20% risk (follow-up every 3–12 months). Erythroplakia: associated with carcinoma in situ or invasive tumour in 40% of cases (highest risk).

Erythroplakia carries the highest malignant potential of the three. Leukoplakia is a white keratotic plaque that cannot be rubbed off (distinguishing it from candidiasis). Dysplasia involving the entire mucosal thickness = carcinoma in situ, which has 15–30% progression to invasive cancer.

**Q:** What is the treatment of choice for lichen planus of the oral mucosa?

**A:** Topical corticosteroids (first-line); topical calcineurin inhibitors (second-line). Follow-up every 6–12 months due to 5–10% malignant transformation risk.

Oral lichen planus presents as lacy white lines (Wickham's striae) with surrounding erythema. The exact cause is unknown but is thought to be immune-mediated (T-cell lymphocyte attack on basal keratinocytes). Symptomatic lesions require treatment; asymptomatic cases need surveillance.

**Q:** What is the general treatment principle for head and neck malignancies by anatomic site?

**A:** Oral cavity: primary surgery with radiotherapy reserved for salvage/poor prognostic indicators. Nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx: primary radiotherapy with surgery reserved for salvage. Advanced (T4) pharyngeal/laryngeal cancer: surgery is standard of care. Metastatic: palliative chemotherapy.

The anatomic site dictates primary treatment modality. Oral cavity tumours are generally resected because they are accessible and well-defined. Laryngeal and pharyngeal tumours are often treated with radiotherapy to preserve function. Laser endoscopic surgery (transoral) is an option for early-stage laryngeal cancer.

**Q:** What is the epidemiology and key risk factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma?

**A:** 90% SCC. Mean age: 50–59 yr; M:F = 2.4:1. 100-fold increased incidence in Southern Chinese. Key risk factors: EBV infection, salted fish consumption, nickel exposure. Poor oral hygiene also contributes.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has a striking geographic and ethnic distribution, highly prevalent in Southern China and Southeast Asia. EBV is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis, particularly for the undifferentiated (non-keratinizing) subtype. EBV serology is used in screening in endemic regions.

**Q:** What proportion of oropharyngeal cancers (OPC) are attributable to HPV, and how does HPV status affect prognosis?

**A:** Up to 70% of OPC are attributable to HPV (primarily HPV-16). HPV+ OPC patients have significantly better prognosis: 82.4% vs. 51.1% 3-year overall survival and a 58% reduction in risk of death compared to HPV-negative tumours.

The rising incidence of HPV-associated OPC (225% increase from 1988–2004) has shifted the epidemiology of head and neck cancer. HPV+ OPC patients tend to be younger (~10 years), non-smokers, with better treatment response. HPV vaccination (quadrivalent) is a key prevention strategy, independent of smoking and alcohol exposure.

**Q:** What is the most common site of laryngeal carcinoma, and what is the gender predominance?

**A:** Glottic larynx (60–65% of laryngeal cancers). Laryngeal cancer has a strong male predominance (M:F = 10:1). Primary risk factors: smoking and alcohol.

Laryngeal cancers arise in three sites: supraglottic (30–35%), glottic (60–65%), and subglottic (1%). Glottic tumours present early (hoarseness) because the vocal cords are directly involved. Supraglottic tumours have poorer prognosis due to late presentation and rich lymphatic drainage. Laryngeal cancer accounts for 45% of all H&N cancers.

**Q:** What is the rule regarding the likelihood of malignancy and salivary gland size?

**A:** The smaller the salivary gland, the greater the likelihood that a mass in that gland is malignant. Parotid: 15–25% malignant; submandibular: 37–43% malignant; minor salivary glands: >80% malignant.

This inverse relationship between gland size and malignancy risk is a key MCCQE1 high-yield fact. While the parotid contains most salivary gland tumours, the vast majority are benign. A sublingual or minor salivary gland mass carries very high malignancy risk and demands urgent investigation.

**Q:** What is the most common malignant salivary gland tumour overall?

**A:** Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (40% of malignant salivary gland tumours), followed by adenoid cystic carcinoma (30%), acinic cell carcinoma (5%), and malignant mixed tumour (5%).

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is also the most common malignant tumour of the parotid. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural invasion and late distant metastases (even decades later). Salivary gland malignancies are associated with radiation exposure as a key risk factor.

**Q:** What is the role of panendoscopy in head and neck oncology?

**A:** Panendoscopy (nasopharyngoscopy, laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy with washings and biopsy) is used to identify the primary tumour when cervical lymph node metastasis is identified (unknown primary). The primary is found ~95% of the time.

When a patient presents with a cervical lymph node containing SCC with no obvious primary, panendoscopy is performed to identify the occult primary tumour in the upper aerodigestive tract. If the primary remains occult (~5%), excisional biopsy of the node for histologic diagnosis guides management (radiotherapy ± neck dissection).

**Q:** What targeted therapy is used for advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck?

**A:** Anti-EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) treatment — cetuximab or panitumumab — as concurrent therapy with radiation for advanced local and regional SCC of the head and neck.

EGFR is overexpressed in most H&N SCC. Cetuximab (a monoclonal antibody against EGFR) improves survival when added to radiation in advanced disease. It is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate cisplatin-based chemoradiation. Concomitant chemotherapy also increases survival in advanced disease.

**Q:** What is the most common risk factor for hypopharyngeal carcinoma, and what is the most common subsitite?

**A:** Smoking and alcohol (synergistic) are the primary risk factors. The most common subsite is the pyriform sinus (60%), followed by the postcricoid region (30%) and posterior pharyngeal wall (10%).

Hypopharyngeal cancers have poor prognosis due to late presentation. They account for 8–10% of all H&N cancers, predominantly affecting males aged 50–70 years. Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron-deficiency dysphagia with esophageal webbing) is associated with postcricoid carcinoma in women.

**Q:** What imaging modality is superior for detecting pathologic cervical lymph nodes and bone cortex invasion in head and neck cancer?

**A:** CT scan is superior to MRI for detecting pathologic nodal disease and bone cortex invasion.

While CT excels at detecting cortical bone invasion and lymph node size/morphology, MRI is superior for discriminating tumour from mucus, detecting bone marrow invasion (medullary spread), and soft tissue characterization. PET scans have an emerging role in H&N neoplasm staging and surveillance.

**Q:** What size criteria define pathologically enlarged cervical lymph nodes?

**A:** Jugulodigastric node >1.5 cm in diameter; retropharyngeal node >0.8 cm in diameter; any node of any size with central necrosis.

Lymph node size alone is imperfect for detecting metastasis. Central necrosis on imaging (seen as a low-density center on CT) is highly specific for metastatic SCC. Retropharyngeal nodes have smaller threshold criteria because they are not normally visible on imaging.

**Q:** What is lymphatic (cystic hygroma) / venolymphatic malformation, and how does its size affect treatment?

**A:** Lymphatic malformations arise from vestigial lymph channels. Macrocystic lesions: soft, painless, compressible, treated by surgical excision or sclerotherapy (doxycycline). Microcystic lesions: noncompressible with mucosal/skin vesicles, difficult to treat — debulking or bleomycin sclerotherapy.

Lymphatic malformations (cystic hygroma) usually present by age 2. They can regress spontaneously after bacterial infection, so surgical intervention should be delayed several months after infection. Sudden enlargement after infection or trauma is a characteristic feature that may cause airway compromise requiring urgent intervention.

**Q:** What is the most common site of oral cavity cancer, and what are its key risk factors?

**A:** Most common site: anterior 2/3 of the tongue (50% of oral cavity cancers). Risk factors: smoking, alcohol, poor oral hygiene, leukoplakia, erythroplakia, lichen planus, chronic inflammation, HPV, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, sun exposure (lip), genetic factors.

Oral cavity SCC (95% of oral cavity cancers) is treated primarily with surgery. The tongue is the most common site, and early lesions of the oral tongue have a good prognosis with surgery. Risk factors are additive; smoking and alcohol have a synergistic relationship in causing oral cavity cancers.

**Q:** What are the 5-year survival rates for oral cavity cancer by T-stage?

**A:** T1/T2: 75%; T3/T4: 30-35%

Oral cavity cancer prognosis is stage-dependent. Poor prognostic indicators include depth of invasion, close surgical margins, and location (tongue has worse prognosis than floor of mouth). Primary treatment is surgery with local resection ± neck dissection ± reconstruction, with secondary radiation.

**Q:** What is the primary treatment for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC)?

**A:** Primary radiation + chemoradiation; surgery reserved for limited or recurrent disease

NPC commonly presents with cervical nodes (60-90%), nasal obstruction, unilateral otitis media with hearing loss, and cranial nerve involvement (III-VI, IX-XII). 5-year survival: T1=79%, T2=77%, T3=50-60%, T4=36-42%.

**Q:** How does HPV status affect oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) prognosis?

**A:** HPV-positive OPC has significantly better outcomes: Stage I 92%, II 87%, III 74%, IV 40% vs. HPV-negative: Stage I 70%, II 58%, III 50%, IV 30%

HPV+ OPC predominantly arises at the base of tongue or tonsillar region. HPV status is determined via RT-PCR (presence of HPV DNA) and p16 overexpression. HPV+ patients are candidates for therapy de-intensification. Transoral robotic surgery has an emerging role.

**Q:** What are the Bethesda categories for thyroid FNA cytology and their associated malignancy risk?

**A:** I Non-diagnostic: 1-4%; II Benign: 0-3%; III Follicular lesion of undetermined significance/AUS: 5-15%; IV Follicular neoplasm: 15-30%; V Suspicious for malignancy: 60-75%; VI Malignant: 97-99%

The Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (TBSRTC) guides management decisions. Categories III-IV often require molecular testing (BRAF, microRNA classifiers) to distinguish high-risk from low-risk nodules and decide whether surgery is needed.

**Q:** Compare the key features of the 5 types of thyroid carcinoma (papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic, lymphoma).

**A:** Papillary (90-92%): lymphatic spread, orphan Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies, positive I-131 uptake, 98% 10-yr survival. Follicular (4-6%): hematogenous spread, capsular/vascular invasion, NOT diagnosable by FNA, 92% 10-yr survival. Medullary (1-2%): associated MEN IIa/IIb, secretes calcitonin, amyloid stroma, 55-80% 5-yr survival Stage I. Anaplastic (<1%): elderly, giant cells/spindle cells, rapid enlarging mass, rapidly fatal. Lymphoma (<1%): associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis (60x risk), diffuse large B-cell most common, non-surgical treatment (CHOP).

Papillary is the most common and has the best prognosis. Follicular cancer is notable for hematogenous spread to lung/bone and cannot be diagnosed by FNA alone (requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion). Medullary cancer can be hereditary (MEN IIa: RET mutation) and requires median/lateral neck dissection based on calcitonin levels. Anaplastic carries the worst prognosis.

**Q:** What is the TI-RADS classification and when is FNA indicated?

**A:** TR1 (0 pts): benign, no FNA. TR2 (2 pts): not suspicious, no FNA. TR3 (3 pts): mildly suspicious, FNA if ≥2.5 cm, follow-up if ≥1.5 cm. TR4 (4-6 pts): moderately suspicious, FNA if ≥1.5 cm, follow-up if ≥1 cm. TR5 (≥7 pts): highly suspicious, FNA if ≥1 cm, follow-up if >0.5 cm.

The ACR Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) uses features including composition, echogenicity, shape, margin, and echogenic foci to score thyroid nodules. Higher scores indicate greater suspicion for malignancy and lower size thresholds for FNA.

**Q:** What are the indications for radioiodine (I-131) therapy in thyroid disease?

**A:** Treatment of hyperthyroidism; adjuvant treatment after surgery for intermediate-to-high-risk papillary or follicular carcinoma

Radioiodine therapy targets thyroid tissue that takes up iodine. For well-differentiated thyroid cancers, postoperative I-131 scanning guides further treatment. Medullary and anaplastic carcinomas do not take up iodine and are not treated with I-131.

**Q:** What is the definition of acute otitis media (AOM) and what is the primary etiology?

**A:** AOM = infection of middle ear space with both presence of middle ear effusion/inflammation (MEE/MEI) AND acute onset of symptoms. Primary defect: Eustachian tube dysfunction/obstruction leading to stasis and pathogen colonization. Most common bacteria: S. pneumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.

AOM is the most frequent diagnosis in sick children and the most common reason for antibiotic prescription. Peak incidence is 6-15 months. Bacterial and viral co-infections are common. Viral pathogens include RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, and rhinovirus.

**Q:** What are the criteria for watchful waiting vs. immediate antibiotics in pediatric AOM?

**A:** Watchful waiting (24-48h): healthy child >6 months with unilateral, non-severe AOM (mild illness, otalgia mild, fever <39°C, <48h symptoms). Immediate antibiotics: infant <6 months; moderately/severely ill; fever ≥39°C; symptoms >48h; immunocompromised; craniofacial abnormalities; perforated TM with purulent drainage.

This reflects Canadian evidence-based guidelines. If not improved or worsening at 24-48h follow-up, treat with antimicrobials. For severe or bilateral AOM with MEE and bulging TM, antimicrobials should be started immediately regardless of age.

**Q:** What is the first-line antibiotic treatment for AOM, and what are alternatives for penicillin allergy?

**A:** First-line (no penicillin allergy): high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/d divided BID. Penicillin allergy (first-line alternatives): azithromycin 10 mg/kg or clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/d divided BID. If initial therapy fails (no improvement after 2-3 days): high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate 45-60 mg/kg/d.

Duration: 5-day course for most children >2 years with uncomplicated AOM; 10-day course for children 6-24 months, perforated TM, or recurrent AOM. Failure of first-line therapy suggests beta-lactamase-producing organisms (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) requiring amoxicillin-clavulanate.

**Q:** What is the most common complication of AOM, and what are the major intracranial complications?

**A:** Most common complication: mastoiditis. Intracranial complications: meningitis, epidural/brain abscess, subdural empyema, lateral and cavernous sinus thrombosis, sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis, carotid artery thrombosis, facial nerve paralysis.

Extracranial complications include hearing loss, TM perforation, cholesteatoma, facial nerve palsy, middle ear atelectasis, ossicular necrosis, and vestibular dysfunction. Other complications include postauricular abscess and Bezold's abscess (extension to neck).

**Q:** What are the criteria for tympanostomy tube insertion in children?

**A:** Recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months OR ≥4 episodes in 12 months with ≥1 in recent 6 months) with unilateral or bilateral MEE at time of reassessment; Chronic bilateral OME and documented hearing loss ≥25 dB after ≥3 months with symptoms attributable to OME; At-risk children (permanent HL, speech/language delay, ASD, craniofacial disorders) with unilateral or bilateral OME with type B tympanogram or persistent effusion >3 months.

Per Canadian/AAO clinical practice guidelines on tympanostomy tubes. Evidence shows tubes improve hearing threshold by ~9 dB at 1-3 months vs. watchful waiting, and reduce recurrent AOM episodes, but benefit diminishes by 12-24 months.

**Q:** What is otitis media with effusion (OME) and how does it differ from AOM?

**A:** OME = presence of fluid in the middle ear WITHOUT signs or symptoms of acute infection. AOM requires both MEE/MEI AND acute onset symptoms (otalgia, fever). OME presents with conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, amber/dull grey TM with immobility on pneumatic otoscopy, and meniscus fluid level.

OME is the most common cause of pediatric hearing loss. 90% of children clear fluid within 3 months following AOM. Watchful waiting for 3 months is recommended before considering surgery. Intranasal steroids, systemic antibiotics, antihistamines, and decongestants are NOT recommended.

**Q:** What is adenoid facies and what causes it?

**A:** Adenoid facies = characteristic facial appearance from chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy: open-mouthed appearance, high arched palate, dental crowding, hypoplastic maxilla, pinched nostrils, short upper lip, and elongated face.

Adenoid hypertrophy peaks around age 5-7 and typically resolves by age 12 (self-resolving due to age-related atrophy). Graded 0 (absent) to 4+ (>75% obstruction). Complications include Eustachian tube obstruction causing serous otitis media, sleep apnea, and orofacial developmental abnormalities.

**Q:** What are the PSG (polysomnography) criteria for OSA severity in children vs. adults?

**A:** Children: AHI >1/h abnormal; mild 2-4/h, moderate 6-10/h, severe >10/h. Adults: mild 5.1-15/h, moderate 15.1-30/h, severe >30.1/h.

Children have a lower threshold for abnormality (AHI >1/h vs. >5/h in adults) because children normally have near-absent apneas during sleep. Pediatric OSA peaks at age 2-8 years when tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the pharyngeal airway.

**Q:** What is the surgical treatment of choice for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)?

**A:** Bilateral tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy

If OSA persists after tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy, consider adenoid regrowth. For refractory cases not tolerant of CPAP/BiPAP, options include lingual tonsillectomy, midline posterior glossectomy, tongue suspension, or other surgeries targeting resistance sites, guided by drug-induced sleep endoscopy or cine-MRI.

**Q:** What is the classic triad (Quinsy triad) of peritonsillar abscess and what is the most reliable diagnostic sign?

**A:** Quinsy triad: trismus, uvular deviation, dysphonia ('hot potato voice'). Most reliable indicator: trismus (due to irritation and reflex spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle).

Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is most common in 15-30 year olds. Most common causative organism is Group A Streptococcus (50%). Complications include aspiration pneumonia (spontaneous rupture), airway obstruction, lateral dissection into parapharyngeal/carotid space, bacteremia, and retropharyngeal abscess.

**Q:** How is peritonsillar abscess treated?

**A:** Secure airway; surgical drainage (incision or needle aspiration with C&S); empiric PO antibiotics for 14-day course; IV penicillin G x10d if GAS on cultures; add PO/IV metronidazole or clindamycin x10d if Bacteroides positive; warm saline irrigation; consider elective tonsillectomy after resolution.

Tonsillectomy may be deferred until after a second episode. The recurrence rate of peritonsillar abscess after needle aspiration alone is higher than after tonsillectomy, but tonsillectomy carries surgical risks.

**Q:** What are the absolute indications for tonsillectomy?

**A:** Sleep-disordered breathing (most common); recurrent tonsillitis (second most common); tonsillar hypertrophy causing upper airway obstruction, OSA, severe dysphagia, or cardiopulmonary complications (cor pulmonale); suspicion of malignancy (lymphoma, SCC); orofacial/dental deformity; hemorrhagic tonsillitis.

The Paradise Criteria define relative indications: ≥7 tonsillitis episodes in past year, or ≥5 per year for 2 years, or ≥3 per year for 3 years, each with documented sore throat plus one of: fever >38.3°C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive GAS test.

**Q:** What are the Paradise Criteria for tonsillectomy?

**A:** Recurrent tonsillitis with: ≥7 episodes in the past year, OR ≥5 episodes per year for 2 years, OR ≥3 episodes per year for 3 years. Each episode must have documented sore throat with ≥1 of: temperature >38.3°C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive test for Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus.

These are relative (not absolute) indications for tonsillectomy to reduce disease burden. The absolute most common indication is sleep-disordered breathing. Hemorrhage (primary within 24h, secondary within 7-10 days) is the major complication of tonsillectomy.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of stridor in neonates/infants?

**A:** Laryngomalacia — the most common cause of stridor in children

Laryngomalacia results from supraglottic collapse during inspiration due to immature or floppy laryngeal cartilage. It typically worsens in the supine position and with feeding. Most cases resolve spontaneously by 12-18 months. Vocal cord palsy (birth trauma or Arnold-Chiari malformation) is the second most common cause.

**Q:** How does the quality and timing of stridor indicate the level of airway obstruction?

**A:** Inspiratory stridor: vocal cords (glottis) or above (supraglottis). Biphasic stridor: glottis, subglottis, or extrathoracic trachea. Expiratory stridor: distal tracheobronchial tree.

Body position is also informative: stridor worse prone suggests double aortic arch; worse supine suggests laryngomalacia or glossoptosis. Biphasic stridor indicates a fixed obstruction at or below the glottis and is more ominous than purely inspiratory stridor.

**Q:** What is acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)? What is the most common cause?

**A:** Croup = inflammation of subglottic space and tracheobronchial tree with mucosal swelling and thick mucopurulent exudate compromising upper airway. Most common cause: parainfluenza type I virus. Croup is the most common infectious cause of stridor in children.

Croup affects children 6 months to 5 years, peaking in fall/winter. Classic presentation: preceded by URTI, worse at night, 'seal-bark' croupy cough, inspiratory or biphasic stridor, sternal/intercostal indrawing. 'Steeple sign' (narrow subglottis) on AP neck X-ray.

**Q:** What is the treatment of croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis)?

**A:** Nebulized epinephrine q1-2h PRN (if severe, Westley Croup Score >2); systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg or prednisone); humidified oxygen and hydration; close observation 3-4h; hospitalize if poor response after 4h with persistent stridor at rest; intubation if severe (use smaller ETT than expected for age).

Corticosteroids reduce mucosal edema and are the mainstay of treatment for moderate-to-severe croup. Nebulized epinephrine provides rapid but transient relief (rebound effect possible). Recurrent croup should prompt evaluation for subglottic stenosis with bronchoscopy.

**Q:** How does acute epiglottitis differ from croup in clinical presentation?

**A:** Epiglottitis: rapid onset, toxic-appearing, high fever, tripod posture, drooling, muffled voice, inspiratory stridor, slow breathing, dysphagia. No cough. 'Thumb sign' on lateral neck X-ray. Croup: gradual onset, less toxic, barking 'seal' cough, worse at night, 'steeple sign' on AP neck X-ray, supraglottis normal.

This is a classic MCCQE1 distinction. Epiglottitis is a medical emergency — do NOT examine the throat as it may precipitate complete obstruction. Ensure anesthesia/ENT present before any airway manipulation. Post-H. influenzae type B vaccine, causes now include S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, and S. aureus.

**Q:** What is the treatment of acute epiglottitis?

**A:** Secure airway (most critical — do NOT examine throat before preparation); IV access with hydration; IV antibiotics: cefuroxime, cefotaxime, or ceftriaxone for 10-14 days; moist air; extubate when epiglottic edema decreases (air leak around ETT) and patient is afebrile; watch for meningitis/sepsis.

The 'thumb sign' on lateral neck radiograph shows swollen epiglottis. Blood and pharyngeal cultures should be taken AFTER intubation. WBC is elevated. The condition was previously most common in children 1-4 years due to H. influenzae type B, but HiB vaccination has made this much less common.

**Q:** What are the contraindications to tonsillectomy?

**A:** Relative contraindications: velopharyngeal insufficiency (overt or submucous cleft palate, impaired palatal function); hematologic (coagulopathy, anemia, hemophilia, leukemia, agranulocytosis); active local infection without urgent obstructive symptoms.

Tonsillectomy in patients with submucous cleft palate can unmask velopharyngeal insufficiency, leading to hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation. In patients with coagulopathy, the risk of hemorrhage (primary within 24h or secondary within 7-10 days) is significantly increased.

**Q:** What syndromes are associated with Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent AOM?

**A:** Down syndrome (horizontal Eustachian tube position), Crouzon syndrome, cleft palate (even after repair), Apert syndrome, Kartagener syndrome (abnormal cilia). Also: CHARGE syndrome (associated with choanal atresia), Pierre-Robin sequence.

Eustachian tube dysfunction is the primary defect in AOM. At-risk populations include those with craniofacial abnormalities, immunodeficiencies, and ciliary dyskinesia syndromes. These children should be monitored closely for OME and may benefit from earlier consideration of tympanostomy tubes.

**Q:** What are the otoscopic findings that most reliably diagnose AOM?

**A:** Bulging tympanic membrane (LR 51, 95% CI 36-73) is most reliable; cloudy TM (LR 34, 95% CI 28-42); immobile TM on pneumatic otoscopy (LR 31, 95% CI 26-37); erythematous TM (LR 8.4, 95% CI 7-11). Ear pain is the most reliable symptom.

The diagnosis of AOM in pediatrics requires both MEE/MEI AND acute onset symptoms. Ear tugging alone is not a reliable indicator of pathology. MEI on otoscopy includes a bulging TM with marked discolouration (hemorrhagic, red, grey, or yellow) with loss of bony landmarks.

**Q:** What is Grisel's syndrome and in what surgical context does it occur?

**A:** Grisel's syndrome = atlantoaxial subluxation following head and neck surgery, particularly tonsillectomy. It is a rare complication.

Grisel's syndrome occurs due to inflammatory ligamentous laxity from local infection or surgical trauma near the atlantoaxial joint. It presents with painful torticollis and limited neck motion post-operatively and requires prompt recognition and treatment.

**Q:** What are the indications for adenoidectomy?

**A:** Chronic upper airway obstruction with sleep-disordered breathing/OSA + cor pulmonale; chronic nasopharyngitis resistant to medical treatment; chronic serous OM and chronic suppurative OM (with second set of tubes); recurrent AOM resistant to antibiotics; suspicion of nasopharyngeal malignancy; persistent rhinorrhea from nasal obstruction; persistent adenoiditis after two courses of antibiotics; hyponasal speech; dental malocclusion or orofacial growth disturbance.

Adenoidectomy combined with tympanostomy tubes is recommended for recurrent AOM in children ≥4 years. Adenoidectomy alone is not recommended in children <4 years unless there is nasal obstruction or chronic adenoiditis. Contraindications include conditions increasing risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency.

**Q:** What is the role of molecular testing in thyroid nodule evaluation?

**A:** Molecular testing (mutational analysis including BRAF, RAS, microRNA classifiers) is used to distinguish 'high-risk' from 'low-risk' thyroid nodules in Bethesda category III (follicular lesion of undetermined significance) and category IV (follicular neoplasm) to determine whether surgical excision is needed.

Nuclear scanning has minimal value in thyroid nodule investigation. All patients with thyroid nodules require serum TSH and thyroid/neck ultrasound. TI-RADS guides FNA vs. ultrasound follow-up decisions. U/S-guided FNA should be used for repeat biopsy of initially non-diagnostic nodules.

**Q:** What are the protective factors and modifiable risk factors for AOM in children?

**A:** Protective factors: breastfeeding, xylitol. Modifiable risk factors: lack of breastfeeding, daycare attendance, household crowding, exposure to cigarette smoke/air pollution, pacifier use, vitamin A deficiency, cochlear implants.

Non-modifiable risk factors include young age, family history of OM, prematurity, orofacial abnormalities, immunodeficiencies, Down syndrome, and lower SES. Breastfeeding provides passive immunity and optimal Eustachian tube positioning during feeding, reducing AOM risk.

**Q:** What are common causes of sudden-onset airway obstruction in infants?

**A:** Foreign body aspiration, croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis), bacterial tracheitis, caustic ingestion, epiglottitis.

Foreign body aspiration should always be considered in sudden-onset stridor in infants and toddlers, especially with a choking episode history. Bacterial tracheitis (Staphylococcal) can mimic croup but is more toxic-appearing and refractory to standard croup treatment.

**Q:** What is the treatment for medullary thyroid carcinoma and why is family screening important?

**A:** Treatment: total thyroidectomy + median and/or lateral compartment neck dissection based on serum calcitonin levels; postoperative thyroxine; radiotherapy; screen relatives. Family screening important because medullary thyroid cancer is associated with MEN IIa and MEN IIb (RET proto-oncogene mutations) — hereditary in 25% of cases.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma secretes calcitonin (diagnostic marker), prostaglandins, ACTH, serotonin, and kallikrein. MEN IIa includes MTC + pheochromocytoma + primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN IIb includes MTC + pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus. Serum calcitonin is used for monitoring.

**Q:** What lymphoid tissues comprise Waldeyer's ring?

**A:** Waldeyer's ring is an interrupted circle of protective lymphoid tissue at the upper ends of the respiratory and alimentary tracts, consisting of: pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), tubal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and lingual tonsil (under mucosa of posterior 1/3 of tongue).

Waldeyer's ring acts as the first line of immune defense at the pharyngeal inlet. Chronic inflammation or hypertrophy of any component can cause airway obstruction. Thyroid lymphoma arising in this ring has a strong association with Hashimoto thyroiditis.

**Q:** What is the Cotton-Myer grading system for subglottic stenosis?

**A:** Grade I: ≤50% obstruction; Grade II: 51-70%; Grade III: 71-99%; Grade IV: no detectable lumen.

The Cotton-Myer grading system standardizes the degree of subglottic obstruction and guides management decisions, ranging from endoscopic dilation for mild stenosis to laryngotracheoplasty for severe cases.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of acquired subglottic stenosis?

**A:** Prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation causing pressure necrosis and subsequent scar formation.

Endotracheal intubation is the most common cause of acquired subglottic stenosis. Nasal intubation is less traumatic than oral intubation for long-term use because of differing tube orientation and less pressure on the subglottis. Stenosis risk is related to both duration of intubation and endotracheal tube size.

**Q:** Which syndromes are frequently associated with congenital subglottic stenosis?

**A:** 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge), Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), and CHARGE syndrome.

Congenital subglottic stenosis is defined as a subglottic diameter <4 mm in neonates or smaller than average for age. It is commonly associated with chromosomal or developmental syndromes, highlighting the importance of airway evaluation in these patients.

**Q:** What are the clinical features of subglottic stenosis?

**A:** Biphasic stridor, respiratory distress, and recurrent or prolonged croup.

Biphasic stridor (both inspiratory and expiratory) reflects fixed airway obstruction at the subglottis. Recurrent croup should prompt evaluation for underlying subglottic stenosis, especially in young children with multiple croup episodes.

**Q:** How is subglottic stenosis treated based on stenosis characteristics?

**A:** Soft stenosis: tissue division with knife or laser, balloon dilation + steroids. Firm stenosis: laryngotracheoplasty.

The consistency of the stenotic tissue determines treatment approach. Soft/mucosal stenosis responds to endoscopic techniques and steroids, while firm/cartilaginous stenosis requires open surgical reconstruction (laryngotracheoplasty) to provide a durable airway.

**Q:** What is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in neonates?

**A:** Laryngomalacia — congenital softening of tissues above the glottis causing collapse into the glottis on inspiration.

Laryngomalacia accounts for approximately 60% of all cases of neonatal stridor. The immature laryngeal cartilage and poor supraglottic tone cause dynamic collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration, producing characteristic high-pitched inspiratory stridor.

**Q:** Describe the pathophysiologic cycle in laryngomalacia that perpetuates airway obstruction.

**A:** Airway obstruction → supraglottic indrawing on inspiration → negative intrathoracic pressure → laryngopharyngeal reflux of acid → supraglottic edema → worsened obstruction.

This self-reinforcing cycle explains why PPI therapy is part of conservative management. By reducing acid reflux, PPIs decrease supraglottic edema, breaking the cycle and improving airway patency. This also explains why laryngomalacia often worsens postprandially.

**Q:** What are the classic laryngoscopic findings in laryngomalacia?

**A:** Omega-shaped epiglottis, short aryepiglottic folds, and redundant mucosa over the arytenoids.

These anatomical findings on flexible laryngoscopy confirm the diagnosis of laryngomalacia. The omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds are the primary structural abnormalities; supraglottoplasty addresses these by dividing the short aryepiglottic folds and/or removing excess arytenoid mucosa.

**Q:** What is the natural history and initial management of laryngomalacia?

**A:** Symptoms typically resolve spontaneously by 12-18 months in >90% of cases. Initial management: observation + PPI therapy.

The vast majority of laryngomalacia is self-limiting. PPIs break the acid-reflux cycle that promotes supraglottic edema. Surgical intervention (supraglottoplasty) is reserved for the ~10% with severe disease causing failure to thrive, significant feeding difficulties, or cyanotic episodes.

**Q:** Where does an ingested foreign body most commonly lodge in a child?

**A:** At the cricopharyngeus muscle (upper esophageal sphincter).

The cricopharyngeus is the narrowest point of the esophagus and the most common site of food and foreign body impaction. Common objects include coins, toys, and batteries. Batteries require emergency removal due to their ability to erode through the esophagus via electrical and chemical injury.

**Q:** Why is a button battery ingestion a medical emergency compared to a coin?

**A:** Button batteries can erode through the esophagus via electrical current and chemical injury; they appear as a 'halo sign' on X-ray (vs. single disc for coin) and must be urgently removed.

Even a brief contact period allows button batteries to generate hydroxide at the negative pole via electrical current, causing liquefactive necrosis of esophageal tissue. Fatal complications (esophago-aortic fistula, tracheoesophageal fistula) can occur within hours. The double-ring or halo sign on X-ray distinguishes a battery from a coin.

**Q:** Where does an aspirated foreign body most commonly lodge and why?

**A:** Right main bronchus — because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

The anatomy of the right main bronchus (more vertical, wider, shorter) makes it the preferential path for aspirated foreign bodies. Right-sided aspiration causes unilateral 'asthma-like' symptoms — wheezing, decreased breath sounds — often leading to misdiagnosis. Complete occlusion can lead to atelectasis, lobar pneumonia, or pneumothorax.

**Q:** What are the radiographic techniques used to evaluate suspected foreign body aspiration in children based on age?

**A:** Older child (stable): inspiratory AND expiratory chest X-ray. Younger child: right and left lateral decubitus chest X-rays (lack of lung deflation on dependent side suggests foreign body).

Air trapping distal to an obstructing foreign body causes the affected lung to remain hyperinflated. In older cooperative children, expiratory films reveal unilateral hyperinflation. In young children who cannot cooperate, gravity-dependent decubitus views serve the same purpose — a normal lung should deflate when dependent, whereas an obstructed lung remains inflated.

**Q:** What is the definitive treatment for a suspected airway or esophageal foreign body?

**A:** Bronchoscopy (airway) or esophagoscopy (esophageal) with removal. Patient must be kept NPO immediately.

Any patient with suspected foreign body ingestion or aspiration should be made NPO immediately to prepare for potential procedural intervention. Rigid bronchoscopy or esophagoscopy under general anesthesia allows direct visualization and extraction.

**Q:** What is the most common source of deep neck space infection in adults vs. children?

**A:** Adults: mandibular dental infection (most common). Children: tonsillar infection (most common).

Deep neck space infections are polymicrobial, involving mixed aerobes and anaerobes from the oral flora. Ludwig's angina is the prototypical deep neck infection involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from dental infections in adults.

**Q:** What is Ludwig's angina and what is its anatomical significance?

**A:** Ludwig's angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis/infection of the submandibular and sublingual spaces — the prototypical deep neck space infection, most commonly from dental sources.

Ludwig's angina can rapidly compromise the airway through floor-of-mouth elevation and tongue displacement. Airway management is the first priority. The infection is typically polymicrobial. CT with contrast aids in assessment, but imaging should be accompanied by the surgeon given risk of sudden airway loss.

**Q:** What is the treatment triad for deep neck space infections?

**A:** 1) Secure the airway; 2) Source control (surgical drainage, tooth extraction, debridement); 3) Maximum-dose IV antimicrobials.

The airway must be secured first in deep neck space infections as progressive swelling can cause sudden airway loss — the worst scenario is losing the airway during imaging. Surgical drainage of fluctuant collections is essential as antibiotics alone are insufficient for established abscesses.

**Q:** What is the clinical warning about imaging in deep neck space infections?

**A:** Investigations (CT/MRI) should be obtained carefully with the surgeon accompanying the patient, as the worst place to lose an airway is during imaging.

Deep neck space infections can cause rapid airway deterioration. The surgeon should accompany the patient to radiology to manage potential acute airway compromise. If airway compromise is imminent, securing the airway takes priority over imaging.

**Q:** What is rhinitis medicamentosa and which nasal decongestants cause it?

**A:** Rhinitis medicamentosa is rebound nasal congestion/decongestant addiction from prolonged use (>5 days) of topical decongestants such as xylometazoline (Otrivin) and oxymetazoline (Dristan).

Topical alpha-adrenergic decongestants cause vasoconstriction of nasal mucosa. With prolonged use, rebound vasodilation occurs upon drug withdrawal, causing worsening congestion. Treatment is gradual cessation, sometimes with topical nasal steroids. Short-term use (<5 days) is recommended to avoid this complication.

**Q:** What is an important caution for ipratropium bromide (Atrovent) nasal spray?

**A:** Avoid spraying into eyes — can cause burning or precipitate narrow-angle glaucoma. Also causes increased epistaxis risk when combined with topical nasal steroids.

Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic used for vasomotor rhinitis. Its systemic anticholinergic effects (mydriasis, cycloplegia) can precipitate acute narrow-angle glaucoma if it contacts the eyes. The combination with nasal steroids increases epistaxis risk, requiring patient education.

**Q:** What is the key finding from the NEJM 2016 trial on AOM treatment duration in children aged 6-23 months?

**A:** 10 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate had more favourable outcomes (16% vs 34% clinical failure) than 5 days; no increase in adverse events or antimicrobial resistance with 10-day course.

This trial demonstrated that shortened courses of antibiotic therapy for AOM in young children (6-23 months) resulted in significantly higher clinical failure rates. Canadian and international guidelines support 10-day courses in this age group to optimize outcomes while limiting resistance.

**Q:** What did the PET-NECK trial (NEJM 2016) demonstrate about surveillance versus planned neck dissection in N2/N3 head and neck SCC?

**A:** PET-CT-guided surveillance is non-inferior to planned neck dissection for overall survival in N2 or N3 SCC (2-year survival 84.9% vs 81.5%), with fewer operations.

The PET-NECK trial changed practice by supporting PET-CT surveillance at 12 weeks post-chemoradiotherapy instead of routine planned neck dissection. This avoids significant surgical morbidity in patients who achieve a complete response on imaging while maintaining equivalent survival outcomes.

**Q:** What did the CheckMate 141 trial demonstrate regarding nivolumab in head and neck SCC?

**A:** Nivolumab resulted in longer median overall survival (7.5 mo vs 5.1 mo) than standard therapy in platinum-refractory recurrent SCC of the head and neck (HR 0.70, p=0.01).

CheckMate 141 established nivolumab (anti-PD-1 immunotherapy) as a treatment option for platinum-refractory recurrent head and neck SCC. This was a landmark trial for immunotherapy in this setting and led to regulatory approval in Canada and internationally.

**Q:** What did the elective vs. therapeutic neck dissection trial (NEJM 2015) show for node-negative oral cavity SCC?

**A:** Elective (upfront) neck dissection had significantly better 3-year overall survival (80% vs 67.5%) and disease-free survival (69.5% vs 45.9%) compared to therapeutic (delayed) neck dissection.

This RCT demonstrated that elective neck dissection at the time of primary tumour resection leads to superior outcomes over watchful waiting with therapeutic neck dissection only when nodal disease becomes clinically apparent. This supports elective neck dissection as standard of care for T1/T2 node-negative oral SCC.

**Q:** What were the key conclusions of the CHAT trial (NEJM 2013) regarding adenotonsillectomy for childhood OSA?

**A:** In children aged 5-9 with OSA, adenotonsillectomy did NOT significantly improve attention or executive function, but DID significantly improve behaviour, quality of life, and polysomnographic findings (normalization: 79% vs 46%).

The CHAT trial is a landmark RCT showing that the primary neurocognitive outcomes (attention, executive function) were not significantly different at 7 months post-surgery versus watchful waiting, but subjective measures and polysomnography improved. This informs shared decision-making about adenotonsillectomy in school-age children.

**Q:** What does the KATE trial conclude about adenotonsillectomy for mild vs. moderate OSA in young children (ages 2-4)?

**A:** Children with MILD OSA (ages 2-4): watchful waiting may suffice. Children with MODERATE OSA: adenotonsillectomy should be considered (meaningful OAHI improvement: -3.1 vs -1.0).

The KATE trial provides evidence for stratifying surgical intervention by OSA severity in very young children. While mild OSA may resolve with watchful waiting, moderate OSA shows a clinically meaningful benefit from adenotonsillectomy, guiding Canadian paediatric otolaryngology practice.

**Q:** What is ciprofloxacin's important safety consideration in children regarding musculoskeletal effects?

**A:** Animal studies suggest systemic quinolones may cause cartilage necrosis (arthropathy) in children; use with caution.

Fluoroquinolones cause arthropathy in juvenile animal studies, raising concerns about use in pediatric populations. In otolaryngology, ciprofloxacin otic drops (Ciprodex) are used topically for otitis externa and complications of otitis media and are considered safe due to minimal systemic absorption, but systemic quinolones are used cautiously in children.

**Q:** What complication is associated with erythromycin (systemic) use in the ear?

**A:** Ototoxicity.

Erythromycin and other macrolides are associated with reversible sensorineural hearing loss, particularly at high systemic doses. This is relevant in ENT practice when erythromycin is used as a penicillin alternative. Erythromycin also commonly causes GI side effects (nausea, cramping) via motilin receptor agonism.

**Q:** What is the risk of neomycin/polymyxin B/hydrocortisone (Cortisporin Otic) otic drops if placed in the inner ear?

**A:** Risk of hearing loss (cochlear toxicity) if placed in the inner ear (i.e., if the tympanic membrane is perforated).

Aminoglycoside-containing otic drops (e.g., neomycin in Cortisporin) are contraindicated when the tympanic membrane is perforated due to potential ototoxicity from direct contact with inner ear structures. Ciprofloxacin otic drops (non-ototoxic) are preferred when a perforation is present.

**Q:** What is the mechanism of hydrocortisone and acetic acid (VoSol HC) otic drops?

**A:** Bactericidal by lowering pH of the ear canal; used for otitis media.

Acidic ear drops work by creating an environment hostile to bacterial growth. Most ear pathogens (including Pseudomonas) cannot survive in a low-pH environment. This mechanism is particularly useful in otitis media and otitis externa management when antibiotic resistance is a concern.

**Q:** What is the advantage of mometasone furoate (Nasonex) and fluticasone (Flonase) nasal sprays regarding systemic absorption?

**A:** Flonase and Nasonex are NOT absorbed systemically, making them safer for long-term use in allergic rhinitis.

Minimal systemic bioavailability (<1%) of these intranasal steroids reduces the risk of HPA axis suppression, growth effects in children, and other systemic corticosteroid side effects with long-term use. This is a key advantage over older intranasal steroids. Nasal steroids typically require up to 4 weeks of consistent use to achieve full therapeutic effect.

**Q:** A 3-week-old infant presents with high-pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens with feeding and crying but improves in the prone position. Flexible laryngoscopy reveals an omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?

**A:** Laryngomalacia. First-line management: observation and PPI therapy. >90% resolve by 12-18 months. Supraglottoplasty if severe (failure to thrive, cyanosis).

This clinical vignette is classic for laryngomalacia — the most common cause of stridor in neonates. Key features include: onset at 1-2 weeks, worsening with feeding/crying/supine position, characteristic laryngoscopic findings. PPIs address the acid reflux cycle. The prone position relieves obstruction by allowing the tongue and supraglottic structures to fall forward.

**Q:** A 2-year-old presents to the ER with sudden onset coughing, wheeze, and decreased breath sounds on the right side without fever. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step?

**A:** Aspirated foreign body in the right main bronchus. Next step: make NPO immediately; right and left decubitus chest X-rays (lack of deflation on dependent side suggests obstruction); urgent rigid bronchoscopy.

The classic triad of sudden onset, unilateral wheeze, and decreased breath sounds without fever in a toddler strongly suggests foreign body aspiration. The right main bronchus is most commonly affected. Absence of fever and elevated WBC differentiates from infectious causes. Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

## Ent Otitis Externa

**Q:** What is malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa and which patients are at risk?

**A:** Osteomyelitis of the mastoid or temporal bone, occurring in elderly patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised patients. It is a rare, severe complication of otitis externa.

Malignant OE is a life-threatening skull base osteomyelitis almost exclusively caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The immunocompromised state (especially DM) impairs neutrophil function, allowing Pseudomonas to invade bone. It is a medical emergency requiring IV antibiotics and surgical debridement.

**Q:** What is the most common causative organism in malignant otitis externa and what cranial nerve is most commonly affected?

**A:** Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common organism. CN VII (facial nerve) is most commonly affected, followed by CN X and CN XI.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa thrives in the warm, moist external auditory canal of diabetic patients. It invades the skull base and damages cranial nerves at the stylomastoid foramen and along the skull base. CN VII palsy in the setting of refractory otitis externa should prompt urgent imaging.

**Q:** How are gallium and technetium scans used differently in malignant otitis externa?

**A:** Technetium scans are used for diagnosis (demonstrate sites of osteomyelitis). Gallium scans are used for follow-up monitoring of active infection because gallium is taken up by PMNs and only shows active infection, not the extent of osteomyelitis.

Technetium bone scans detect areas of increased bone turnover (osteomyelitis), while gallium is taken up by white blood cells (PMNs), making it a marker of active infection. Gallium normalization on follow-up scans indicates treatment response, making it the preferred monitoring tool during and after antibiotic therapy.

**Q:** A 68-year-old diabetic man presents with severe otalgia, purulent otorrhea refractory to topical antibiotics, and granulation tissue on the floor of the auditory canal. What is the diagnosis and management?

**A:** Diagnosis: malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa (skull base osteomyelitis). Management: medical emergency — hospitalization, IV antibiotics (anti-pseudomonal), surgical debridement. Imaging: high-resolution temporal bone CT, gadolinium-enhanced MRI, technetium scan.

The combination of elderly age, diabetes, refractory OE, granulation/necrotic tissue on auditory canal floor, and purulent otorrhea unresponsive to topical therapy is classic for malignant OE caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CN VII palsy indicates spread to the skull base. Failure to treat aggressively risks cranial nerve palsies, systemic infection, and death. Technetium scan diagnoses osteomyelitis; gallium scan monitors treatment response.

## Ent Middle Ear

**Q:** What is a cholesteatoma and what are the two main types?

**A:** A cyst composed of keratinized desquamated epithelial cells occurring in the middle ear, mastoid, and temporal bone. The two types are congenital and acquired (primary and secondary).

Congenital cholesteatoma appears as a 'small white pearl' behind an intact TM (anterior and medial to the malleus) due to aberrant migration of external canal ectoderm during development. Acquired cholesteatoma is more common and results from retraction pockets or epithelial migration through TM perforations. The progressive destruction of surrounding bone leads to serious complications.

**Q:** What are the intracranial complications of cholesteatoma?

**A:** Meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, intracranial abscess (subdural, epidural, cerebellar), and facial paralysis (CN VII).

Cholesteatoma causes progressive enzymatic and pressure-induced destruction of surrounding bone structures. Erosion through the tegmen can lead to meningitis or intracranial abscess. Sigmoid sinus erosion causes thrombosis. Facial canal erosion causes CN VII palsy. Early surgical intervention (mastoidectomy + tympanoplasty) is essential to prevent these life-threatening complications.

**Q:** What are the local (non-intracranial) complications of cholesteatoma?

**A:** Ossicular erosion causing CHL, inner ear erosion causing SNHL/dizziness/labyrinthitis, temporal bone infection (mastoiditis, petrositis), and facial paralysis.

Cholesteatoma's keratinizing epithelium produces collagenases that erode bone. Ossicular chain destruction is the most common complication, causing conductive hearing loss. Extension into the labyrinth causes sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular symptoms. These complications indicate the need for urgent surgical management.

**Q:** What is the definitive treatment for cholesteatoma?

**A:** Surgical: mastoidectomy + tympanoplasty + ossicular reconstruction.

There is no medical treatment for cholesteatoma. Surgical excision is required because the lesion is locally destructive and will continue to erode surrounding structures. Mastoidectomy removes infected mastoid air cells and the cholesteatoma. Tympanoplasty repairs the TM, and ossicular reconstruction restores hearing. Audiogram and non-contrast CT of temporal bones are performed preoperatively.

**Q:** What is acute mastoiditis, what organisms cause it, and what is the classic clinical triad?

**A:** Infection (usually subperiosteal) of mastoid air cells, most commonly ~2 weeks after untreated or inadequately treated AOM. Caused by same organisms as AOM: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus, P. aeruginosa. Classic triad: (1) tenderness to pressure over the mastoid, (2) retroauricular swelling with protruding ear, (3) otorrhea.

Mastoiditis is a complication of AOM when bacteria spread from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells. Coalescence occurs when infection destroys the bony septa between air cells. CT shows opacification and interruption of normal trabeculations. Complications of AOM are rare due to widespread antibiotic treatment but mastoiditis is the most common serious complication when AOM is undertreated.

**Q:** What are the indications for surgical intervention (cortical mastoidectomy) in acute mastoiditis?

**A:** Failure of medical treatment after 48 hours, symptoms of intracranial complications, and aural discharge persisting for 4 weeks resistant to antibiotics.

Most acute mastoiditis cases respond to IV antibiotics with myringotomy and ventilation tubes. Cortical mastoidectomy (debridement of infected tissue for aeration and drainage) is reserved for treatment failures. Incision and drainage may be needed for postauricular abscess. Intracranial complications such as meningitis, brain abscess, or sigmoid sinus thrombosis require urgent surgical exploration.

## Ent Inner Ear

**Q:** What is otosclerosis, what is its inheritance pattern, and what is Carhart's notch?

**A:** Fusion of the stapes footplate to the oval window preventing vibration. Autosomal dominant with ~40% penetrance, F>M, progresses during pregnancy. Carhart's notch is a characteristic dip at 2000 Hz on audiogram.

Otosclerosis is the 2nd most common cause of CHL in 15-50 year olds (after cerumen impaction). The abnormal bone remodeling fixes the stapes, causing conductive hearing loss. Schwartz's sign (pink blush through TM) reflects neovascularization of otosclerotic bone. The Carhart notch at 2000 Hz is a mechanical artifact of stapes fixation on bone conduction testing, not true sensorineural loss.

**Q:** What are the treatment options for otosclerosis?

**A:** Monitor with serial audiograms, hearing aid (BAHA), or definitive surgical treatment: stapedectomy or stapedotomy (using laser or drill) with prosthesis.

Stapedectomy/stapedotomy is the definitive treatment and highly effective, restoring conductive hearing. A prosthesis is placed to bypass the fixed stapes and transmit sound. BAHA (bone-anchored hearing aid) is an alternative for those who cannot or choose not to have surgery. Monitoring is appropriate for patients coping well with mild loss.

**Q:** What gene mutation is the most common cause of non-syndromic hereditary sensorineural hearing loss?

**A:** Connexin 26 (GJB2 gene) is the most common cause. It is often idiopathic and autosomal recessive.

Non-syndromic SNHL accounts for 70% of hereditary hearing loss. GJB2 mutations disrupt gap junction communication in the cochlea, impairing potassium recycling essential for hair cell function. This is the most commonly identified genetic cause of congenital SNHL. Testing for GJB2 mutations is part of the workup for unexplained bilateral SNHL in children.

**Q:** Name 4 syndromes associated with hereditary sensorineural hearing loss and their key distinguishing features.

**A:** 1. Waardenburg: white forelock, heterochromia iridis, wide nasal bridge, increased intercanthal distance. 2. Pendred: euthyroid goiter, SLC26A4 gene, enlarged vestibular aqueducts. 3. Treacher-Collins: first and second branchial cleft anomalies. 4. Alport: hereditary nephritis.

Syndromic SNHL accounts for 30% of hereditary hearing loss. Waardenburg involves pigmentation abnormalities from neural crest migration defects. Pendred is the most common cause of syndromic SNHL; goiter is typically euthyroid. Treacher-Collins involves mandibulofacial dysostosis. Alport syndrome manifests as nephritis plus SNHL, pointing to type IV collagen defects in both the kidney and cochlea.

**Q:** What TORCH infections and postnatal infections are risk factors for congenital/acquired SNHL?

**A:** Prenatal TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19), Rubella, CMV, HSV, and Zika virus. Postnatal: bacterial meningitis, mumps, measles.

CMV is the most common congenital infection causing SNHL. Rubella was historically significant but vaccination has reduced its incidence. Bacterial meningitis (especially S. pneumoniae) causes SNHL through labyrinthitis ossificans. Early ABR testing is performed for any at-risk neonates before NICU discharge and at 3 months adjusted age.

**Q:** What is presbycusis and what are its characteristic audiologic features?

**A:** SNHL associated with aging (starting in the 5th and 6th decades). Features: progressive bilateral hearing deterioration initially at high frequencies, followed by middle and lower frequencies; loss of speech discrimination especially with background noise; recruitment phenomenon (inability to tolerate loud sounds); tinnitus.

Presbycusis results from cumulative hair cell degeneration, age-related basilar membrane degeneration, cochlear neuron damage, and inner ear ischemia. The high-frequency loss explains difficulty with consonants (speech understanding). The recruitment phenomenon is due to outer hair cell loss with preserved inner hair cells at the outer hair cell recruitment threshold. Hearing aids are indicated when HL >30-35 dB and speech discrimination is adequate.

**Q:** What is sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL) and what is the recommended treatment according to Canadian guidelines?

**A:** Sudden onset significant SNHL (usually unilateral) ± tinnitus, vertigo, aural fullness. 80-90% are idiopathic. Treatment: intratympanic or oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/d for 7-14 days), started within 3 days (ideal), up to 14 days of onset.

SSHL is defined as loss of at least 30 dB affecting three consecutive frequencies. MRI to rule out tumour and/or CT for ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke is indicated if focal neurological signs are present. Routine labs, CT, or MRI are not required unless indicated by history and physical. 70% resolve within 10-14 days, 20% partial resolution, 10% permanent loss. Idiopathic SSHL may be confused with ischemic brain events — keep high index of suspicion in elderly patients.

**Q:** What is the prognosis of sudden SNHL?

**A:** 70% resolve within 10-14 days; 20% experience partial resolution; 10% experience permanent hearing loss.

Prognosis depends on degree of hearing loss at presentation. Spontaneous recovery is common, but corticosteroids are started empirically to improve outcomes in idiopathic cases. Intratympanic steroids are an alternative when systemic steroids are contraindicated. Delays beyond 14 days significantly worsen prognosis.

**Q:** What is autoimmune inner ear disease and how does it present?

**A:** AIIED is an idiopathic condition (ages 20-50) causing rapidly progressive or fluctuating bilateral SNHL ± tinnitus, aural fullness, vestibular symptoms (ataxia, disequilibrium, vertigo). May be associated with systemic autoimmune diseases (RA, SLE) or vasculitides (GPA, polyarteritis nodosa).

AIIED is distinguished from idiopathic sudden SNHL by its bilateral nature and rapid progression over weeks to months. Autoimmune workup includes CBC, ESR, ANA, and rheumatoid factor. Treatment involves high-dose corticosteroids for at least 30 days. Cytotoxic medication (e.g., methotrexate, cyclophosphamide) may be used for steroid non-responders.

**Q:** Which aminoglycosides are vestibulotoxic vs. cochleotoxic, and what is the mechanism of ototoxicity?

**A:** Vestibulotoxic: streptomycin and gentamicin. Cochleotoxic: kanamycin and tobramycin. Mechanism: destroys sensory hair cells (outer first, then inner); toxic by any route (oral, IV, topical) especially if TM is perforated.

Aminoglycoside ototoxicity occurs days to weeks post-treatment. High-frequency hearing loss develops earliest because outer hair cells (lost first) are most numerous in the basal turn (high-frequency region). Otoacoustic emissions are lost first since they require intact outer hair cells. Once-daily dosing (q24h determined by creatinine clearance) reduces ototoxicity because aminoglycoside toxicity displays saturable kinetics. Duration of treatment is the most important predictor of ototoxicity.

**Q:** What is noise-induced SNHL and at what frequency is the classic audiogram notch seen?

**A:** SNHL caused by cochlear damage from sounds 85-90 dB over months/years, single impulses >135 dB, or repetitive vibratory insults. Classic audiogram shows bilateral SNHL with a notch at 4000 Hz ('boilermaker's notch'), the resonant frequency of the temporal bone.

The 4000 Hz notch is pathognomonic for noise-induced hearing loss. Speech reception is not affected until HL >30 dB at speech frequencies, so significant cochlear damage can occur silently. Temporary threshold shift (reversible) occurs with acute noise exposure; permanent threshold shift is irreversible. Prevention includes ear protectors (muffs, plugs), noise exposure limits, and regular audiologic follow-up.

## Ent Trauma

**Q:** Compare otic capsule-involving vs. otic capsule-sparing temporal bone fractures regarding hearing loss, CN VII involvement, and incidence.

**A:** Otic capsule-involving (10-20%): SNHL from direct cochlear injury, CN VII palsy in 50%, frontal/occipital trauma. Otic capsule-sparing (70-90%): CHL from ossicular injury, CN VII palsy in 10-20%, lateral skull trauma. Otic capsule-sparing is more common.

Temporal bone fractures are traditionally described as transverse or longitudinal relative to the petrous long axis, but most are mixed. Otic capsule-involving fractures are severe and carry a high rate of profound SNHL and facial nerve injury. Otic capsule-sparing fractures may present with hemotympanum, TM perforation, and step formation in the EAC. Battle's sign (mastoid ecchymosis) and raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis) are signs of basilar skull fracture.

**Q:** What are the surgical indications for exploring temporal bone fractures?

**A:** CN VII palsy (immediate and complete), gunshot wound, depressed fracture of external auditory meatus, early meningitis (mastoidectomy), bleeding intracranially from sinus, and CSF otorrhea (may resolve spontaneously but may require surgery).

Immediate and complete CN VII palsy suggests direct nerve transection and warrants early exploration. Delayed or incomplete facial palsy may be managed conservatively as it suggests neuropraxia with potential for recovery. Prevention of otogenic meningitis is the primary medical management goal. Facial nerve anastomosis, interpositional grafts, or anastomosis to other motor nerves may be needed for reanimation.

## Ent Facial Nerve

**Q:** Differentiate central vs. peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) paralysis clinically.

**A:** Central: spares the forehead (frontalis) because of bilateral cortical representation of upper face muscles; associated with lateralizing signs (hemiparesthesias, hemiparalysis, aphasia). Peripheral: involves all ipsilateral facial muscles including frontalis; no lateralizing signs.

The key clinical distinction is frontalis involvement. In central facial palsy (UMN lesion, e.g., stroke), the contralateral hemisphere also provides input to the upper face, so forehead movement is partially preserved. Peripheral facial palsy (LMN lesion, e.g., Bell's palsy) affects all branches of CN VII equally, causing complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including forehead. This distinction prevents misattributing a stroke to Bell's palsy.

**Q:** Using the KITTENS mnemonic, list the causes of peripheral facial nerve palsy.

**A:** K - Congenital; I - Infection/Idiopathic (Bell's palsy, HSV; otitis media, mastoiditis, varicella-zoster); T - Trauma/Toxins; T - Tumour; E - Endocrine (diabetes, preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism); N - Neurologic (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis, MS); S - Systemic (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hyperostoses).

Bell's palsy (idiopathic, possibly HSV) accounts for 80-90% of peripheral facial palsy. The KITTENS mnemonic ensures a systematic differential. Red flags suggesting non-Bell's cause include: palpable mass over the parotid gland, unilateral middle ear effusion in adults, no spontaneous remission beginning within 3 weeks, or presence of vesicles (suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome).

**Q:** Compare Bell's palsy and Ramsay Hunt syndrome in terms of etiology, incidence, clinical features, and prognosis.

**A:** Bell's palsy: idiopathic (possibly HSV), 80-90% of PFP; acute onset, postauricular pain, hyperacusis (30%), decreased lacrimation; >90% recovery. Ramsay Hunt: varicella-zoster infection of CN VII/VIII, 4-5% of PFP; severe otalgia, SNHL, vesicles on pinna/EAC (3-7 days after pain onset), herpes zoster ophthalmicus; worse prognosis — only 22% recover completely, 10% complete paralysis.

Ramsay Hunt (herpes zoster oticus) is distinguished by the triad of peripheral facial palsy, ear pain, and ipsilateral auricular vesicles. SNHL and vestibular symptoms may occur due to CN VIII involvement. Treatment includes systemic steroids (reduce pain and postherpetic neuralgia) and acyclovir (may lessen pain and aid healing). Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion with MRI showing PIE enhancement of CN VII. Spontaneous remission should begin within 3 weeks in Bell's palsy; delayed recovery (3-6 months) portends functional loss.

**Q:** A 45-year-old woman presents with acute onset complete right-sided facial droop including forehead, postauricular pain, and hyperacusis. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

**A:** Most likely diagnosis: Bell's palsy (idiopathic peripheral facial nerve palsy, possibly HSV). Treatment: corneal protection (artificial tears, nocturnal lid taping), systemic corticosteroids (prednisone), consider antiviral (acyclovir). Monitor for spontaneous remission within 3 weeks.

Involvement of the forehead (frontalis) distinguishes peripheral from central facial palsy. Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion accounting for 80-90% of peripheral facial palsy. Postauricular pain and hyperacusis are characteristic features. MRI with gadolinium shows PIE enhancement of CN VII. If no voluntary EMG motor unit potentials are present in >90% testing, consider surgical decompression. Prognosis is good — most patients recover completely but recovery of delayed onset (3-6 months) portends functional loss.

## Ent Rhinitis

**Q:** What is rhinitis medicamentosa and how is it treated?

**A:** Rebound nasal congestion caused by overuse of intranasal vasoconstrictors (topical decongestants). Treatment: limit topical decongestant use to no more than 3-5 days; treat with saline irrigations and intranasal corticosteroid.

Rhinitis medicamentosa occurs when prolonged use of vasoconstrictors (e.g., oxymetazoline) causes tachyphylaxis and rebound vasodilation upon discontinuation. Patients become dependent on the decongestant to breathe. The mainstay of treatment is intranasal corticosteroids which reduce mucosal inflammation and allow gradual withdrawal of the decongestant.

**Q:** What nasal discharge character suggests neoplasia vs. allergic/viral rhinitis?

**A:** Serosanguinous discharge suggests neoplasia. Bloody discharge suggests trauma, neoplasia, bleeding disorder, or HTN/vascular disease. Watery/mucoid suggests allergic, viral, vasomotor rhinitis, or CSF leak. Mucopurulent suggests bacterial infection or foreign body.

The character of nasal discharge guides the differential diagnosis. Unilateral serosanguinous or bloody discharge in an adult should raise concern for sinonasal malignancy until proven otherwise. CSF leak (e.g., from skull base fracture) can mimic watery rhinorrhea — the halo sign and beta-2 transferrin testing help confirm CSF. Mucopurulent discharge from one side in a child suggests foreign body.

**Q:** What is allergic rhinitis, and what is the first-line treatment?

**A:** IgE-mediated hypersensitivity rhinitis to foreign allergens (seasonal or perennial). First-line treatment: intranasal corticosteroid (INCS) — mainstay of treatment, combined with allergen identification and avoidance, nasal saline irrigation, and oral antihistamines.

Allergic rhinitis affects people usually under 20 years with personal/family history of atopy. Seasonal triggers include pollen (trees, grass, ragweed); perennial triggers include dust mites, cockroach residue, animal dander, moulds, tobacco. Physical exam shows gray/blue congested turbinates and nasal tip transverse crease ('allergic salute'). Allergen immunotherapy is used for patients not adequately controlled with pharmacotherapy. Decongestants carry rhinitis medicamentosa risk. Complications include chronic sinusitis/polyps and serous otitis media.

**Q:** What is vasomotor rhinitis and how does its treatment differ from allergic rhinitis?

**A:** Rhinitis from dysregulation of nociceptors and autonomic nerves causing increased vascular permeability, triggered by temperature changes, alcohol, dust, smoke, or stress. Treatment: eliminate irritants; congestion-predominant — intranasal antihistamine/INCS; rhinorrhea-predominant — intranasal anticholinergic (ipratropium) ± INCS/antihistamine.

Vasomotor rhinitis is non-allergic and non-infectious; allergy must be ruled out. It causes chronic intermittent nasal obstruction that varies from side to side. Unlike allergic rhinitis, IgE testing is negative. The key distinction in treatment is the use of ipratropium (anticholinergic) for rhinorrhea-predominant symptoms, which reduces parasympathetic-driven glandular secretion. Exercise provides symptomatic relief via increased sympathetic tone.

## Ent Sinusitis

**Q:** What is the osteomeatal complex and why is it important in rhinosinusitis?

**A:** A common drainage area under the middle meatus where all sinuses drain. Ostial obstruction at the osteomeatal complex leads to stagnant mucus, dysfunctional cilia, and subsequent bacterial infection — the central pathogenesis of rhinosinusitis.

The osteomeatal complex is a key anatomical concept in sinusitis. Obstruction can be mechanical (septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy, polyps, tumours) or inflammatory (allergy, URTI). All paranasal sinuses drain through this area, so obstruction predisposes to pansinusitis. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) targets the osteomeatal complex to restore drainage while preserving mucosa.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria and time-based classification for rhinosinusitis?

**A:** Classification: acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), chronic (>12 weeks). Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis diagnosis requires at least 2 major symptoms (P: facial pain/pressure; O: nasal obstruction; D: purulent/discoloured nasal discharge; H: hyposmia/anosmia — at least 1 must be O or D) plus symptoms >7 days or worsening >5 days or purulence with high fever (>39°C) for 3-4 days.

The PODS criteria distinguish acute bacterial rhinosinusitis from viral URTI (course <10 days, peaks by day 3). The distinction matters because antibiotics are indicated for bacterial rhinosinusitis but not viral. CT of paranasal sinuses is indicated only if complications are suspected, not for routine diagnosis. Predisposing factors include viral URTI, allergy, dental disease, and anatomical defects.

**Q:** What is the most commonly affected sinus in acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and what are the most common organisms?

**A:** The maxillary sinus is most commonly affected. Organisms: S. pneumoniae (35%), H. influenzae (35%), M. catarrhalis, S. aureus, and anaerobes (dental source).

The maxillary sinus is most prone to infection because its ostium is located superiorly (poorly positioned for gravity drainage) and it receives drainage from the osteomeatal complex. In immunocompromised patients, mucormycosis must be ruled out — painless black or pale mucosa on exam should raise this concern. Children are more prone to bacterial etiology than adults but viral rhinosinusitis is still more common in children.

**Q:** What are the orbital complications of acute rhinosinusitis according to Chandler's classification?

**A:** I - Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis; II - Orbital cellulitis; III - Subperiosteal abscess; IV - Orbital abscess; V - Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Chandler's classification describes the progression of orbital complications from ethmoid sinusitis (the ethmoid sinus lies medial to the orbit). Stages I-II may be managed medically with IV antibiotics; Stages III-V generally require surgical drainage. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (Stage V) is life-threatening with bilateral eye involvement, septic emboli, and high mortality. Hospitalization is warranted for any suspected orbital or intracranial complication.

**Q:** What is the antibiotic management for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (first-line and second-line)?

**A:** Mild-moderate: INCS; if no response in 72h, add antibiotics. Severe: INCS + antibiotics. First-line: amoxicillin x 10 days (TMP-SMX or macrolide if penicillin allergy). Second-line (no response to 1st line within 72h): fluoroquinolones or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.

INCS reduces mucosal inflammation and ostial obstruction, the primary pathogenesis. Antibiotics are added based on severity and response. The shift from amoxicillin to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or fluoroquinolones addresses beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Adjuvant therapy (saline irrigation, analgesics, decongestants) provides symptomatic relief but does not treat the underlying infection.

**Q:** What is the management approach for chronic rhinosinusitis with and without nasal polyps?

**A:** With polyps: INCS, oral steroids + antibiotics (if signs of infection), refer to otolaryngologist/H&N surgeon. Without polyps: INCS, antibiotics (3-6 weeks: amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, fluoroquinolone, macrolide, clindamycin, or metronidazole), saline irrigation, oral steroids (severe). Surgery (ESS or balloon sinuplasty) if medical therapy fails or fungal sinusitis.

Chronic rhinosinusitis requires 2 major symptoms for >12 weeks plus objective inflammation on CT or endoscopy. Contributing factors must be identified and addressed (allergy, dental disease, anatomic factors, ciliary disorders, biofilms). Clarithromycin (macrolide) has anti-inflammatory as well as antibiotic properties. ESS (endoscopic sinus surgery) restores sinus drainage while preserving mucosa, targeting the osteomeatal complex. Complications include those of acute sinusitis plus mucocele.
